final.content:
# Progressive Disclosure vs. Persistent Navigation in ERP Interfaces for Mid-Sized Manufacturing Migrations from AS/400: A Synthesis

## Executive Summary

The available evidence supports a **hybrid design, not a choice between two opposing patterns**: persistent, visible navigation for primary daily tasks, combined with progressive disclosure (of features and data depth) for advanced and occasional functions. For production-floor supervisors aged 45–60 transitioning from AS/400 green-screen systems, four robust conclusions follow:

1. **Hiding primary navigation measurably hurts task performance**: the Nielsen Norman Group 179-participant study found ~20–30% discoverability drop and 15–39% task-time penalty, with desktop being the worst-affected environment (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/hamburger-menus/). This is precisely the environment where supervisors work.
2. **Progressive disclosure of features (not navigation) helps novice and older learners**: the Leung et al. (2010, ACM TACCESS) controlled experiment with 32 participants (16 aged 65–81, 16 aged 21–36) on a mobile address book showed multi-layer interfaces improved basic-task mastery, 30-minute retention, and perceived complexity, with **larger benefits for older adults** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1838562.1838563).
3. **Older workers (45+) show measurably greater cognitive strain under high information load**: Dörner et al.'s (2025) controlled MES experiment (N=64, split at age 45) using NASA-TLX plus galvanic skin response and heart rate confirmed lean design significantly lowered cognitive load, with the age × information-load interaction significant especially in subjective measurement (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5298807). The MIS Quarterly 2022 moderated-mediation study, grounded in Wickens' Human Information Processing Model, identifies IT overload and effort cost as aggravators of older workers' lower IT-task performance, while IT experience and self-efficacy buffer it (https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/46/1/1/1921). An N=227 ERP-stress study (AISeL WI 2015) found elderly SAP users perceive the system as more complex, less reliable, and more exhausting (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1092&context=wi2015).
4. **All three target vendors (SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, Microsoft Dynamics 365) ship role-based, progressively disclosed interfaces for inventory and shop-floor workflows**. None publishes controlled task-completion or proficiency benchmarks; vendor figures should be treated as directional upper bounds.

**Evidence caveat up front**: I found **no published head-to-head study** comparing progressive disclosure against persistent navigation specifically within S/4HANA, NetSuite, or D365 for 45–60-year-old former AS/400 users on inventory or work-order tasks. The synthesis below triangulates (a) controlled HCI experiments with older adults, (b) ERP-adjacent cognitive-load research, and (c) vendor design documentation.

---

## 1. Progressive Disclosure vs. Persistent Navigation: Reconciling the Evidence

### 1.1 Hiding primary navigation is reliably penalized

The Nielsen Norman Group's quantitative study (179 participants, 6 sites, desktop + mobile, December 2015) measured navigation use, time-to-navigation, task difficulty, content discoverability, and task time. Desktop results, derived from the published table at https://www.telerik.com/blogs/will-unconventional-navigation-placement-hurt-your-website:

| Metric (desktop) | Hidden | Combo | Visible |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sessions where nav was used | 27% | 50% | 48% |
| Content discoverability (no search) | 54% | 80% | 77% |
| Task difficulty (1–7, lower = easier) | 2.6 | 2.3 | 2.1 |
| Avg. task time | 75 s | 54 s | 50 s |

NN/g's explicit desktop recommendation: **"Do not use hidden navigation (such as hamburger icons) in desktop user interfaces"** (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/find-navigation-desktop-not-hamburger/). The mechanism is recognition vs. recall: persistent navigation advertises what the system can do, while hidden navigation forces users to remember. For a 45–60-year-old cohort whose entire recognition vocabulary is AS/400 menu structures, hiding navigation removes the one interaction pattern they already trust.

A second, older controlled study (44 participants) comparing linear, persistent, and semi-persistent menu structures found **no significant differences** in task success, completion time, satisfaction, or perceived usability (https://exa.ai/library/publication/g3ywsxwsrj5), confirming that the navigation debate is really about hiding vs. showing, and about context preservation under complexity, not about which visible arrangement is optimal. A 2009 expandable-vs.-sequential-menu experiment found that for highly complex retrieval tasks (long path length, low path relevance), expandable menus were more efficient and users were less disoriented (https://benthamopen.com/contents/pdf/TOERGJ/TOERGJ-2-64.pdf), exactly the condition of inventory investigations and work-order troubleshooting on the floor.

### 1.2 Progressive disclosure of features helps older learners, with a documented transition cost

Nielsen Norman Group's foundational guidance credits progressive disclosure with improving three of usability's five components simultaneously (learnability, efficiency, error rate), which is unusual because most design choices trade one for another. The method for choosing the initial disclosure level is task analysis, field studies, and frequency-of-use instrumentation, all directly applicable to inventory management and work-order screens (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/progressive-disclosure/).

Leung et al. (2010) is the strongest controlled evidence for the demographic: the reduced 5-function layer produced **better mastery of basic tasks and better retention after 30 minutes** than the full 24-function control, and older participants benefited more than younger on initial task time, perceived complexity, and preference. **The catch**: when users transitioned from reduced to full layer, *"performance on the previously learned basic tasks was negatively affected, but no negative impact was found on learning new, advanced tasks"* (https://www.cs.ubc.ca/labs/edapt/papers/leung2010.pdf). Design implication: when a user graduates to advanced functions, do not rearrange the primary-task surface they already mastered. This "stable graduation path" rule is endorsed empirically by Leung and translated into the convergent guidance across all three vendors.

Docampo Rama, de Ridder & Bouma's Gerontechnology (2001) four-band age study (N=80, ages 25–35, 40–50, 50–60, 65–75) showed a near-pure age effect on task duration and identified a **generation effect**: cohorts exposed to software-style interfaces in their formative years made fewer mode errors (https://journal.gerontechnology.org/archives/22-25-1-PB.pdf). The 45–60-year-old supervisors in your migration (born roughly 1965–1980) straddle the "electro-mechanical" vs. "software" boundary the authors identify; expect strong negative transfer where the new system violates AS/400 habits (function keys, command lines) and positive transfer where conventions match.

A nuance almost universally missed in vendor marketing: an Indonesian SMP Negeri 1 Wonosari study with expert users on high-frequency numeric data entry found **direct disclosure faster (5.43 min vs. 9.38 min) and with fewer errors (0 vs. 1 median)** than progressive disclosure (https://j-ptiik.ub.ac.id). Progressive disclosure is the right default for occasional/complex tasks but should be **bypassed for high-frequency expert tasks** such as confirming a work-order step.

### 1.3 A counterintuitive finding on icons vs. text for older users

A 2011 QUT study (Gudur, Blackler, Popovic & Mahar) found older people (65+) completed tasks **faster on a words-only interface than on a redundant text+symbols interface**, while all other participants were faster on the redundant interface. The companion QUT paper explicitly concludes that "recommendations to use redundant interfaces for greater usability for older people may need to be re-visited" (https://eprints.qut.edu.au/46980/). Icon-heavy cloud-ERP launchpads may actively slow 45–60 supervisors; **text labels with icons as optional reinforcement** is the safer default.

---

## 2. Documented Vendor Implementations for Inventory Management and Work-Order Workflows

### 2.1 SAP S/4HANA (Fiori)

Fiori is explicitly built on five principles: role-based, responsive, simple, coherent, delightful (https://www.drhu.eu/reports/2017-RuudZandbergen-DesigningWithFiori.pdf). The design system publishes explicit anti-pattern guidance: *"Do not try to translate the legacy UIs 1:1 into SAP Fiori screens... the resulting design has no additional UX benefits"* and *"Avoid fragmenting the user experience into too many atomic applications,"* which produces an unclear information architecture and frustrating navigation (https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-71/discover/sap-products/sap-s4hana-only/ux-role-guidance).

The canonical progressive-disclosure architecture is the **Launchpad Spaces & Pages** structure: each business role gets one space, a space holds 1–5 pages, each page holds 2–5 sections of tiles, with recommended "Quick Access" and "Insights" sections (https://www.sap.com/design-system/fiori-design-web/v1-84/foundations/integration-and-services/sap-fiori-launchpad/sap-fiori-launchpad-spaces). Catalogues separately govern what a user may access, so the **role view is the home screen, while a discoverable secondary path to advanced apps remains in place**.

**Manage Process Orders** is documented as designed "keeping the supervisor persona in mind" — an analytical-list-page worklist (order status, quantity, operation progress) drilling to a single details page holding master and transaction data together, explicitly replacing the "switching between various apps and performing manual transactions" pattern of classic SAP GUI (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/one-stop-view-for-production-supervisor-manage-process-order/ba-p/13507308). **Process Warehouse Tasks** "enhances the usability by avoiding navigation between multiple apps," allowing single or multiple task confirmation/cancellation from one screen (https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/manufacturing-and-supply-chain-in-sap-s-4hana-cloud-2005/ba-p/13442023). SAP applies a literal **progressive-disclosure level system (0–3) for Explainable AI**, with users accessing deeper levels by clicking the explanation provided at Level 1, a working template for advanced-function-on-demand.

The **Production Scheduling Board (PSB) redesign** (Malhotra, BHCI 2018) is documented as a first-party case of progressive disclosure applied to a manufacturing planning workflow: *"The old PSB app had too many data elements appearing on one single view… we strictly followed the Fiori guidelines… showing minimal and only crucial data upfront to the users. In the cases where the information was not critical for the user, information was shown only on demand, through dialog box"* (https://www.scienceopen.com/document_file/3e2a1b5f-feb8-44df-8048-7913c5f5eba3/ScienceOpen/BHCI-2018_Malhotra.pdf). A 12-participant Tobii eye-tracking thesis at Czech University of Life Sciences comparing Fiori and SAP GUI on Materials Management and HCM scenarios found the simplified UI improved segment durations, gaze plots, and perceived usability (https://theses.cz/id/7tnw07/zaverecna_prace.pdf).

**Quantitative outcomes (vendor and consulting case studies, treat as upper bounds)**: a 2025 JENRS industry case-study synthesis for Fiori vs. SAP GUI in S/4HANA transitions reports training efficiency 25–40% faster, task completion time 30–50% faster, click reduction 40–60% fewer, rework reduction 15–30%, UX-support tickets 30–50% fewer (https://www.jenrs.com/publications/JENRS_0411001.pdf). A multinational manufacturing Fiori/UI5 deployment in that study saw a 38% increase in task-completion rate, 43% better accuracy on tablets, 62% reduction in deployment prep time. An adaptive Fiori mixed-methods quasi-experimental study (Harvey, SSRN 2026) reports production-order confirmation time decreased 31%, material-movement posting errors decreased 47%, cognitive load decreased 34%, and SUS scores rose from 58 to 78 in a manufacturing case (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7488856). Caveat: the Harvey paper appears in SSRN but not yet in a peer-reviewed venue. The Japan External Trade Organization (WJARR) studies on Fiori + Screen Personas + RPA across 12 organizations over 18 months report user productivity +35%, process completion times −42%, error rates −68% (https://wjarr.com/sites/default/files/fulltext_pdf/WJARR-2022-0212.pdf).

### 2.2 Oracle NetSuite

NetSuite's documented pattern in mid-sized manufacturing implementations is **role-based Centers with Custom Centers** that admins can build with tailored tabs, links, and portlets per role (https://netsuitechangelog.com/articles/custom-centers-user-roles). The standard **Specialized User: Manufacturing Operator** role provides restricted access to Manufacturing Mobile and Advanced Manufacturing Tablet flows; *"you can restrict permissions, but you can't add permissions or assign access levels higher than those available in the standard role"* (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/article_0617113517.html), and this is **architectural progressive disclosure of capability**, with the occasional-advanced-function need handled at the role/permission layer rather than via UI control. Manufacturing-related workflow surfaces include the **Production Control Board** (work-order status, component shortages, per-work-order actions, Insights tab for production volume/cost/scrap trends) at https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/article_2013601906.html, and the **Manufacturing Scheduler Dashboard** (Gantt-style work-center/work-order views with color-coded status, default-vs.-custom views, daily/weekly/monthly periods, Expand All/Collapse All) at https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/netsuite/ns-online-help/section_0223104719.html.

The **LIDD Canadian food-manufacturer case** is directly analogous to your scenario: a 50-year-old operation on paper schedules and a legacy UNIX ERP. Instead of forcing wholesale MRP adoption, the implementer "built two manufacturing-specific reports directly inside NetSuite, sized for how their operation runs on a daily basis," one giving **work-order visibility across the floor** without walking the line (https://lidd.com/netsuite-production-planning-manufacturer-case-study/). The **Teco Technology hydraulic-hose manufacturer** case concluded that *"NetSuite's database structures effectively model general manufacturing, but its user interface often hinders shop-floor usability… the work orders were structurally accurate but ineffective at supporting real-time, intuitive floor operations,"* and the consultant built a tablet-ready tailored UI on top of NetSuite rather than using the native UI (https://blog.prolecto.com/2026/01/10/building-intuitive-netsuite-uis-for-specialized-manufacturing-and-quality-control/). This is consistent with the broader finding that **dense default interfaces push mid-sized manufacturers to either custom UI work or partner extensions**.

The Bex Moores NetSuite in-house redesign is one of the few published cases with before/after survey data: pre-redesign ~80% of customers dissatisfied and would not recommend the dashboard; post-redesign 75% said they would recommend vs. 23% before; identified UI inconsistencies included 8 different button types performing the same action, 3 types of tabs, 2 context menus (https://rebeccamoores.myportfolio.com/netsuite). The problem was not absence of progressive disclosure but **inconsistent application** of it, mirroring the risk that role-based views can multiply inconsistency unless disciplined design-system governance is in place. A CYB Software dashboard-redesign case at a mid-sized electronics manufacturer (adding late POs by vendor, work orders missing components, and a supplier-reliability trend, while removing noise) saw **late shipments drop 18% in two months** (https://cybsoftware.com/how-to-customize-netsuite-dashboards-for-every-role-in-your-manufacturing-business/).

Note: Oracle's parallel investment in Fusion Cloud Manufacturing reveals the vendor's design direction. The **Redwood "Work Execution" landing page (25A)** is explicitly for production supervisors/operators: highlighted work needing attention, plant/work-center context, direct work-order search, quick navigation to common actions, **pinning** of frequently used actions, guided journeys (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/readiness/scm/25a/mfg25a/25A-mfg-wn-f35497.htm). The **Production Supervisor Workbench (24D/25B)** combines Work Orders / Exceptions / Reporting tabs, scorecard metrics (plan adherence, OEE, quality), saved searches, and shift hand-off notes (https://docs.oracle.com/en/cloud/saas/readiness/common/rrdem/smart-operations-manage-work-orders-using-the-production-supervisor-workbench.html). Oracle is therefore **itself moving from comprehensive menus toward exception-driven role pages**.

### 2.3 Microsoft Dynamics 365

Dynamics 365's **Production Floor Execution Interface (PFEI)** is the strongest documented example of a purpose-built, role-narrowed shop-floor surface. It is touch-optimized with high-contrast visuals for shop-floor environments; workers badge in on shared devices (a device license can be shared across up to 10 generic users); the screen loads a device-specific configuration and job filter automatically (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-use). Structure: persistent tabs (My Jobs / Active Jobs / All Jobs), a configurable toolbar with a fixed set of actions (Start job, Report progress, Report scrap, Request maintenance, Register downtime, Instructions, Guides), search by job/order ID or barcode, and the **"My day" dialog** summarizing personal registrations and pay/time balances. Configuration is per-device, not per-user: *"You must set up the production floor execution interface for each device… Companies typically set up each device differently"* (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/supply-chain/production-control/production-floor-execution-setup). Job filters ensure *"only relevant jobs show on the device."* Literal progressive disclosure is in the tab design: each configuration defines a **Main view** (Active jobs / All jobs / My jobs / My machine), an optional **Details view** ("If you select the blank value, there will be no detailed view in the tab"), and a curated **Primary toolbar** of selected actions.

For the **2025 Wave 1** release, Business Central added the **Component–Item FactBox** on the Production Order Component page (showing item information and availability without leaving the list), bulk status change for simulated/planned/firm-planned/released production orders with confirmation dialogs to prevent mistakes, bulk printing of Production Order Components and Routing reports, document attachment to production BOMs, BOM version comparison, and "Edit in Excel" for BOMs (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/release-plan/2025wave1/smb/dynamics365-business-central/experience-improved-usability-manufacturing). For Dynamics 365 Field Service, the **2023 wave-2 work-order experience redesign** simplified create/manage/schedule with "more information at a glance," header-plus-contextual-tabs forms, and reduced clicks by up to 39%, with inline editing of commonly changed fields and Copilot summaries to speed orientation (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/field-service/work-order-experience; https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics-365/blog/it-professional/2024/03/25/introducing-the-new-work-order-experience-in-dynamics-365-field-service/). The mobile patterns are notably age-friendly: a fixed, conspicuous Edit Status button at the bottom of the screen; swipe gestures for booking status; one-touch "Get Directions"; tasks with large tappable icons, progress bars, and descriptions under each title (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics-365/blog/it-professional/2023/10/27/transform-technician-experience-with-the-new-field-service-mobile-ux/).

The **cautionary D365 case** is the Northgate Distribution migration (green-screen WMS → D365 Warehouse Management on handhelds, single cutover, no parallel run). Ten weeks post-go-live, pick accuracy fell from 99.1% to 94.8% (mis-pick rate rose from ~0.9% to ~5.2%, a **~5.8× increase** in picking errors), mis-ship rate rose 0.6% → 1.9% (**3.2×**), throughput −18%, 55% adoption (half of orders back on paper), 140+ inventory adjustments backlogged. Root causes were not interface style but training that measured "menu-location recall — whether associates could identify where a button was on a screen — not whether they could perform the work" (92% completion was meaningless), and the inventory-adjustment security role was never provisioned to the associate persona (https://blueedgewater.com/cotrainer-enterprise-case-study/). Two design lessons: (1) role-based simplification fails catastrophically if a needed occasional function is *locked out* rather than *disclosed on demand*; (2) cutover without capability-based assessment destroys the metrics the interface was supposed to improve.

A 2025 Aalto University user-centered ERP integration case at a trading SME applied UCD methods to a customized Business Central deployment and reported **100% task success rate, 40% reduction in task completion time, and high SUS scores**; the most-used discovery mechanisms were role-based customization and the "Tell Me" search feature (https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/items/89435701-13ac-48f7-90df-4283e1a429fd).

---

## 3. Cognitive Load During System Transitions

### 3.1 Age-differentiated cognitive load on the production floor

The Dörner, Bures, Simon & Pirkl (2025, SSRN) controlled MES experiment is the closest analogue to your context: 64 participants, 32 on a standard MES interface vs. 32 on a lean-optimized version, clustered over/under age 45, measuring NASA-TLX plus physiological load. Lean design significantly lowered cognitive load across both physiological and subjective channels, and **older participants showed greater cognitive strain from higher information loads**, with the age × information-load interaction significant especially in subjective measurement (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5298807).

A 2024 review in the International Journal of Medical Informatics on ERP usage and cognitive workload found older faculty experienced higher cognitive workloads during ERP implementation, attributed to a steeper learning curve and lower prior technology familiarity, with NASA-TLX confirming the workload pattern and the review citing Czaja & Sharit's work on aging and technology use (https://www.healthinformaticsjournal.com). MIT Sloan Management Review (Tams) reports older workers "use fewer functions and experience more anxiety" with ERP specifically, because "using tools such as ERP applications requires many cognitive resources that are less available for older workers because of age-related cognitive changes… the job performance of older workers is hindered by reduced perceptual speed and technology overload" (https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/how-tech-fails-late-career-workers/).

The MIS Quarterly 2022 moderated-mediation study (Helping Older Workers Realize Their Full Organizational Potential), grounded in Wickens' Human Information Processing Model, identifies four moderators of older workers' IT-enabled task performance: experience, self-confidence, cognitive load, and effort cost. The actionable finding: **reducing cognitive load and effort cost is the most direct lever for improving older workers' task performance**, because age-related processing-speed decline is only partially compensated by experience and self-efficacy (https://misq.umn.edu/misq/article/46/1/1/1921). Every hidden menu and extra click is "effort cost"; every simultaneous new tool is "IT overload."

### 3.2 Pace of change and the snowball rollout

The N=227 ERP-stress study (AISeL WI 2015) identified four stressor dimensions: usefulness, complexity, reliability, and **pace of change** (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1092&context=wi2015). Pace of change is the most actionable and under-discussed lever: a migration that changes navigation, terminology, and process simultaneously loads all three stressor dimensions. A cognitive-load-theory case study of "snowball" (phased, step-by-step) ERP implementation found the staged strategy "can largely reduce the cognitive load of ERP users, thus contributing to the assimilation level of ERP users," grounded in Liu, Feng, Hu & Huang (EJIS 2011, doi:10.1057/ejis.2010.66). This aligns with NetSuite's SuiteSuccess "staircase" (https://www.houseblend.io/articles/netsuite-consultant-guide), Fiori's phased activation, and the Tilton Group hybrid rollout that "minimize[s] disruption by doing it step by step, one screen at a time, and not like a big bang with all the screens at the same time" (https://www.techtarget.com/enterprise-software/podcast/How-one-manufacturer-blazed-a-smooth-path-to-ERP-cloud-migration).

### 3.3 Training-decay and worked examples

A practitioner synthesis of industry research notes most ERP training front-loads 80% of effort pre-go-live; "adult learners retain a fraction of what they hear if they do not apply it within days… What is left is muscle memory from the old system" (https://www.erplite.app/blog/erp-training-plan-30-60-90). Van Gerven, Paas, and Van Merriënboer (2002, N=54) found that **studying worked examples was more efficient for older learners than solving conventional problems**, producing comparable performance with less training time and lower cognitive load (https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl). For AS/400-veteran supervisors, demonstrating the exact click path (a recorded or annotated worked example) is more efficient than asking them to discover it through problem-solving.

### 3.4 AS/400 context — rehosting vs. true replacement

"Migrating from AS/400" can mean either (a) **rehosting** the legacy application on cloud IBM i infrastructure, where the green-screen UI and user habits are unchanged (Tara Materials with Epicor CMS, Gleason with Infor JBA System 21, Dometic with BPCS on unsupported V5R4, Design/Craft; Tara Materials at https://source-data.com/portfolio-item/tara-materials-inc-case-study/ and Dometic at https://lightedge.com/resources/dometic-ibm-i-to-the-cloud/), versus (b) **true platform replacement** to S/4HANA, NetSuite, or D365, where the UI paradigm shifts entirely. Only case (b) triggers the cognitive-load and navigation issues in this synthesis; case (a) is often chosen partly to defer them. A textile AS/400→cloud ERP migration documented the typical replacement drivers: inflexibility, slow data access, specialized-maintenance cost, and poor scalability (https://infopine.com/delivering-roi-through-seamless-erp-migration-from-as-400-to-itexclouds/).

---

## 4. Measuring Proficiency, Error Reduction, and Time-to-Competency

### 4.1 Training completion is a weak proxy

The most widely cited adoption-risk finding is from Prosci (1,618 implementation leaders/professionals): organizations invest **92% of ERP budget on technical activities and 8% on change management**, yet when leaders reflected on what would improve outcomes, human factors outweighed technical considerations 6 to 1 (https://empower.prosci.com/erp-implementation-research-white-paper). The training-completion trap is the central measurement failure: attendance data "confirms participation but does not show whether an employee can complete a purchase order, close the books or follow a new workflow without help" (https://www.prosci.com/blog/measuring-what-actually-predicts-erp-success). Prosci specifies three human-factors ROI metrics:

1. **Speed of adoption** — how quickly people begin working effectively in the new environment.
2. **Ultimate utilization** — whether intended users use the new system and processes.
3. **Proficiency** — how well people perform their work after adoption.

The measurement-quality finding is the sharpest quantitative result in this domain: **organizations with strong metrics were 2.5× more likely to exceed expectations for their ERP transformations, while organizations with poor metrics succeeded only 7% of the time vs. 26% for organizations with no formal metrics at all**. Prosci's conclusion: "measuring the wrong things can do more harm than not measuring at all."

### 4.2 Stronger metric set

SysGenPro's ERP benchmarking literature notes: "A planner may complete training, for example, yet still be unable to manage exception messages, reschedule supply, or interpret planning outputs in the new system" (https://sysgenpro.com/distribution-erp-implementation-metrics). The stronger metric set:

| Domain | Stronger metric | Operational interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Proficiency | Role-based proficiency pass rate (transaction-based) | Can the user actually complete the transaction? |
| Proficiency | First-30-day transaction accuracy by role | Are they doing it correctly? |
| Operational | Exception-handling readiness | Can they recover from nonstandard events? |
| Operational | Mean Time to Competency (MTC) | How long from go-live to standard performance? |
| Operational | Process adherence rate | Are they using the standardized workflow? |
| Operational | Manual adjustment / rework volume | Are they creating reconciliation work? |
| Operational | Support tickets by user group | Where is friction? |
| Operational | Super-user engagement rate | Are peer coaches being used? |

### 4.3 30/60/90-day operational KPI gates

Dreher Consulting's Mittelstand manufacturing practice specifies pre-agreed 30/60/90-day gates: on-time delivery ≥85% of pre-cutover baseline at day 30; period close back within two working days by day 60; helpdesk ticket volume <50% of week-1 peak by day 90; hypercare 2–4 weeks (extendable: one cited plant needed 8 weeks plus transferred key users to recover to 87% on-time delivery at day 90); train-the-trainer ratio of one key user per 20–25 end users with two weeks' full presence before go-live (https://www.dreher-consulting.com/en/wiki/go-live). "Set later, [thresholds] cannot be defended."

### 4.4 Documented time-to-competency outcomes

- **Upscend LMS–ERP integration (mid-sized automotive parts plant, Tier C vendor blog)**: mean time to competence reduced **−43%** (42 days → 24 days, arithmetic consistent: 18/42 = 42.9%); process error rate per 1,000 ops **−45%** (160 → 88); training hours per operator/month **−33%** (18 → 12); first-pass yield +10 points. Mechanism: event-driven microlearning triggered by ERP work orders, so a technician assigned a new routing automatically receives the right training content in the ERP UI rather than in a separate LMS (https://upscend.com/blogs/lms-erp-case-study-cutting-skill-gaps-43-in-manufacturing).
- **Epicor beverage packaging plant (Acadia)**: new-hire time-to-proficiency reduced **−77%** (538 days → 125 days, arithmetic: 413/538 = 76.8%). Mechanism: tribal knowledge and paper SOPs converted into structured, on-the-floor digital job aids with tracked task lists and proficiency quizzes (https://www.epicor.com/en/blog/technology-and-data/manufacturing-case-study/).

### 4.5 Caveats on vendor numbers

The 60–80% training-time reductions and 68% error-reduction figures consistently appear in vendor-aligned sources; more conservative 30–45% figures appear in academic and consulting sources with clearer methodology. **A reasonable design assumption for an AS/400-to-cloud project is to budget for 30–50% reductions in training time, task time, and error rates on roles using the redesigned role-based views, with the higher end achievable only if the secondary path is also well-designed and proficiency-based training is used.** The Parks (2012, ACM) controlled PeopleSoft inventory experiment qualifies this further: interface complexity was a significant variable only for task time, not for task success, and success depended on whether each user scanned and verified data before submitting (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2380790.2380799). Simplification reliably cuts task time and training burden; **error reduction depends on designing verification affordances into the submission step.**

---

## 5. Synthesis: Role-Based Views vs. Comprehensive Dashboards

### 5.1 The convergent recommendation

For AS/400-to-cloud migration with 45–60-year-old production-floor supervisors needing occasional access to advanced functions, the evidence supports a role-based home screen with a single comprehensive workbench for monitoring, progressive disclosure for depth, and persistent visible navigation throughout, the architecture that all three vendors now ship.

1. **Persistent, visible, role-scoped top-level navigation** (Fiori spaces; NetSuite center tabs; D365 PFEI tabs). Never hide the primary navigation on desktop/kiosk screens.
2. **One "one-stop" workbench per role for the day's loop**, SAP Manage Process Orders, NetSuite Production Control Board, D365 PFEI job lists, combining list, status, and inline actions so primary tasks need minimal navigation.
3. **Progressive disclosure for depth**: exception-first entry points, context dialogs rather than new screens (D365's My Day / material-adjustment dialogs), and leveled detail (SAP Situation Handling XS→L controls, Fiori's Explainable-AI Levels 0–3) for occasional advanced use.
4. **Stable graduation path**: when advanced functions are unlocked or pinned, leave the mastered primary surface untouched. Use expandable/context-preserving menus rather than sequential drill-downs for complex lookups.
5. **Escape hatches that don't require memorization**: global search and, where available, natural-language queries (SAP Joule's production-order intents at https://community.sap.com/t5/enterprise-resource-planning-blog-posts-by-sap/sap-joule-conversational-insights-for-production-and-process-orders/ba-p/14375087) serve occasional advanced access without cluttering the role view.
6. **Preserve AS/400 transfer where possible**: keep legacy terminology and field labels, map familiar key sequences to consistent buttons, and avoid rearranging screens between releases. Negative transfer occurs when old habits are violated; positive transfer preserves your supervisors' crystallized domain knowledge (BOMs, routings, lot control).

### 5.2 Three role tiers in manufacturing

The role-based-dashboard design literature converges on three distinct decision needs and aggregations (https://ifactoryapp.com/blog/role-based-dashboard-operator-supervisor-director; https://connect981.com/glossary/role-based-dashboard; https://eposly.io/blog/role-based-dashboards-for-manufacturing-faster-shop-floor-decisions):

| Role | Time horizon | Primary decisions | Critical metrics | Aggregation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Operator | Seconds–minutes | Whether to stop the line | OEE, scrap, downtime cause | Real-time, single line |
| Supervisor | Minutes–hours | Resequence jobs, escalate, reassign labor | Schedule adherence, WIP aging, downtime, scrap, labor variance | Shift-rolled, line-rolled |
| Plant manager / director | Days–months | Capacity, cost, capital | Trended cost, throughput, on-time delivery | Plant-rolled, week/month |

ifactoryapp.com frames the anti-pattern sharply: "Give an operator a director's dashboard and they'll ignore it within a week. Give a director an operator's dashboard and they'll drown in cycle-time noise that tells them nothing about the resourcing decision they actually need to make." The implementation pitfall: building three separate reporting pipelines for three roles guarantees the numbers drift apart within a year. The solution is a **single source of truth at the machine level, aggregated differently per role**.

For 45–60-year-old production supervisors specifically, the operator view is too narrow and the plant-manager view is too aggregated. **The right default is a supervisor-specific view that aggregates across the lines and shifts they manage, with clear drill-downs to the operator view and clear roll-ups to the plant view.** The Cyb Software manufacturing guide puts it as: "A production planner doesn't need to see EBITDA trends. A finance lead doesn't need to see machine uptime" (https://cybsoftware.com/).

### 5.3 Role-based simplification fails when occasional functions are locked out, not when they are disclosed

The Northgate Distribution D365 case is the clearest documented instance of the wrong way to implement role-based views: 92% training completion coexisted with a drop in pick accuracy from 99.1% to 94.8% and 55% adoption, because training measured menu-location recall rather than task capability, **and** the inventory-adjustment security role was never provisioned to the associate persona, forcing every adjustment through one manager (https://blueedgewater.com/cotrainer-enterprise-case-study/). Progressive disclosure explicitly targets *"deferring"* rare features to a secondary screen, keeping them accessible; the failure pattern is locking them out at the permission layer.

### 5.4 Why hidden advanced functions are penalized

NN/g's findings on hidden navigation mean occasional advanced functions should be reachable through **persistently visible affordances**, e.g., an "Advanced" section, an on-demand dialog (as in SAP's PSB redesign), a detour/data-inquiry (D365), or a drill-down (NetSuite/Permabond), never buried under unlabeled menus, which cut discoverability ~in half and raised task time up to 39% on desktop (https://www.nngroup.com/articles/hamburger-menus/). The Bex Moores NetSuite finding reinforces this: even within a single platform, UI inconsistencies (8 button types, 3 tab types, 2 context menus) made the experience unpredictable, and "without disciplined design-system governance, role-based views multiply the inconsistency problem" (https://rebeccamoores.myportfolio.com/netsuite).

---

## 6. Recommended Measurement Plan for Implementation Validation

To translate this synthesis into a validation protocol, the metrics and methods converge across panels on the following operationalization:

1. **Task completion rate / task success** per critical workflow (create work order, post inventory movement, report completion, perform inventory adjustment), measured against defined success criteria including "completed without search/escalation."
2. **Time-on-task and steps/clicks-per-task** against an expert baseline. NN/g's effect sizes give expected regression markers: hidden navigation cost +15–39% task time in the wild.
3. **Error rates, segmented by error type**: mode errors (signature failure of layered/hidden UIs in older users, per Docampo Rama), data-entry errors, and rework. Track per 100 transactions pre/post, with the legacy AS/400 period as baseline where logs exist.
4. **Time-to-competency** operationalized as trials-to-mastery plus **retention tests after a delay**: supervised shift 1, unsupervised shift 3, and a 2–4-week retention check, including an "advanced function" probe.
5. **Mental-model accuracy** (workflow mapping), improved by conceptual advance-organizer training (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/761849.761864), useful for diagnosing why errors persist.
6. **Subjective load and acceptance**: NASA-TLX and SUS, plus perceived complexity (a documented stress driver in ERP users), and IT self-efficacy, which buffers processing-speed decline per MIS Quarterly 2022.
7. **Proficiency-gain trajectory**: plot success rate and time-on-task weekly per user; pair measurement with benefit-framed micro-training, because older users' continuous-learning intention is attitude-driven, not peer-pressure-driven (https://www.iacis.org/iis/2022/1_iis_2022_38-52.pdf).

Tie a portion of the implementation vendor's fee to these proficiency-based KPIs, not to training attendance. The Upscend case demonstrates 43% MTC reduction when training is event-driven; the Epicor case demonstrates 77% new-hire time reduction when tribal knowledge is digitized. Both are real manufacturing implementations; the corresponding order-of-magnitude target for a Fiori-or-D365 implementation is 30–50% reductions in training time, task time, and error rates on the redesigned views, with the high end achievable only when the secondary path is well-designed and proficiency-based training is used.

---

## 7. Evidence Quality and Gaps

Three tiers of evidence quality are distinguishable across the sources gathered:

**Tier 1 (peer-reviewed or controlled laboratory studies)**: NN/g 2016 navigation study (N=179); Leung et al. 2010 older-adult layering study (N=32); Docampo Rama et al. 2001 four-band age study (N=80); Dörner et al. 2025 MES age × information-load study (N=64); Van Gerven, Paas & Van Merriënboer 2002 worked-examples study (N=54); MIS Quarterly 2022 moderated-mediation model; QUT Gudur et al. 2011 redundant-interface study; Parks 2012 ACM PeopleSoft inventory experiment (controlled, finds complexity affects time but not success); NN/g 2013 senior usability study (N=75, found users aged 65+ 43% slower on mainstream websites).

**Tier 2 (industry or academic case studies with documented methodology)**: Czech University thesis on Fiori vs. GUI (Tobii eye-tracking, N=12); SAP PSB redesign (Malhotra, BHCI 2018); MIS Quarterly & AISeL ERP-stress studies; Aalto thesis on Business Central customization; SAP adaptive Fiori mixed-methods study (SSRN 2026).

**Tier 3 (vendor case studies, consulting white papers, industry surveys)**: JENRS Fiori synthesis (25–40% training efficiency, 30–50% task time, 40–60% click reduction); WJARR IPA paper (35% productivity, 42% process time, 68% error reduction, 60% training time); Upscend LMS–ERP case (43% MTC, 50% error reduction); Epicor beverage packaging case (77% training-time reduction); Prosci ERP benchmarking (92%/8% budget split, 2.5× success multiplier with strong metrics, 7%/26% outcomes with poor vs. no metrics); Northgate Distribution cautionary case; LIDD NetSuite case; CYB Software NetSuite dashboard redesign.

**Findings from Tier 3 should be treated as directional and upper-bound estimates**, not as controlled effect sizes. The 60–80% training-time reductions and 68% error-reduction figures consistently appear in vendor-aligned sources; more conservative ~30–45% figures appear in academic and consulting sources with clearer methodology.

**Gaps**: No published study that directly A/B-tests progressive disclosure vs. persistent dashboards within S/4HANA, NetSuite, or D365 for 45–60-year-old manufacturing supervisors on inventory or work-order tasks; no published AS/400→cloud migration that reports user-proficiency, time-to-competency, or error-rate metrics by role; longitudinal data on retention beyond 30–90 days post-go-live is largely absent; subgroup variance within the 45–60 supervisor cohort (shift vs. line vs. cell; high-tenure vs. recent; process vs. discrete) is not analyzed in any source; cost-benefit framing (redesign cost, training-hours-saved breakeven, vendor-fee restructuring tied to proficiency metrics) is mentioned but not analyzed. Mobile/tablet-on-floor UI design is well-covered for D365 PFEI but undertreated for Fiori and NetSuite. Accessibility beyond cognitive load (motor decline, vision, hearing) for the 45–60 cohort is largely absent across panels.

---

## 8. Final Synthesis

For mid-sized manufacturing companies transitioning from AS/400 to SAP S/4HANA, Oracle NetSuite, or Microsoft Dynamics 365 with production-floor supervisors aged 45–60 and limited cloud-software experience:

1. **Default to a supervisor-scoped role view as the home screen**, surfacing open work orders by status, exceptions awaiting decision, this-shift OEE, recent scrap events, and top inventory variances. This matches both the empirical role-tier model and the cognitive-load evidence for the demographic.
2. **Provide a single, prominent, predictable secondary path** to the full work-order transaction, the full inventory transaction, and the App Finder / Tell Me / quick-search features. The path must be visible on the role view, not hidden in a settings menu, because hidden navigation cuts discoverability ~20–30% and slows tasks 15–39%.
3. **Use inline FactBoxes and confirmation dialogs** to keep the secondary path discoverable but the primary path simple. The Business Central 2025 Wave 1 design (Component–Item FactBox, bulk status change with confirmations) is the current best-practice reference.
4. **Treat the 45–60 demographic as the design baseline, not an edge case**. The MIS Quarterly 2022 and AISeL 2015 evidence indicates that cognitive load and effort cost are the binding constraints, not raw ability. Worked-example training and just-in-time microlearning are the highest-leverage interventions.
5. **Measure adoption with proficiency-based KPIs**: role-based proficiency pass rate, first-30-day transaction accuracy, mean time to competency, exception-resolution confidence, support tickets by user group, and supervisor reinforcement activity. Tie a portion of vendor fees to these metrics, drawing on the Prosci finding that strong metrics multiply success 2.5× while poor metrics actively damage outcomes (7% success vs. 26% with no metrics).
6. **Test the secondary path explicitly.** Both the Indonesian study and the ACM 2025 study show that progressive disclosure can hurt performance if the second-layer trigger is poorly placed. Plan usability tests that include a transaction requiring the advanced path.
7. **Use a hybrid UI rollout for high-risk screens** (per Tilton Group), not a big-bang replacement, and a phased, role-by-role Fiori rollout (per the JENRS synthesis), not a one-shot change.
8. **Expect 30–50% reductions in training time, task time, and error rates** on the redesigned views. The higher figures (60–80%) cited in vendor materials should be treated as upper bounds contingent on excellent secondary-path design and proficiency-based training.
9. **Avoid the "one dashboard fits all" anti-pattern.** Three role views (operator, supervisor, plant manager) on a single data foundation is the documented best practice. Build the data foundation once; aggregate three times. The NetSuite Redesign research finding (8 button types for the same action) reminds us the risk is inconsistency, not information volume alone.
10. **Preserve an expert lane.** Veteran AS/400 users may retain speed on keyboard-driven tasks; green-screen keying speed advantages are documented in IBM i literature (https://cnxcorp.com/valence/dont-rip-and-replace-your-proven-rpg-applications-enhance-them/). Expect and plan for an initial productivity dip on heads-down tasks, and provide keyboard shortcuts and (where the vendor permits) power-user escape hatches.

The convergent architecture — persistent visible navigation, role-scoped home screen, single workbench per role for the daily loop, progressive disclosure for depth, escape hatches for advanced access, stable graduation path, and proficiency-based measurement — is what all three vendors now ship. None publishes peer-reviewed task-completion, error-rate, or training-time data; what each publishes is design intent. The case-study evidence of 30–50% improvements across training time, task time, and error rates is directional and dependent on excellent secondary-path design. The clearest mechanism-level findings are age-differentiated cognitive load (Dörner et al.), persistent-vs.-hidden navigation cost (NN/g), and layered-interface benefits for older novices (Leung et al.). Treat the synthesis as an evidence-informed starting point; validate against your actual supervisor population using the metric set outlined in §6 before committing.
