# The Anthropology of Gift Economies: A Literature Review

## I. Introduction and Central Argument

The anthropological study of gift exchange rests on a small canon of foundational texts—Bronisław Malinowski's *Argonauts of the Western Pacific* (1922), Marcel Mauss's *Essai sur le don* (1925), and Marshall Sahlins's *Stone Age Economics* (1972)—subsequently codified by C. A. Gregory's *Gifts and Commodities* (1982) into a durable analytic opposition. A sustained feminist intervention (Annette Weiner, Marilyn Strathern, Gayle Rubin, Lisette Josephides, Genevieve Vaughan) revealed that the canon rested on unexamined gendered labor. Today, practitioners routinely describe open-source software, social-media platforms, and cryptocurrency networks in the vocabulary of the gift. The literature reviewed here indicates that digital practices *empirically confirm* many classical mechanisms (obligation, reputation, rank, inalienability) while simultaneously *collapsing* the clean gift/commodity dichotomy—precisely as the feminist critics predicted.

---

## II. The Classical Foundations

### A. Malinowski and the Kula Ring (1922)

*Argonauts of the Western Pacific* established the kula as the paradigmatic case of non-market exchange. The system spans **18 island communities** of the Massim archipelago, involving thousands of individuals, and consists of two classes of valuables moving in opposite directions around a closed circuit: red shell-disc necklaces (*soulava*) traveling clockwise, and white shell armbands (*mwali*) traveling counterclockwise (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kula_ring; https://anth1001.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/08/malinowski_excerpts.pdf). Crucially, **"no man ever keeps any of the articles for any length of time in his possession"**; each holder receives, holds briefly, and passes on to permanent partners (*karayta'u*) in dyadic relationships. Exchange cycles (*keda*) run between two and five years, while partnerships are lifelong (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/social-sciences-and-humanities/kula-ring/).

Malinowski posed the founding puzzle: "Why would men risk life and limb to travel across huge expanses of dangerous ocean to give away what appear to be worthless trinkets?" His answer, that the system was "clearly linked to political authority," established that the valuables were neither consumable nor media of exchange outside the ceremonial system but were held "to acquire prestige and rank" (https://www.britannica.com/topic/kula-trade). He carefully distinguished the kula from *gimwali*, ordinary utilitarian barter (https://hraf.yale.edu/teach-ehraf/reciprocity-exchange-the-kula-ring/index.html), and thereby inaugurated both participant observation as method and the analytic separation of prestige exchange from market transaction.

Subsequent ethnography extended kula analysis. Nancy Munn's *The Fame of Gawa* (1986) theorized value production through "transformative actions" that extend persons across inter-island spacetime; fame is the yield of giving, anticipating with uncanny precision the reputation economies of the internet (https://dukeupress.edu/the-fame-of-gawa). The kula's scholarly footprint is measurable: Macintyre's (1983a) bibliography lists **625 publications** on the phenomenon, and the kula has been described as "a paradigmatic example of the difference between 'economic exchange' and 'social exchange'" (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S037887330700072X).

A historicizing critique now complicates Malinowski's synchronic account. Steinmüller argues that "the Kula he observed was the historical result of colonial pacification": once colonial authorities banned warfare, "valuables previously used for ransom and peace-making were instead directed into it," while steel tools raised garden production (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/120022/1/Steinmuller_archaeology_of_the_kula_and_malinowski_accepted.pdf). The canonical "gift economy" was thus already entangled with money, colonialism, and commodity relations—a point that recurs forcefully in the digital debates.

### B. Mauss and the *Hau* (1925)

Marcel Mauss's *Essai sur le don* was published in *L'Année Sociologique* in 1925—the first issue after World War I, in which **twelve of Mauss's colleagues died, including his uncle Émile Durkheim** (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gift_(essay)). Mauss asked: "What is the principle of right and interest which, in societies of primitive or archaic type, requires that the gift received must be repaid? What force is there in the thing given which compels the recipient to make a return?" (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf).

His famous answer decomposed the gift cycle into three obligations: **to give, to receive, and to reciprocate** (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Gift_(essay)). The essay's "master concept" is the Māori *hau*, "the spirit of the gift," drawn from the informant Tamati Ranaipiri (via Elsdon Best): "Suppose you have some particular object, *taonga*, and you give it to me... Now this *taonga* I received from him is the spirit (*hau*) of the *taonga* I received from you and which I passed on to him... I must give them to you since they are the *hau* of the *taonga* which you gave me. If I were to keep this second *taonga* for myself I might become ill or even die" (https://web.mit.edu/allanmc/www/mauss1.pdf). On Mauss's reading, "to present something to someone is to present something of oneself"—the thing given has a soul and seeks to return to its origin.

Mauss extended the framework to the potlatch of the American Northwest (Tlingit, Haida, Kwakiutl), where "honor and credit" replace mere utility, and to total prestation between collectivities: "ceremonies, feasts, rites, military services, women, children, dances, celebrations, fairs" (https://web.stanford.edu/class/ihum54/odyssey/mauss_gift.htm). He located gift exchange as a "total social fact" spanning religion, law, economy, and morality, and ended with a political-moral conclusion: that the essay was, from birth, "a mixed-economy manifesto"—a model of how modern societies might rebuild solidarity after the war (https://haubooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Marcel-Mauss-The-Gift-Expanded-Edition-Selected-Annotated-and-Translated-by-Jane-Guyer.pdf).

The essay's reception is enormous: it became "not only a founding text of economic anthropology" but a touchstone for Lévi-Strauss, Bataille, Baudrillard, Bourdieu, and Derrida, and the starting point for Mary Douglas, Godelier, Gregory, Sahlins, and Strathern (https://histanthro.org/reviews/peripeteia-of-the-gift/). Critical receptions include Mary Douglas's "No Free Gift" declaration; Jacques Derrida's counter-claim that a gift recognized or reciprocated is annulled as gift—the gift is "impossible" (https://histanthro.org/reviews/peripeteia-of-the-gift/); James Laidlaw's ethnography of Jains showing unreciprocated giving exists precisely where social relationship is refused (https://anthrosource.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/anhu.12014); and Bourdieu's reading of the gift as structured misrecognition—"The objective truth of the gift is exchange; its subjective truth is disinterestedness" (https://shs.cairn.info/article/E_RDM_052_0074/pdf?lang=en).

### C. Sahlins and the Sociology of Primitive Exchange (1972)

Marshall Sahlins's *Stone Age Economics* both canonized and corrected Mauss. In "The Spirit of the Gift," Sahlins argued that Mauss's *hau* was a "mystic cement" that addressed only why gifts are repaid, not the obligations to give or to receive, and that fragmented exchange into discrete acts rather than grasping it as "a unified and integral principle" (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf). Sahlins's secularist re-reading proposes that *hau* "really means something on the order of 'return on' or 'product of'"—the *yield* of a good—and that the ethical principle is "one man's gift should not be another man's capital... the fruits of a gift ought to be passed back to the original holder" (https://faculty.fairfield.edu/dcrawford/sahlins_2012.pdf).

The enduring contribution is "On the Sociology of Primitive Exchange," which classifies reciprocity along a continuum indexed by social distance:

| Type | Social location | Return expectation |
|---|---|---|
| **Generalized reciprocity** | Close kin / fictive kin | Altruistic, indefinite, uncalculated |
| **Balanced reciprocity** | Intermediate distance | Equivalent return within a specified time |
| **Negative reciprocity** | Strangers / enemies | Attempt to take without reciprocating |

(Typology from https://hraf.yale.edu/teach-ehraf/reciprocity-exchange-the-kula-ring/index.html; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reciprocity_(cultural_anthropology))

David Graeber called this tripartite scheme "one of the most consequential theoretical devices in modern social theory," adopted across archaeology, history, psychology, philosophy, and beyond—though lamenting that "the only discipline that has never made significant use of the theoretical tools provided in this collection is economics itself" (https://davidgraeber.org/articles/foreword-to-the-routledge-classics-edition-stone-age-economics-marshall-sahlins/). Sahlins also theorized how generosity underwrites political rank: "If friends make gifts, gifts make friends. Or more appropriate to the present context, 'gifts make slaves,' as the Eskimo say, 'just as whips make dogs'" (https://fieldnotesandfootnotes.wordpress.com/2011/12/29/marshall-sahlins-exchange-and-sociability-thoughts-on-yolngu-sociality/).

### D. Gregory and the Gift/Commodity Binary (1982)

Christopher Gregory's *Gifts and Commodities* crystallized the implicit opposition into a precise schema synthesizing Marx with Mauss (https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/G/bo20551269.html). Its canonical propositions:

- "Gift exchange establishes a relation between the transactors, while commodity exchange establishes a relation between the objects transacted."
- "Commodities are alienable objects transacted by aliens; gifts are inalienable objects transacted by nonaliens"—gift transactors in a state of *reciprocal dependence*; commodity transactors in *reciprocal independence*.
- In gift economies, "things and persons... assume the social form of persons," the mirror image of Marx's commodity fetishism.
- Gifts have "exchange-order rather than exchange-value… ordinal rather than cardinal"—on Rossel Island, over twenty different ranks of shell-gifts are distinguished (http://haubooks.org/viewbook/gifts-and-commodities/10_ch03).

**Quantitative illustration (Gregory's Table 3.1, Enona clan, Irian Jaya, 1955):** the clan gave 2,638 shell-gifts of a certain rank on interclan account and received 759 in return—a net credit of **1,879 (a giving-to-receiving ratio of ≈ 3.48:1)**. A single big-man's household accounted for a net credit of 1,210, i.e., **≈ 64.4% of the entire clan's net credit**—a striking demonstration that prestige accrues to those who *give away the most* (http://haubooks.org/viewbook/gifts-and-commodities/10_ch03).

Gregory's crucial empirical point was that in colonial Papua New Guinea, gift and commodity economies expanded simultaneously—contrary to neoclassical assumptions that gifts would simply give way to markets (https://researchportal.helsinki.fi/en/publications/reprises-chris-gregorys-gifts-and-commodities-and-the-frontier/). His definition, that gift exchange is "an exchange of inalienable things between transactors who are in a state of reciprocal dependence," has become the standard benchmark, critically employed by Strathern and Weiner (https://www.soas.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2022-10/economics-wp127.pdf). Lewis Hyde's *The Gift* (1983) popularized the same binary for the arts (https://lewishyde.com/the-gift/).

---

## III. Feminist Critiques

### A. Gayle Rubin and the Traffic in Women (1975)

Gayle Rubin's *The Traffic in Women* (1975) turned Lévi-Strauss's gift theory against itself, arguing that the **incest taboo** functions as "a rule obliging the mother, sister, or daughter to be given to others. It is the supreme rule of the gift" (https://glc.yale.edu/sites/default/files/pdf/rubin_the_traffic_in_women.pdf). Marriage, on this account, is "a most basic form of gift exchange, in which it is women who are the most precious of gifts." Rubin's intervention showed that the classic theory of reciprocity **presupposes women as objects of exchange rather than as subjects**, founding gender studies as a field (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Traffic_in_Women:_Notes_on_the_Political_Economy_of_Sex).

### B. Annette Weiner: Women's Wealth and Keeping-While-Giving

Annette Weiner's *Women of Value, Men of Renown* (1976) restudied the very site of Malinowski's fieldwork and found the canonical account structurally gender-blind: "While Malinowski and others have focused on men, dismissing 'women's work' as unimportant, Weiner shows that women play a vital role in Trobriand society" (https://books.google.com/books/about/Women_of_Value_Men_of_Renown.html?id=AdXtAAAAMAAJ). On her first day of fieldwork, she observed a mortuary ceremony in which women distributed **up to 30,000 bundles in one day, each worth about one Australian cent**—a vast wealth of "ephemeral plant-fiber fluff" that Malinowski's writings had ignored (https://www.academia.edu/35663879/Women_of_Value_Men_of_Renown). These women's wealth—banana-leaf bundles and skirts (*doba*)—circulated in *sagali* mortuary distributions and embodied "womanness": sexuality, reproduction, and nurture (https://press-files.anu.edu.au/downloads/press/n2571/pdf/epilogue.pdf).

Weiner's *Inalienable Possessions* (1992) generalized the critique into a theory of "keeping-while-giving": "Reciprocity is only the superficial aspect of exchange, which overlays much more politically powerful strategies of 'keeping-while-giving'" (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/inalienable-possessions/paper). Inalienable possessions—objects, land, ancestral myths, sacred knowledge that must return to the giver—"have the power to create lasting social divisions." The theory "places women at the heart of the political process," because women possess a wealth of their own that gives them power.

The framework was contested. A *Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute* critique argued that "Weiner's ethnographic illustrations do not lend support to her theory of inalienable possessions... and that the paradox of keeping-while-giving is more appropriately seen as deriving from Western presuppositions of individual boundedness, subjectivity, possession, ownership, and hierarchy" (https://researchportalplus.anu.edu.au/en/publications/inalienable-ethnography-keeping-while-giving-and-the-trobriand-ca/).

### C. Marilyn Strathern and the Dividual Person

Marilyn Strathern's *The Gender of the Gift* (1988) radicalized the critique by attacking the analytical categories themselves. Drawing on Gregory's gift/commodity distinction for Melanesian material, she argued that "gender relations have been a particular casualty of unexamined assumptions held by Western anthropologists and feminist scholars alike" (https://www.ucpress.edu/books/the-gender-of-the-gift/pdf). Her famous conclusion is the *dividual* or *partible person*: Melanesian persons are not bounded individuals but composites of the gendered relations and gifts that produced them; a gift is a detached part of a person, so all exchange is gendered at its root (https://ebrary.net/286501/sociology/strathern_s_gender_gift_distributed_personhood_strathernograms). The book simultaneously mounts "one of the most sustained critiques of cross-cultural comparison"—the "Western"/"Melanesian" contrast itself being a Western construction.

David Lipset challenged the empirical adequacy of the concept, arguing that Strathern mistook "a virulently anti-female ideology... for benign accommodation between the sexes," and that the dividual "paradoxically affirms Lévi-Strauss' classic demonstration... that 'the gender of the gift' is invariably female" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/dbsjqhp8dpm).

### D. Josephides, Irigaray, and Vaughan

**Lisette Josephides** (*The Production of Inequality: Gender and Exchange Among the Kewa*, 1985) named appropriation directly in a Marxist/Bourdieusian register: among the Kewa, "male dominance of the exchange system, control of land, female labour and resources, patriliny, and patrilocal residence" render women "peripheral sojourners," and big-men mobilize female production as male prestige (https://cas-sca.journals.uvic.ca/index.php/anthropologica/article/download/1751/1523/2741).

**Luce Irigaray** ("Women on the Market," 1977) reads Lévi-Strauss's exogamous exchange of women through Marx: "our entire society is predicated" on men circulating women among themselves as commodities, with women divided into use value and exchange value (https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9780203760369-13/women-market-luce-irigaray).

**Genevieve Vaughan** (*For-Giving: A Feminist Criticism of Exchange*, 1997) inverts the valuation: the gift paradigm "derives from mothering and is therefore woman-based," is need-oriented rather than profit-oriented, and is systematically rendered invisible. Her "unilateral gift"—the one-way nurture of infants who cannot reciprocate—is analytically prior to exchange and exposes the Maussian model as built on the invisible exception of non-reciprocal care (http://gift-economy.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/forgiving_english_rev2016.pdf).

The feminist corpus converges on three findings: (1) the canon fetishized circulation and ignored production—disproportionately women's work; (2) the "gift" was never gender-neutral; (3) visibility itself is a theoretical bias.

---

## IV. Contemporary Digital Practices

### A. Open-Source Software as Gift Culture

Eric Raymond's *Homesteading the Noosphere* (1998) explicitly imported anthropological gift theory: hacker culture is "a 'gift culture' in which participants compete for prestige by giving time, energy, and creativity away" (https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/view/1474). Raymond mapped the analogy precisely:

- **Abundance, not scarcity**: "Gift cultures are adaptations not to scarcity but to abundance... In gift cultures, social status is determined not by what you control but by what you give away. Thus the Kwakiutl chieftain's potlatch party... And thus the hacker's long hours of effort to produce high-quality open-source code" (https://www.free-soft.org/literature/papers/esr/homesteading/homesteading-6.html).
- **Reputation as the secularized *hau***: "peer repute in the gift culture of hackers" is the yield, enforceable by the three taboos—illegitimate forking, rogue patches, and "surreptitiously filing someone's name off a project," which "steals the victim's gift to be presented as the thief's own" (http://catb.org/~esr/writings/cathedral-bazaar/homesteading/ar01s09.html).

David Zeitlyn's "Gift Economies in the Development of Open Source Software" (2003) cautioned against too literal a translation: while Raymond's metaphor captures the "axiom of kinship amity" within developer subgroups paralleling lineages, Bourdieu's symbolic-capital framework is needed to track reputation flows (https://sci-hub.st/storage/2024/1746/0d168596d46d06ac105718d7fac3fe2d/zeitlyn2003.pdf). Christopher Kelty's *Two Bits* (2008) introduced the "recursive public"—"a public that is vitally concerned with the material and practical maintenance and modification of the technical, legal, practical, and conceptual means of its own existence as a public" (https://twobits.net/pub/Kelty-TwoBits.pdf). Free software is given by a *reconfiguration of property* (copyleft) rather than by suspending it.

Richard Barbrook's "The Hi-Tech Gift Economy" (1998) added the crucial qualification: on the Net, "the same piece of information could exist both as a commodity and a gift" (https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/download/631/552?inline=1). The challenge from Greger Petersen and others is that FOSS lacks Mauss's three-party structure and obligatory reciprocation: code is "left at a publicly accessible place for anyone to take" rather than given to a particular person or group, so it may be better described as social sharing than as gift economy (https://fahrplan.events.ccc.de/congress/2006/Fahrplan/attachments/1171-GiftOfSharingGregersPetersen.pdf).

**The feminist audit of open source** applies with brutal quantitative force. Survey-based studies "up to 2003 reported 95–99% man dominance in FOSS; a 2013 survey observed a ratio of 10% women respondents," and in one widely used survey "only three percent of respondents identified as women" (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2011.08488). A widely cited comparison found **1.5% of F/LOSS participants were women versus 28% in proprietary technical roles**—women approximately **18.7 times less represented** in FLOSS (https://culturedigitally.org/2012/06/engendering-change-gender-advocacy-in-open-source/). A 2022 systematic review of 51 articles found "only about **5% of projects** were reported to have women as core developers," and "women authored **less than 5% of pull-requests**, but had similar or even higher rates of pull-request acceptances than men" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3510460). Dawn Nafus's "'Patches don't have gender'" argues that "'openness' is a complex construct" that "weaves together ideas about authorship, agency, and the circumstances under which knowledge and code can and cannot be exchanged" and that men monopolize code authorship while de-legitimizing the social ties necessary for women's inclusion (https://culturedigitally.org/2012/06/engendering-change-gender-advocacy-in-open-source/). This is a direct **reproduction of the canonical feminist finding**: as Weiner showed that Malinowski's kula-centric gaze rendered women's *doba* invisible, so the FLOSS "gift culture" renders relational, maintenance, and non-code labor invisible.

### B. Social Media and the Attention Economy

Drawing on Mauss rather than Malinowski, recent work has treated social media as a "digital gift economy" structured by the obligation to give, receive, and repay attention. A *Theory, Culture & Society* article argues that the Like button and Twitter Mention are recoded as gifts of mutual recognition, "the interference between gift exchange and market economy which is daily at work online" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0263276415619474).

The most important critical intervention is *A Maussian bargain: Accumulation by gift in the digital economy* (2020), which proposes the regime of "accumulation by gift": "The economic relation that develops as a result of a digital gift offering not only masks the structural asymmetry between giver and gifted but also permits the creation of the new commodity of personal data, obfuscates its true value, and naturalizes its private appropriation" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/2053951719897092). Oliver Nachtwey and Simon Schaupp's "The valorization of interactions" (2024) proposes a three-step process of data commodification: appropriation as use-value, secondary commodification, and cybernetization (https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1177/20539517241259639).

TikTok ethnography shows how virtual gifts operate in "dual manifestation": they "contribute to the construction of the influencers' self because they reflect the appreciation and attention received from users," while the platform "monitors and calculates the gifts obtained by influencers to remunerate them," transforming "the work of the influencer" into "monetization of the self... within an economic system centered on the attention of others" (https://revistasociologieromaneasca.ro/sr/article/view/1809). Work on KakaoTalk, LINE, and WeChat finds that platform design interacts with deeply rooted gifting traditions—WeChat's Hongbao enables "playful, communal monetary exchanges largely detached from traditional, obligation-driven gifting"—and proposes a "Channel-Oriented Gifting Cycle model" that "extends classical gift-exchange theory" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3757689). Across these cases, the digital gift is "a gift that creates a debt the recipient cannot repay"—closer to a Marxian extraction than to Maussian reciprocity.

### C. Cryptocurrency Governance

The blockchain case is the most theoretically generative because its designers cite the anthropological problem directly. Buterin, Weyl, and Ohlhaver's "Decentralized Society: Finding Web3's Soul" (May 2022) diagnoses that "Web3 today centers around expressing transferable, financialized assets, rather than encoding social relationships of trust" (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4105763). Their proposed primitive—non-transferable **"soulbound tokens" (SBTs)** representing "the commitments, credentials, and affiliations of 'Souls'"—is, in anthropological terms, a designed instrument of **inalienability**: tokens that "must not be given or, if they are circulated, must return finally to the giver" (cf. Weiner, https://www.ucpress.edu/books/inalienable-possessions/paper). The stated goal is to let Web3 "eschew today's hyper-financialization in favor of a more transformative, pluralist future."

A *Tribal Governance* paper makes the technical point: "before the blockchain, all copies were the same. With blockchain it has become possible to **differentiate something from something else (like who owns a bitcoin) without relying on non-digital authorities.** This property... is allowing to move **from openness and gift economy, well exemplified by FOSS, to a digitally native economy**, at the expense of the non-rivalry that used to characterize information goods" (https://scholarspace.manoa.hawaii.edu/bitstreams/4f9b5036-92e9-4920-839c-90264d63a8a3/download). Blockchain thus reintroduces **rivalry and alienability** into a domain previously characterized by abundance and non-rivalry—precisely re-creating the conditions the gift/commodity distinction presupposed.

Ellie Rennie, Jason Potts, and Joshua Tan's "The 'natural state' of blockchains: An ethnography of validator governance" frames validator governance as a transition "from a Limited Access Order to an Open Access Order," tracking how blockchain networks attempt to constrain elite power through impersonal rules (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4741076). Annaliese Milano Merfield's LSE ethnography argues that Bitcoin and Ethereum "are not simply protest movements—or worse, unbridled gamblers—but rather serious experiments in alternative forms of governance" (https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/135613/1/Merfield_201649740.pdf). The Duniter / Ğ1 libre currency case shows how a blockchain can be designed "specifically... for the needs of the Ğ1 ecosystem," operationalizing Ostrom's principles for commons governance and supporting a "universal dividend" (https://revuesim.org/index.php/sim/article/view/1131). "When Ostrom Meets Blockchain" identifies six blockchain affordances relevant to Ostromian commons: tokenization, formalization and decentralization of rules, autonomous automatization, decentralization of power over infrastructure, transparency, and codification of trust (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3272329).

Cryptocurrency "airdrops" distribute digital tokens "to users at zero cost," and "billions of dollars of tokens have been airdropped for reasons such as marketing and decentralisation" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00191-024-00874-6). Airdrops are "most effective at facilitating decentralisation" and create "a claim on future governance and value" rather than a purely relational bond—a hybrid form closer to equity than to the Maussian gift.

---

## V. Synthesis: Challenge or Reinforcement?

The three contemporary sites do not align with classical models in the same way:

| Dimension | Open-source software | Social media attention | Crypto governance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Maussian obligation to reciprocate** | Reinforced: fork/patch norms, reputational credit (Raymond) | Simulated at user level; captured at platform level | Absent by design in token systems; re-engineered via SBTs |
| **Sahlins's social-distance spectrum** | Reinforced: core maintainers (generalized) vs. drive-by contributors (balanced) | Blurred: intimacy simulated at scale | Challenged: pseudonymity collapses social distance; SBTs attempt to restore it |
| **Gregory's gift/commodity binary** | Challenged: same code is gift and commodity (Barbrook) | Challenged: same content is gift and commodity | Challenged, then partially restored by inalienable tokens |
| **Weiner's keeping-while-giving** | Reinforced: reputation and namespace control kept while code is given | Partially reinforced: identity/followers kept, content given | Explicitly reinforced: SBTs are designed inalienables |
| **Feminist critique of invisible labor** | Reinforced: 1.5% women, ~18.7× underrepresentation | Reinforced: affective labor monetized by platforms | Unaddressed: governance design ignores reproductive labor |

**Gregory's 1982 gift/commodity binary is the principal casualty.** None of the digital phenomena sit cleanly on either side: open-source code is given but legally constrained; the Like is gift and surveillance instrument simultaneously; tokens are simultaneously commodity and political voice. Yet the digital cases also *reinforce* the classical models' deepest claim—that exchange constitutes persons and obligations, not just allocations. Barbrook's observation that the same digital object can be gift and commodity simultaneously (https://firstmonday.org/ojs/index.php/fm/article/download/631/552?inline=1) validates Gregory's historical point that gifts and commodities transform into one another (https://haubooks.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Chris-Gregory-Gifts-and-Commodities-Foreword-by-Marilyn-Strathern-New-Preface-by-the-Author.pdf) while undermining any static dichotomy.

Three unresolved tensions persist:

1. **Whether gift and commodity are analytical types or historical residues.** Gregory, Bourdieu, and much digital scholarship have pushed toward a typology, while Mauss's later interpreters hold that the gift names a primary social phenomenon irreducible to interest-maximizing exchange.
2. **Whether feminist anthropology has adequately resolved gendered labor.** Weiner foregrounded women as producers of inalienable wealth; Strathern relocated gender to the texture of personhood itself; Lipset argues that the dividual conceals rather than describes indigenous male ideologies of female containment.
3. **Whether digital "gifts" reproduce or invert classical logics.** The "accumulation by gift" literature suggests inversion through structural asymmetry; the crypto-commons scholars suggest continuity through modified logics; Derrida-influenced work suggests the gift was always constitutively impossible and digital conditions simply expose this.

---

## VI. Conclusion

Roughly a century on from Malinowski's *Argonauts*, the kula remains the discipline's most cited single ethnographic case, but its analytical uses have multiplied. Mauss's *hau* provoked Sahlins's secularist counter-reading; Lévi-Strauss universalized reciprocity; Gregory formalized it as a binary; Weiner challenged its gendered silences; Strathern challenged its ontological premises; Rubin, Josephides, Irigaray, and Vaughan extended the critique into political philosophy. The contemporary digital applications—open source, attention economies, cryptocurrency—are not merely new ethnographic sites for old theory. They are simultaneously phenomena that require extensions (recursive publics, engineered inalienability, Ostrom-style commons governance) and phenomena that re-expose the unresolved tensions at the heart of a literature that began with an attempt to explain "worthless trinkets" that Trobriand Islanders nonetheless risked their lives to give.

The feminist critique remains the least absorbed lesson in digital design. As Weiner showed that the celebrated male circuit of Kula rested on women's banana-leaf wealth and mortuary labor, as Josephides showed prestige exchange appropriating female production, and as Vaughan identified unilateral care as the invisible gift substrate of all economies, so the open-source "gift culture" (1.5% women), the attention economy (affective labor extracted by platforms), and cryptocurrency governance (silent on reproductive work) reproduce the same structure: the visible gift economy is subsidized by invisible, gendered, or devalued labor. The task the feminist critics set, of making the invisible labor of the gift visible, remains open in the digital economies that now depend on it.

# Cold-Weather Fleet Selection for Mongolian Mining at −40°C: Caterpillar vs. Komatsu vs. Volvo CE, with Russian/CIS Alternatives

## Executive Summary

For sustained −40°C mining operation in Mongolia, the evidence supports a **two-vendor shortlist between Caterpillar (Barloworld Mongolia) and Komatsu (Transwest Mongolia)** as the only Western OEMs with (a) factory cold-weather packages validated at or below −40°C, (b) staffed Ulaanbaatar service and component-rebuild bases, (c) in-country parts warehousing, and (d) Mongolian-language training pipelines. **Volvo CE cannot be recommended as a primary mining fleet** because no verified dedicated CE dealer for mining-class equipment has been confirmed in-country; only Volvo Trucks Mongolia (on-highway) and aftermarket Indian/Chinese parts traders are confirmed. **BelAZ (Belarus) and UZTM-Kartex (Russia) are legitimate regional alternatives**: BelAZ has 200+ units operating in Mongolia via United BelAZ Machinery (UBM) since 2012, with a 2,289 m² Ulaanbaatar service center, and UZTM-Kartex electric rope shovels have run at Erdenet since 1978; both carry sanctions-adjacent supply-chain risk for internationally financed projects.

**Critical context**: Mongolia imports ~95% of its diesel from Russia, and Mongolian market diesel carries sulfur content 22–23× higher than Euro 4 (https://exa.ai/library/publication/kkxrvmjz29q). This means **specify Tier 2-equivalent engines** (no DEF/DPF aftertreatment), because DEF freezes at −40°C (Komatsu thaw takes ~70 minutes) and Tier 4 aftertreatment will fail on Mongolian fuel (https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20230718-37cae-7058a; https://www.komatsu.com/content/dam/komatsu/sales-and-marketing-documents/brochures/excavators/pc7000/ultra_excavator_pc7000-11_brochure-en.pdf; https://www.constructionequipment.com/earthmoving/rigid-frame-trucks-off-highway/product/10752402/komatsu-komatsu-930e-5-haul-truck).

---

## 1. Cold-Weather Operation at −40°C

### 1.1 Caterpillar

Caterpillar publishes a dedicated system-level cold-weather manual (SEBU5898-19, March 2019) covering starting procedures, fluid selection, batteries, and tire inflation (https://catpublications.com/previews/SEBU5898.pdf). Standard cold-start capability for large hydraulic mining equipment is −18°C, with cold-start block-heater options extending the 395 excavator to **−32°C (−25°F)** (https://www.cat.com/en_US/products/new/equipment/excavators/large-excavators/126440.html; https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20210601-35dac-75766). The 6020B hydraulic mining shovel was validated for modular field assembly at −30°C in 14 days (https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20160201-48357-52819). The 824 Wheel Dozer supports antifreeze rated to **−50°C (−58°F)**, the deepest OEM-published cold-fluid rating found in this research (https://www.fabickcat.com/new-equipment/824-wheel-dooser/).

Specific truck provisions: Cat 793/797F carry coolant protection to **−50°C**, fuel filter with water separator and heater, engine coolant/oil heaters, 240V shore power, heated mirrors, Mesabi flexible-core radiator, 36,510 BTU/hr (10.7 kW) cab heater rated to −30°C ambient, and an engine delay shutdown timer to prevent turbo coking (https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20221205-dfa81-b707a?%24Type1%24=; https://www.kellytractor.com/eng/images/pdf/earthmoving/offhighway_trucks/797F.pdf). The 789D specalog lists coolant heater, fuel filter with water separator and heater, ether starting aid, pre-lube, variable-speed fan, and antifreeze protection to −35°C standard / −50°C optional (https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20230718-37cae-7058a). Cat 6040/6050 mining shovels offer formal Cold Weather Packages: engine coolant heater, engine oil heater with thermostat, hydraulic oil heater with thermostat, fuel blender, auxiliary cab pre-heating, requiring ~50 kW external power at 400V three-phase (https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20260211-22a73-3be06; https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20210601-35dac-75766). The 6020B's engine avoids DEF/urea secondary fluid entirely, eliminating DEF-freezing failure mode (https://s7d2.scene7.com/is/content/Caterpillar/CM20160201-48357-52819).

### 1.2 Komatsu

Komatsu Mining Germany (KMG) explicitly rates its hydraulic shovels for ambient temperatures **down to −50°C** when equipped with preheating for diesel engine, water, hydraulic oil, and lubrication systems. Below −25°C, ordinary operation must halt and external electrical preheating engaged; hydraulic oil must reach −20°C (viscosity ~1,000 cSt) before the main drive engine can be started, with engine crankshaft speed held at half-rated until hydraulic oil viscosity drops to 100–10 cSt. Arctic-package components include cast/forged structural elements, bolted connections in special steel grades, special-insulation electric cables, and ICE-Champion flexible high-pressure hoses (https://onemine.org/documents/adaptation-of-hydraulic-shovels-for-arctic-temperature-of-yakutia-region). This is the only OEM in this comparison with a documented **−50°C structural rating for excavators**.

For haul trucks, the 930E-5/930E-5SE, 980E-5, 830E-5, and 860E-1K all support cold-weather packages: electric heaters for coolant, engine oil, and hydraulic oil (220V), double-wall exhaust tubes, radiator shutters, cold-weather suspensions, and (for 980E-5/830E-5) **heated exhaust-body routing** to prevent payload freeze-sticking, a feature engineered for Canadian oil sands but directly applicable to Gobi coal (https://www.komatsu.com/en-us/products/equipment/trucks/electric-drive-mining-trucks/980e-5; https://www.komatsu.com/en-us/products/equipment/trucks/electric-drive-mining-trucks/830e-5; https://www.komatsu.com/en-us/products/equipment/trucks/electric-drive-mining-trucks/860e-1k; https://www.komatsu.jp/en/-/media/home/aboutus/innovation/technology/techreport/2017/en/180330_06e.pdf). The 785-7/-8 lists "batteries for cold area arrangement" and dedicated "cold weather operation" chapters in the O&M manual (https://www.manualslib.com/manual/395073/Komatsu-Hd785-7.html; https://www.komatsu.com/content/dam/komatsu/sales-and-marketing-documents/brochures/trucks/hd785/hd785-8-aess936-01-v4.pdf). The PC4000-6 carries a KIM HOTSTART coolant heating system with thermostat, engine oil reserve-tank heater, and HYDRONIC engine-independent auxiliary cab heater with programmable start times (https://www.manualslib.com/manual/3641219/Komatsu-Pc4000-6.html?page=151; https://www.manualslib.com/manual/3641219/Komatsu-Pc4000-6.html?page=95). Komatsu also produces factory "EXTREME COLD TERRAIN SPEC" excavators such as the PC400-7 (JPN) (https://manuals-komatsu.com/shop/komatsu-pdf-download-1/pc400-7jpn-extreme-cold-terrain-spec-s-n-50001-up-field-assembly-manual-english/).

Field proof: Oyu Tolgoi has operated **28 Komatsu 930E-4SE trucks since August 2012** in the South Gobi, where winter nights reach −35 to −40°C (https://en.eot.mn/open-pit-mine; https://www.linkedin.com/posts/oyutolgoi_otunfiltered-activity-7425115077701398528-F-Q0). Erdenet Mining Corporation accumulated ~16,000 operating hours on Komatsu HD1500-8 (142 t) over two years, with haulage volume +7.9% and cost per m³ −5.8% after introduction (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/transwest-mongolia_komatsu-komatsuhd1500-hd1500-activity-7500022394456092672-Wf2J; https://erdenettoday.mn/art/7169). 

Reliability caveat: a study of Komatsu D-375A/A5 dozers in northern Russia indicates failure flow on basic components rises 2× to 6× at low temperatures relative to warm-season operations, with −25°C as a critical threshold for rubber/polymer embrittlement (https://exa.ai/library/publication/9vvm1yl0lv4).

### 1.3 Volvo CE

The EC950F operates 10+ hours/day, 7 days/week at Boliden's Aitik open-pit copper mine in Arctic Sweden, year-round at −20 to −30°C; the contractor reports "fuel consumption is reasonable" (https://www.volvoce.com/global/en/news-and-events/news-and-stories/2021/ec950f-swecon_sweden-jobstory/). ## 4. Fuel Efficiency in Extreme Cold

### 4.1 Physics at −40°C

Four compounding mechanisms drive the winter fuel penalty:

1. **Fuel gelling/waxing**: No. 2 diesel cloud point is ~−10°C; the Cold Filter Plugging Point (CFPP) is only a few degrees below that, at which wax crystals plug filters (https://www.keycoop.com/news/key-cooperative-news/stop-diesel-gelling-this-winter-2024; https://www.z.co.nz/assets/zenergy/products-services/documents/technical-data-sheets/Diesel-fuel-in-winter.pdf). Arctic-grade diesel with depressant additives is required for sustained −40°C operation (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1755-1315/459/5/052009/pdf).
2. **Tier 4/Stage V injection vulnerability**: common-rail systems run >30,000 psi with clearances under 2 microns; gelled fuel or ice shuts machines down and can score high-pressure pump plungers and stick injector needles (https://www.constructionequipment.com/equipment-maintenance-and-repair/article/55409927/how-to-prevent-diesel-fuel-gelling-in-construction-equipment). DEF thawing at −40°C takes **up to 70 minutes** before urea flows (https://www.constructionequipment.com/earthmoving/rigid-frame-trucks-off-highway/product/10752402/komatsu-komatsu-930e-5-haul-truck). Hence: **specify Tier 2-equivalent engines** for all brands.
3. **Arctic-diesel energy density**: switching from summer to arctic winter diesel reduces engine power by **~10%** because low-temperature fuel is less dense and volumetric injection delivers less energy (https://exa.ai/library/publication/f52xp10r1xq).
4. **Warm-up/idle burn**: Cat guidance requires extended warm-up to ≥71°C coolant under no load and warns against short-cycle operation (https://avsmanual.com/i.caterpillar/240574-cold-weather-operation-3516b-hd-generator-set/). Winter fleet telematics show idling at ~23% of operating hours, consuming 4.3% of total fuel (https://www.cts.umn.edu/publications/report/reducing-winter-maintenance-equipment-fuel-consumption-using-advanced-vehicle-data-analytics). Days with heavy snow/cold show >25% higher fuel use vs. mild days.

### 4.2 Worked Example

A truck burning 100 L/h baseline over a 6,000-h year = 600,000 L. Winter scenario with 10% arctic-fuel penalty on ~50% of annual hours (+30,000 L) plus 4.3% idling overhead (+25,800 L) → **~655,800 L, a +9.3% annual uplift** before snow/grade effects that can push individual winter days +25%. At US$1.00/L landed diesel, that is **~US$56,000 per truck per year** (https://exa.ai/library/publication/f52xp10r1xq; https://www.cts.umn.edu/publications/report/reducing-winter-maintenance-equipment-fuel-consumption-using-advanced-vehicle-data-analytics). Fuel-system specification (heated filters/lines, coolant-heat exchangers, diesel-fired or electric preheaters to eliminate idle) pays back faster than almost any other winter option.

### 4.3 OEM Cold-Weather Fuel Strategies

- **Caterpillar**: Fuel blender/heater elements in the Cold Weather Package keep wax crystals small and prevent fuel-filter icing; auto-warm-up, cold-start block heaters (Cat 395 rated −32°C), arctic hydraulic oil, antifreeze to −50°C (https://www.cat.com/en_US/products/new/equipment/excavators/large-excavators/126440.html; https://www.fabickcat.com/new-equipment/824-wheel-dozer/). Cat runs a **Fuel Promise Program** in Mongolia tied to Customer Value Agreements (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/barloworldmongolia_%D1%82%D2%AF%D0%BB%D1%88%D0%BD%D0%B8%D0%B9-%D0%B0%D0%BD%D0%B4%D0%B3%D0%B0%D0%B9-fuelpromiseprogram-activity-7313018085832081408-jm-R), a contractual fuel-efficiency guarantee unique among the three OEMs in Mongolia.

- **Komatsu ThermaStart**: autonomous idle management on the 830E, field-tested through Canadian tundra at −30°C, eliminates unnecessary idling and warm-up cycles via continuous monitoring of block temperature, battery voltage, and air pressure; reportedly delivers ROI within days (https://www.roscomining.com/post/thermastart-komatsu-830e-cold-weather). For oil-sands transport, the 980E routes engine exhaust through the dump body to keep ore from freezing to the body, reducing wasted fuel on stuck-payload cleanup (https://www.komatsu.jp/en/-/media/home/aboutus/innovation/technology/techreport/2017/en/180330_06e.pdf). HD785-8 incorporates Variable HorsePower Control, optimized shift control, reduced hydraulic losses, and auto idle stop (https://www.komatsu.jp/en/-/media/home/aboutus/innovation/technology/techreport/2019/en/200331_05e.pdf). 830E-5 claims 3–5% fuel savings from on-demand cooling (https://www.komatsu.com/en-us/products/equipment/trucks/electric-drive-mining-trucks/830e-5).

- **Volvo CE**: drain fuel/water separators nightly, fill fuel tanks nightly, regenerate DPF before cold shutdown, arctic-grade engine/hydraulic oils; Volvo A60 carries a fuel-efficiency claim of "up to 15% more fuel efficiency" vs. prior generation (https://www.volvoce.com/en-ca/discover/guides-and-advice/2021/diesel-engine-dos-and-donts-to-prep-for-winter-season/; https://www.volvoce.com/united-states/en-us/products/articulated-haulers/a60/). EC350E claims up to 9% better fuel efficiency than prior generation (https://www.volvoce.com/united-states/en-us/products/excavators/ec350e/).

- **BelAZ**: Specific fuel consumption at nominal power is 196–201 g/kWh (75710: 198; 75605: 196; 7513A: 201), competitive with Western diesel-electric drives (190–200 g/kWh typical). BelAZ has piloted LNG cryogenic fuel systems on dump trucks to reduce diesel dependence in Russian coal regions (https://www.matec-conferences.org/articles/matecconf/pdf/2019/46/matecconf_ispcime18_03002.pdf).

### 4.4 Mongolian Diesel Context

Mongolia imports ~95% of petroleum products from Russia; Western sanctions on Russian energy companies and banks have created payment difficulties and supply uncertainty (https://www.intellinews.com/hit-indirectly-by-sanctions-mongolia-struggles-to-find-workarounds-351043/; https://www.trtworld.com/asia/mongolia-is-feeling-weight-of-western-sanctions-on-russia-over-ukraine-war-18214964). In 2026 Russian export controls disrupted supply, prompting Mongolia to secure winter-diesel delivery agreements from October, hold ~85,600 t of diesel (~21 days of national supply at ~4,076 t/day), and diversify to China/South Korea via slow rail-gauge transfers (https://mn.ibtimes.com/mongolia-expands-fuel-supply-beyond-russia-china-south-korea-1812481). **At −40°C, source Arctic-grade diesel meeting GOST R 55475-2013 grade A with limiting filtration temperature ≤ −44°C** (https://meganorms.com/gost-r-55475-2013.html; https://www.russiangost.com/p-59774-gost-r-55475-2013.aspx). Without this, fuel filters will gel and shut machines down regardless of brand.

- **Immersive Technologies PRO3 simulator** at Oyu Tolgoi (installed 2011, five-year gold support, Custom Mine Site) for Komatsu haul-truck operator training (https://www.immersivetechnologies.com/news/news2011/news_2011_21.htm).
- **Mongolia Polytechnic "Mining Machinery Operation Technician" program** in Ömnögovi province, delivered via public-private partnership with Germany's Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development and Ministry of Education, with >80% of students from Umnögovi and a blended learning/internship model (https://mcpg.mn/en/9281/).
- **South Gobi Underground Mass Mining Institute** launched March 2025 by Rio Tinto and the University of Queensland, based at Oyu Tolgoi, 2025 cohort of 28 participants; 2026 curriculum will open to local and international mining companies (https://www.australianmining.com.au/rio-tinto-debuts-world-class-training-program-at-oyu-tolgoi/).

---

## 6. Russian-Made Alternatives and Regional Trade Realities

### 6.1 BelAZ Product Range (Belarusian; CIS-Aligned)

BelAZ is the largest supplier of mining dump trucks in the CIS and the dominant Russian-bloc alternative in Mongolia, with **200+ units operating** since the 1970s at Erdenet (30/45/55/130-t fleets), Nariin Sukhait, Tsagaan Suvarga, and **130-t BelAZ-75135 at Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi "equipped for the extreme climatic conditions of the Gobi Desert"** (https://www.belarus.by/en/business/business-news/belaz-dump-trucks-put-into-use-at-coal-minefield-in-gobi_i_9931.html; https://www.kopyl.gov.by/en/news/oblast/item/20638-zhodino-dump-trucks-belaz-will-work-in-the-gobi-desert.html; https://eng.belta.by/economics/view/belaz-to-ship-3m-worth-of-haul-trucks-to-mongolia-103863-2017/). Cost signal: 130-t trucks at roughly US$1 M per unit (3 trucks ≈ US$3 M, 2017) (https://eng.belta.by/economics/view/belaz-to-ship-3m-worth-of-haul-trucks-to-mongolia-103863-2017/).

**Sanctions risk (decisive)**: BelAZ was **EU-sanctioned in June 2021** (https://www.debevoise.com/insights/publications/2021/06/eu-imposes-new-comprehensive-sanctions-on-belarus) and designated under **OFAC's BELARUS-EO14038** program; BelAZ appears on the US OFAC SDN list, EU financial sanctions, UK, Swiss, Belgian, and French regimes — 15 sanction sources per OpenSanctions aggregation (https://www.opensanctions.org/entities/NK-hDr2CxmhFmDRjCisQete2c/; https://ofac.treasury.gov/recent-actions/20211202). Consequences already documented: **Cummins and Rolls-Royce/MTU, BelAZ's two main engine suppliers, terminated supply**, as did Liebherr, Danfoss, Becker, and Yokohama; BelAZ is substituting Chinese and Russian engines (https://www.e-mj.com/departments/suppliers-report/belaz-feels-sting-of-sanctions/; https://charter97.org/en/news/2021/9/3/435602/). A Lithuanian intermediary faced sanctions-violation exposure merely for arranging BelAZ truck delivery to Chile (https://www.occrp.org/en/investigation/ex-prison-warden-in-lithuania-struck-1m-deal-with-sanctioned-belarusian-state-truckmaker). US secondary-sanctions authority over non-US financial institutions facilitating prohibited transactions was explicitly expanded in December 2023 (https://www.clydeco.com/en/insights/2024/03/the-u-s-expands-secondary-sanctions-regime-to-non).

Mongolia is not an EU/US jurisdiction, so purchase is legal for a Mongolian entity, but **Western-bank financing, insurance, resale to international operators, and OEM-engine parts for legacy Cummins/MTU-engined trucks are all impaired**, and future engine standardization is uncertain. Governance allegations: EU Reporter reported claims that UBM functioned as a hard-currency channel linked to the Lukashenko regime, including an MNT 18.6 billion Development Bank loan to Baganuur tied to BelAZ equipment never repaid, and MNT 27 billion of BelAZ equipment supplied to Erdenet amid alleged document falsification (https://www.eureporter.co/world/mongolia/2021-04-13/the-mongolian-connection-to-lukashenkos-money/). UBM denied the allegations (https://ikon.mn/n/272t). Treat as allegations but include in counterparty due diligence.

### 6.2 UZTM-Kartex (Russian)

Electric rope shovels and draglines with deep cold-climate DNA and decades of Mongolian operational history. Erdenet has run their machines since 1978 (11 currently); four EKG-12K shovels added 2018–2020; ESH 25.90 dragline at Shivee-Ovoo since 2003; Baganuur's stripping fleet entirely Russian-built; 2019 strategic agreement to co-manufacture spare parts at Erdenet's repair-mechanical plant. Risk: UZTM-Kartex is controlled by Gazprombank, itself under Western sanctions (https://www.interfax-russia.ru/index.php/ural/news/uztm-karteks-zavershila-postavku-ekskavatorov-mongolskoy-mednoy-kompanii-erdenet).

### 6.3 Liebherr (German-Swiss; European Cold-Climate Track Record)

For excavator alignment with BelAZ trucks, the R 9100 Gen 8 (100 t) and R 9150 G7 (150 t) carry an Arctic Package validated at ALROSA's Udachny mine (−55 to +40°C) with on-site 24/7 service. No dedicated Mongolian CE dealer is identified.

### 6.4 Regional Trade Context

Mongolia imports ~28% of goods from Russia and depends on Russia for ~95% of petroleum products (https://www.trtworld.com/asia/mongolia-is-feeling-weight-of-western-sanctions-on-russia-over-ukraine-war-18214964). December 2024 saw an interim EAEU-Mongolia trade agreement; February 2026 saw the Mongolia-Russia Business Forum with 70+ Mongolian and 100+ Russian businesses meeting (https://russiancouncil.ru/en/analytics-and-comments/analytics/russia-and-mongolia-forging-stronger-trade-relations/; https://thediplomat.com/2026/02/with-speaker-uchrals-trip-mongolia-and-russia-look-to-expand-economic-links/). China dominates Mongolia's construction-machinery import market at 65–70% by value (2026), with Japanese OEMs (Komatsu, Hitachi) in the large mining segment and second-hand imports at ~20% (https://www.ibicrossborder.com/upload/ai_report/en/html/20260718003522-f2bb78fbbc.html). For Mongolia's fixed mining equipment market, the top-five manufacturers (Metso, Sandvik, FLSmidth, Caterpillar, Weir Group) collectively command ~65% of revenue (2026), with Komatsu in the second tier (https://www.marknteladvisors.com/research-library/mongolia-fixed-mining-equipment-market.html).

---

## 7. Side-by-Side Comparison Table

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| **Ulaanbaatar dealer** | Barloworld Mongolia (since 1996, Wagner legacy; 600+ staff; 5 branches; US$130M after-sales) | Transwest Mongolia (exclusive; 120+ service specialists; 300+ rebuilds/yr; Khanbogd facility 2022; KLTD 2025–2026) | No verified CE mining dealer; Volvo Trucks via MNTTT; Central Asia Equipment LLC unverified depth | UBM (sole since 2012; 160 staff, 130 technical; 2,289 m² UB service center) | No dedicated dealer; Erdenet co-manufactures parts |

## 8. Recommendations

1. **Primary haul trucks (rigid 100-t+ class)**: **Komatsu** 930E-5/5SE (290–320 t electric drive) for large operations or **Cat 785/789/793** (139–194 t mechanical drive) for mid-size. Specify cold-weather suspensions, body-heating kits, 220V hot-start oil/coolant/hydraulic, radiator shutters, non-emissionized engines (Komatsu for non-NA markets), and −50°C antifreeze. Both have proven in-Mongolia fleets with the deepest service footprints.

2. **Primary excavators (mining class)**: **Cat 6040/6050/6060** or **Komatsu PC2000/PC4000/PC7000-11** with the factory Cold Weather Package (coolant/oil/hydraulic heaters, cab pre-heater, fuel blender, ~50 kW shore power). Cat's 6040 package documentation is the most detailed; Komatsu's PC4000 HYDRONIC independent cab heater is a genuine −40°C shift-start advantage. Choose based on which haul-truck brand you standardize to minimize dealer fragmentation.

# The State of Deepfake Detection Research Since 2022

## Headline Finding: The Deployment Gap

Since 2022, deepfake detection research has matured architecturally but exposed a persistent generalization crisis. The central empirical result, anchored by **Deepfake-Eval-2024** (Chandra et al., CVPR Workshops 2026; https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4), is that detectors scoring near-perfect AUC on controlled benchmarks collapse by roughly 40–57% when evaluated on deepfakes actually circulated online in 2024. The benchmark collected 45 hours of video, 56.5 hours of audio, and 1,975 images across 88 websites in 52 languages. Per-model AUC drops:

| Modality | Model | Original AUC | In-the-wild AUC | Drop |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Video | GenConViT | 0.96 | 0.63 | −34.4% |
| Video | FTCN | 0.87 | 0.50 | −42.5% |
| Video | Styleflow | 0.95 | 0.51 | −46.3% |
| Audio | AASIST | 1.00 | 0.43 | −57.0% |
| Audio | RawNet2 | 0.99 | 0.53 | −46.5% |
| Audio | P3 (SSL) | 1.00 | 0.58 | −42.0% |
| Image | UFD | 0.94 | 0.56 | −40.4% |
| Image | DistilDIRE | 0.99 | 0.52 | −47.5% |
| Image | NPR | 0.98 | 0.53 | −45.9% |

The paper reports aggregate AUC drops of approximately 50% (video), 48% (audio), and 45% (image). Even tuned CLIP-based baselines reach at most ~81% accuracy, and best commercial detectors reach ~82%—still below expert forensic analysts (who themselves show 6.6–9% inter-annotator disagreement). An estimated 500,000 deepfakes circulated on social media in 2023, with a fourfold increase in deepfake fraud cases from 2023 to 2024 (Chandra et al., 2025).

---

## Technical Methods

### Video and Image Detection

The architectural center of gravity has shifted from CNN backbones (Xception, EfficientNet-B4, MesoNet) to Vision Transformers and hybrid designs. Khan et al. ("A Timely Survey on Vision Transformer for Deepfake Detection," 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2405.08463) catalogued 14 ViT-based detectors and reported transformer architectures exhibit ~11.33% cross-dataset AUC decline versus >15% for CNN-based approaches, at 3–5× higher compute cost. Notable benchmarks from that survey:

- **UIA-ViT (2022)**: AUC 99.33 on FaceForensics++ HQ; cross-dataset AUC 94.68 (DFD), 82.41 (Celeb-DF-v1), 86.59 (Celeb-DF-v2), 75.80 (DFDC).
- **ISTVT (2023)**: 99.0% accuracy on FF++ (HQ), 96.15% (LQ), 99.8% Celeb-DF, 92.1% DFDC.
- **M2TR (2022)**: AUC 99.51 (FF++ HQ), 99.92 (FF++ RAW), 95.5 (Celeb-DF), 86.7 (SR-DF).
- **FA-ViT** (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.11092): 93.83% AUC on Celeb-DF and 78.32% AUC on DFDC in cross-dataset evaluation.

The SoK systematization (Yan et al., 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2401.04364v4) reviewed 51 detectors and identified 18 critical factors, building the first white-box deepfake dataset to evaluate 16 leading systems under black/gray/white-box attacks. DF40 (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks; https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13495) covers 40 distinct generation techniques (10 face-swapping, 13 face-reenactment, 12 entire-face-synthesis, 5 face-editing)—~10× the diversity of FaceForensics++—and concludes that "the dataset, not the algorithm, is the primary culprit" for the generalization gap. DeepfakeBench (NeurIPS 2023; https://github.com/SCLBD/DeepfakeBench) standardized evaluation of 36 detectors across 9 datasets, documenting 15–30% accuracy drops on unseen test sets.

GAN-image forensics transferred poorly to diffusion-generated images; Ricker et al. (2024; https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2024/124220/124220.pdf) showed re-training on diffusion samples yields near-perfect detection that generalizes back to GANs. New diffusion-oriented detectors include:

- **ZED** (Zero-shot Entropy-based Detector; https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.15875): 3%+ accuracy gain without AI-generated training data.
- **APN** (Artifact Purification Network; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1016/j.cviu.2024.104078): 5.6–16.4% higher accuracy on GenImage.
- **Community Forensics** (https://arxiv.org/html/2411.04125v1): 2.7M images from 4,803 generators; diversity-driven generalization.
- **Wavelet-CLIP** (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.18301v3): AUC 0.749 (cross-data), 0.893 (unseen deepfakes).
- **D³** (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.04584v1): 5.3% accuracy improvement in out-of-domain testing.

### Audio Deepfake Detection

RawNet2 (SincNet filters on raw waveforms) and AASIST (RawNet2 encoder + heterogeneous stacking graph attention) remain the dominant end-to-end backbones. Recent refinements:

- **ARawNet2** (Interspeech 2023; https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/li23h_interspeech.pdf): EER 4.61% on ASVspoof 2019 LA, 8.36% on ASVspoof 2021 LA, 19.03% on ASVspoof 2021 DF.
- **TO-RawNet** (https://www.isca-archive.org/interspeech_2023/wang23w_interspeech.pdf): 66.09% relative EER reduction on ASVspoof 2019 LA.
- **AASIST3 with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks** (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/borodin24_asvspoof.pdf): minDCF 0.5357 closed / 0.1414 open on ASVspoof 5—a >2× improvement.
- **AASIST2** (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.08279): Res2Net blocks + Dynamic Chunk Size + Adaptive Large Margin Fine-Tuning.
- **CoNSIST** (KIPS 2024; https://www.manuscriptlink.com/society/kips/conference/ask2024): adds Squeeze-and-Excitation + positional encoding to AASIST.

The dominant paradigm since 2023 is **self-supervised speech front-ends**. Frozen wav2vec 2.0 + logistic regression with under 2,000 learned parameters reduced average EER from 30.9% (RawNet2) to 8.8% across 8 deepfake benchmarks (https://arxiv.org/html/2309.05384v2). Fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 achieved ~90% relative EER improvement on ASVspoof 2021 LA and DF (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2202.12233). Whisper+AASIST (https://faculty.cs.gwu.edu/xiaodongqu/papers/HCII_2024_572_Whisper_Qian.pdf) reports EERs of 24.73% (ASSERT+LPS) and 34.81% (AASIST) on In-the-Wild audio, despite strong academic benchmark performance.

#### ASVspoof 5 (2024)

ASVspoof 5 (Wang et al., 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2408.08739v1) rebuilt the benchmark with crowdsourced data from ~2,000 speakers, 32 attack algorithms (including neural codecs and adversarial attacks for the first time), and two tracks: standalone CM (Track 1) and spoofing-robust ASV (Track 2). The primary metric moved from EER to minDCF (using Cmiss=1, Cfa=10, πspf=0.05). Reported results:

- **ParallelChain Lab ensemble**: minDCF 0.2660 closed (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/tran24_asvspoof.pdf).
- **USTC-KXDIGIT**: 0.3948 minDCF / 14.33% EER closed; 0.0750 minDCF / 2.59% EER open (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/chen24_asvspoof.pdf).
- **SHADOW team's FwSE-ResNet34 with codec augmentation**: minDCF 0.44 (Track 1 Eval), 47% improvement over baseline (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/villalba24_asvspoof.pdf).
- **Fraunhofer SIT**: minDCF 0.589 closed / 0.174 open with SSL front-end (https://www.isca-archive.org/asvspoof_2024/schafer24_asvspoof.pdf).
- Top open-condition systems reached minDCF 0.13–0.20 using wav2vec 2.0/WavLM. Organizers note "performance degrades under adversarial attacks and the application of neural encoding/compression schemes."

---

## Cross-Dataset Generalization

Cross-dataset generalization is the field's central open problem. XceptionNet trained on FF++ scores AUC 0.997 in-dataset but only 0.482 on Celeb-DF, a ~52% relative drop (Nadimpalli et al., CVPRW 2022; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2022W/WMF/papers/Nadimpalli_On_Improving_Cross-Dataset_Generalization_of_Deepfake_Detectors_CVPRW_2022_paper.pdf). A systematic review (https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/2/68) found an average 10–15% cross-dataset performance decline across all methodological classes, with strong evidence that models learn "dataset-specific compression artifacts rather than deepfake characteristics that are generalizable."

Strategies include self-blended images (SBI, CVPR 2022), latent-space augmentation (LSDA, CVPR 2024), identity/inconsistency cues (IID, UCF, RECCE, Face X-ray), and temporal modeling (TALL, ICCV 2023; FTCN; AltFreezing, CVPR 2023). Kamat et al. (ICCVW 2023) found that leading detectors generalize best when they *abandon* certain detection modes—spatial-, temporal-, and lip-reading-based detectors scored 96%/75%/51% AUC on diffusion fakes but 80%/99%/92% on talking-head fakes (https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/ICCV2023W/DFAD/papers/Kamat_Revisiting_Generalizability_in_Deepfake_Detection_Improving_Metrics_and_Stabilizing_Transfer_ICCVW_2023_paper.pdf).

---

## Foundation Model Integration

CLIP-based adaptation is a major research direction since 2023:

- **UFD (Ojha et al., CVPR 2023)**: frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 + linear probe generalizes across GAN and diffusion generators (https://arxiv.org/html/2410.11835v1).
- **CLIPping the Deception** (Khan & Dang-Nguyen, ICMR 2024; https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.12927): +5.01% mAP and +6.61% accuracy over prior SOTA with <⅓ training data (200k vs. 720k images).
- **FatFormer** (CVPR 2024; https://arxiv.org/html/2312.16649v1): forgery-aware adapters over CLIP—98% accuracy on unseen GANs, 95% on unseen diffusion.
- **CLIPMoLE** (https://arxiv.org/html/2404.04883): only 0.08% of parameters fine-tuned via mixture-of-LoRAs; +3.64% mAP and +12.72% average accuracy on unseen diffusion/autoregressive generators.
- **GenD** (https://arxiv.org/html/2508.06248v4): tunes only 0.03% (LayerNorm) of CLIP/Perception Encoder/DINO; paired real-fake training is essential to mitigate shortcut learning.
- **AIDE (ICLR 2025; https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/b0303773962ea1b5394c3a83cc7dd066-Paper-Conference.pdf)**: +3.5% (AIGCDetectBenchmark) and +4.6% (GenImage) over SOTA.
- **MFCLIP** (https://arxiv.org/html/2409.09724) and **M²F²-Det** (https://arxiv.org/html/2503.20188v1) extend to LLM-augmented detection and explanation.

For audio, the ASVspoof 5 winners explicitly credit wav2vec 2.0/WavLM/HuBERT foundation features. A 2026 frozen-features study (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.01738v2) found Perception Encoder, MetaCLIP 2, and DINOv3 plus a linear classifier match or beat specialized detectors in realistic settings.

---

## Multimodal Audio-Visual Detection

Multimodal analysis has emerged as a primary generalization strategy. AVFF (Oorloff et al., CVPR 2024; https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2024/papers/Oorloff_AVFF_Audio-Visual_Feature_Fusion_for_Video_Deepfake_Detection_CVPR_2024_paper.pdf) uses two-stage cross-modal self-supervision on real videos (contrastive learning, autoencoding, complementary masking) followed by supervised fine-tuning, reaching 98.6% accuracy and 99.1% AUC on FakeAVCeleb—14.9 and 9.9 percentage-point gains over prior SOTA. **SpeechForensics** (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/9c7900fac04a701cbed83256b76dbaa3-Paper-Conference.pdf) uses self-supervised masked-prediction on real videos and outperforms SOTA on cross-dataset generalization without any fake training data.

The **AV-Deepfake1M** benchmark (ACM MM 2024, >1M videos, >2,000 subjects, LLM-driven transcript manipulations; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664647.3680795) showed SOTA methods suffer "a significant drop" compared to prior datasets. The follow-up **AV-Deepfake1M++** (2M clips, https://arxiv.org/html/2409.06991) and the 1M-Deepfakes Detection Challenge extended to a long-running competition; **MFMS** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3664647.3688984) won top performance via modality-fused plus modality-specific features. **MSOC** (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.14176) extends one-class learning to four FakeAVCeleb splits (RAFV, FAFV, FARV, Unsynced). The survey "Evolving from Single-modal to Multi-modal Facial Deepfake Detection" (https://arxiv.org/html/2406.06965v1) documents the field's June 2024 transition.

---

## Privacy-Preserving Detection

Federated learning (FL) dominates privacy-preserving work:

- **FedForgery** (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2210.09563): variational autoencoder for residual feature maps + generalized FL.
- **Dynamic-Aware FL for Face Forgery Video Detection** (ACM TIST 2022; https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3501814): first FL framework for face-forgery video, with an Inconsistency-Capture module matching centralized performance.
- **Blockchain-based FL with SegCaps + CNN** (Cognitive Computation 2024; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12559-024-10255-7): +6.6% accuracy / +5.1% AUC over six baselines.
- **FL-TENB4** (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/d97c/1fd280a818f9a30435c07717effc18a1cc08.pdf): Tiny EfficientNetB4-Lite + FL for CCTV edge deployment.
- **FedMaxAdapt** (https://researchonline.gcu.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/113968862/113434712.pdf): 90.1% video / 91.0% audio accuracy at 50% sparsity, reducing bandwidth by 43.1% (video) and 40.3% (audio).
- **FLADD** (https://eurekamag.com/research/110/713/110713846.php): dual-branch Res2Net + Rawformer; EER 0.285% on ASVspoof 2019 LA, 2.045% on ASVspoof 2021 LA.

Differential privacy and secure multi-party computation are emerging: **DDFed** (NeurIPS 2024; https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/824f98c4e9bb301b0b96fa2ae071360b-Paper-Conference.pdf) combines FHE-secure aggregation with poisoning defense; **SecDFDNet** (https://oulurepo.oulu.fi/bitstream/handle/10024/44041/nbnfi-fe20231025141349.pdf) implements additive secret sharing with SecReLU/SecSigm/SecSpatial protocols. A 2024 TPAMI work (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1109/TPAMI.2023.3332428) showed multi-stage adaptive DP in asynchronous FL improves the privacy–utility trade-off by up to 24% accuracy at equal privacy loss.

---

## Benchmarks vs. Real-World Deployment

Beyond Deepfake-Eval-2024, corroborating evidence is robust:

- **Evaluating Deepfake Detectors in the Wild** (SumSubstance 2025; https://arxiv.org/html/2507.21905): on 500,000+ deepfake images, fewer than half of tested detectors achieved AUC > 60%, with the lowest at 50%.
- **Concept drift quantification** (https://arxiv.org/html/2511.07009): models trained on 2024 deepfakes suffer a >30% recall drop when evaluated on fakes generated six months later.
- **WildRF** (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.09398): best method reaches only 93.7% mAP on Reddit/X/Facebook deepfakes. The authors diagnose a benchmark artifact: real images stored lossy (JPEG) vs. fakes lossless (PNG), letting detectors key on format rather than forgery.
- **A zero-shot "out-of-the-box" evaluation** of 16 methods (23 pretrained variants) across 12 datasets, 2.6M images, and 291 generators (https://arxiv.org/html/2602.07814v1): best detector (Community-Forensics ensemble) reaches 75.0% mean accuracy; worst (CNNSpot) 37.5%. Modern commercial generators—Flux Dev, Firefly v4, Midjourney v7—defeat most detectors, achieving only 18–30% average detection accuracy.
- **Compression/robustness** (Frontiers in AI 2026; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/artificial-intelligence/articles/10.3389/frai.2026.1835651/text): five face-swap detectors averaged 94.7% accuracy on clean data vs. 67.8% under distortion—a 26.9 percentage-point drop (relative decline ≈ 28.4%); JPEG and motion blur cause up to 35% drops.
- **RedFace** (https://arxiv.org/html/2510.08067v1): 60,000 forged images from 9 commercial platforms; existing detectors fail to generalize.

Four mechanisms drive the gap: (1) **benchmark staleness** (FF++'s forgery techniques are 4–5 years old per DF40), (2) **shortcut learning** (compression/format/face-crop pipeline signatures), (3) **resolution and platform transformations** erasing low-level cues, and (4) **post-processing enhancement tools** (CodeFormer, GPEN) that erase artifacts. The literature increasingly frames deepfake detection not as a forensic arms race but as a socio-technical system requiring detection, provenance (C2PA), regulation, and media literacy operating together.

---

## Ethical Concerns

Researchers have identified a consistent cluster of issues:

1. **Non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII)**: A 10-country survey of 16,000+ respondents (https://dl.acm.org/doi/full/10.1145/3613904.3642382) found 2.2% victimization and 1.8% perpetration rates. NCII remains the dominant documented harm category in Deepfake-Eval-2024 (https://arxiv.org/html/2503.02857v4).
2. **Election/political misinformation**: Recorded Future identified 82 deepfakes impersonating public figures (July 2023–July 2024) across 38 countries: 26.8% financially motivated scams, 25.6% fabricated misleading statements, 15.8% electioneering (https://assets.recordedfuture.com/insikt-report-pdfs/2024/ta-2024-0924.pdf). A Knight First Amendment Institute analysis of 78 election deepfakes found non-AI "cheap fakes" were used 7× more often than AI content—but AI deepfakes pose disproportionate risks via the "liar's dividend" (https://knightcolumbia.org/blog/we-looked-at-78-election-deepfakes-political-misinformation-is-not-an-ai-problem).
3. **Liar's dividend**: Politicians may falsely dismiss real evidence as AI-generated (https://www.brookings.edu/articles/watch-out-for-false-claims-of-deepfakes-and-actual-deepfakes-this-election-year/).
4. **Bias and fairness**: Legacy datasets (LFW, Celeb-DF) are demographically skewed; FakeAVCeleb was built explicitly to counter racial bias. The German AI Inequalities survey (https://a-mcc.eu/backend/gpt/pdfs/deepfakes-in-the-context-of-ai-inequalities-analysing-disparities-in-knowledge-and-attitudes.pdf) found gender, age, and educational attainment predict deepfake knowledge, raising equitable-protection concerns.
5. **Dual-use dynamics**: Detection research informs better generators (the "tug-of-war"; https://arxiv.org/html/2407.06174v3); white-box evaluation and published detector weights create adversarial roadmaps.
6. **Privacy tensions in detection**: Centralized training requires uploading sensitive biometric media, motivating FL/DP—yet FL itself remains vulnerable to poisoning (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-981-99-8024-6_14).
7. **Free-expression concerns**: Critics of the TAKE IT DOWN Act argue its broad language risks First Amendment conflict (https://apnews.com/article/take-it-down-deepfake-trump-melania-first-amendment-741a6e525e81e5e3d8843aac20de8615).
8. **Detection reliability as evidence**: A reliability-perspective survey (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.10881v4) warns that without statistical reliability guarantees, detector outputs are inadequate for prosecutions.

---

## Regulatory Frameworks

### European Union — AI Act

**Regulation (EU) 2024/1689** (https://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), adopted 13 June 2024. Article 50 transparency obligations apply from **2 August 2026** (https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-50):

- **Art. 50(2)**: Providers of AI generating synthetic audio/image/video/text must mark outputs in machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated—solutions must be "effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible."
- **Art. 50(4)**: Deployers generating deepfakes (Art. 3(60) defines as AI-generated/manipulated image, audio, or video that would falsely appear authentic) must disclose artificial origin; artistic/satirical works receive lighter-touch disclosure.
- **Art. 50(5)**: Disclosure must be "clear and distinguishable" at latest at first interaction/exposure.
- Penalties: up to €15 million or 3% of worldwide annual turnover (Art. 99(4)).

The Commission has published Guidelines on Article 50 implementation and a voluntary Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content (with a standard disclosure icon). The Digital Services Act (Regulation 2022/2065) Art. 35(1)(k) requires VLOPs to mark AI-generated/manipulated content as part of systemic-risk mitigation.

### United States — TAKE IT DOWN Act

**Pub. L. 119-12** (https://www.congress.gov/119/plaws/publ12/PLAW-119publ12.htm), sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz, passed Senate by unanimous consent 13 February 2025 and House 409-2 on 28 April 2025; signed by President Trump on **19 May 2025**:

- **Section 2**: Amends §223 of the Communications Act of 1934 to criminalize knowing publication of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, including "**digital forgeries**" created via software/ML/AI "indistinguishable from an authentic visual depiction." Penalties: up to 2 years' imprisonment (3 years for minors).
- **Section 3**: Requires covered platforms to establish notice-and-removal by **19 May 2026** and remove flagged content + known identical copies within **48 hours**, enforced by the FTC.

Comprehensive federal activity is otherwise limited. According to one review (https://exa.ai/library/publication/dtbv24df4gm), 46 US states have enacted deepfake legislation since 2022, with 169 laws total and 146 bills introduced in 2025 alone, including Texas Election Code § 255.004 (election deepfakes), Minnesota Statutes § 609.771 (90-day pre-convention coverage), Virginia Code § 18.2-386.2 (NCII), and the Tennessee ELVIS Act (first state law protecting voice as right of publicity in AI context). The FCC has separately banned AI-generated voices in robocalls.

### China — Deep Synthesis Provisions

**Provisions on the Administration of Deep Synthesis of Internet-based Information Services** (Order No. 12; https://www.cac.gov.cn/2022-12/11/c_1672221949318230.htm), adopted 25 November 2022 by the CAC, MIIT, and MPS; **effective 10 January 2023**:

- **Art. 9**: Mandatory real-identity verification of users via mobile number, ID, or national network-identity authentication.
- **Art. 10**: Content moderation via technical or manual review; illegal-content feature databases required.
- **Art. 14**: Training-data management; safety assessments for tools generating biometric features (face/voice).
- **Arts. 16–17**: Mandatory non-intrusive marks on all outputs; prominent public labeling for services "may lead to public confusion" (voice generation, face generation/swap/manipulation, immersive virtual scenes).
- **Art. 18**: Deletion or tampering with these marks is illegal.
- **Arts. 19–20**: Algorithm filing for services with opinion-forming or social-mobilization capabilities; security assessments before launching new products.

The companion **Interim Measures for the Management of Generative AI Services** (Order No. 15; effective 15 August 2023; https://www.gov.cn/gongbao/2023/issue_10666/202308/content_6900864.html) extends labeling duties (Art. 12, cross-referencing the Deep Synthesis Provisions) to generative AI providers.

### International

- **Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI (CETS No. 225)**: opened for signature **5 September 2024**; first legally binding international AI treaty (https://www.coe.int/en/web/artificial-intelligence/the-framework-convention-on-artificial-intelligence). Mandates human-rights/democracy/rule-of-law consistency across the AI lifecycle, with transparency, accountability, documentation enabling affected persons to challenge decisions, iterative risk assessments, and possible bans ("red lines").
- **G7 Hiroshima Process International Guiding Principles and Code of Conduct** (30 October 2023); OECD AI Principles (2019, updated November 2023); UNESCO Recommendation on AI Ethics (November 2021).

---

## Synthesis

Since 2022, deepfake detection has shifted from a niche forensic problem to a regulatory-compliance infrastructure with sophisticated technical foundations. In-distribution performance is near-saturated (AUC ~0.95–0.99 on FF++; ASVspoof 5 minDCF as low as 0.13 open condition; 98.6%/99.1% accuracy/AUC for AVFF on FakeAVCeleb). But a roughly 40–57% AUC collapse in real-world deployment, combined with concept drift (30% recall loss on fakes six months post-training), means detection alone cannot carry the full societal burden. The most promising generalization levers are foundation-model features (CLIP intermediate layers, wav2vec 2.0/WavLM), artifact-simulation training (SBI/LSDA), multimodal inconsistency cues (AVFF, SpeechForensics, AV-Deepfake1M line), and privacy-preserving collaborative training (FL/DP). The EU AI Act, US TAKE IT DOWN Act, and China Deep Synthesis Provisions together establish a global baseline of disclosure-and-labeling obligations, shifting part of the burden from *detection* to *provenance and disclosure*—a tacit acknowledgment that purely reactive detection cannot yet carry the weight of the problem.
