# The Glaser–Strauss Divergence and Its Constructivist Resolution: A Comparative Analysis of Grounded Theory Methodology

## 1. The 1967 Common Ground and Its Latent Contradictions

Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss published *The Discovery of Grounded Theory* in 1967 as a deliberate challenge to the dominance of quantitative verification in mid-century sociology. The book aimed to establish qualitative research as a rigorous alternative capable of generating theory from data. As they wrote in the preface: "We have linked this position with a general method of comparative analysis…with various procedures designed to generate grounded theory. Although our emphasis is on generating theory rather than verifying it, we take special pains not to divorce those two activities, both necessary to the scientific enterprise" (Glaser & Strauss, 1967, Preface; http://www.sxf.uevora.pt/wp-content/uploads/2013/03/Glaser_1967.pdf).

The book was, however, a coalition document marrying two distinct intellectual traditions. Glaser's Columbia training under Lazarsfeld and Merton emphasized quantitative methods and middle-range theory; Strauss's Chicago-school pragmatism and symbolic interactionism emphasized human agency, emergent processes, and subjective meanings (https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?httpsredir=1&article=1085&context=dberspeakers).

Udo Kelle's reconstruction of the debate demonstrates that the 1967 text contained two unreconciled epistemological positions that seeded the later split (https://d-nb.info/1186821515/34; https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/download/467/1001):

- **Emergence**: researchers should "literally ignore the literature of theory and fact on the area under study, in order to assure that the emergence of categories will not be contaminated" (Glaser & Strauss 1967, p. 37).
- **Theoretical sensitivity**: "Of course, the researcher does not approach reality as a tabula rasa. He must have a perspective that will help him see relevant data" (p. 3).

The entire subsequent history of grounded theory, including the Glaser/Strauss split and Charmaz's reformulation, can be read as successive attempts to reconcile "emergence" with "theoretical sensitivity." The methodological split was not, as sometimes claimed, a product of early estrangement—Glaser and Strauss continued to co-publish through the 1970s (*Anguish*, *Status Passage*, *Chronic Illness and the Quality of Life*). The rupture became public only after the 1990 publication of Strauss and Corbin's *Basics of Qualitative Research*, what Holton (2008) called "the flagship event that marks the split" (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/16094069221149486).

---

## 2. Glaser's Theoretical Sensitivity (1978): Emergence Hardened into Doctrine

Glaser's *Theoretical Sensitivity: Advances in the Methodology of Grounded Theory* (Sociology Press, 1978; ~24,252 Google Scholar citations per https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=mq4fkIUAAAAJ, ~6,120 per OpenAlex https://explore.openalex.org/authors/a5044483808) extended the 1967 framework with theoretical sampling, theoretical coding, and theoretical memos. Its core commitments were:

**Objectivist epistemology.** Glaser treated data as "discovered" rather than constructed. He wrote that through constant comparison, "Personal input by a researcher soon drops out as eccentric and the data become objectivist not constructionist" (Glaser, 2002, p. 6, cited in Rieger, 2019, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6559166/). The very title *The Discovery of Grounded Theory* encodes the assumption that an external reality exists to be found (Charmaz, 2000, https://qualquant.org/wp-content/uploads/text/Charmaz%202000.pdf).

**Emergence over forcing.** Glaser (1978) wrote: "The first step in gaining theoretical sensitivity is to enter the research setting with as few predetermined ideas as possible—especially logically deducted, a prior[i] hypotheses" (https://science-education-research.com/research-methodology/grounded-theory/theoretical-sensitivity/). "Categories emerge upon comparison and properties emerge upon more comparison. And that is all there is to it" (Glaser, 1992, quoted in Charmaz, 2000, p. 512).

**Coding families as late sensitizers.** Glaser offered at least 18 theoretical coding families (causes, contexts, contingencies, consequences, covariances, conditions, plus the degree family, dimension family, cultural family, etc.), but these are deployed *after* substantive coding, not before (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nin.12261). He wrote: "He moves in with the abstract wonderment of what is going on that is an issue and how it is handled" (Glaser 1992, p. 22).

**Delayed literature review.** Classic GT "generally prohibits preliminary literature reviews…arguing that they might affect emergence…If the researcher is aware of existent concepts, found in the literature, these might contaminate the theory, distorting its social reality" (https://uwe-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/6003806). Reading in unrelated fields is permitted; the substantive-area literature is deferred until later analysis.

**Limited role for verification.** Glaser and Strauss (1967) had written: "Comparative analysis both subsumes and assumes verification and accurate description, but only to the extent that the latter are in service of generation" (p. 28, cited in Rieger, 2019). For Glaser, a theory that fits, works, and is relevant is self-verifying through constant comparison; formal verification imports hypothetico-deductive logic that GT was invented to escape. Evaluation criteria: *fit, work, relevance, modifiability* (Glaser, 1978; Rieger, 2019, Table 3).

Glaser later launched the Grounded Theory Institute and the journal *Grounded Theory Review* to defend this orthodox reading (Kenny & Fourie, 2014, cited in Rieger, 2019).

---

## 3. Strauss & Corbin's Basics of Qualitative Research (1990): Systematization and Verification

Anselm Strauss's collaboration with Juliet Corbin produced *Basics of Qualitative Research: Grounded Theory Procedures and Techniques* (Sage, 1990), which Glaser's camp later labeled "Full Conceptual Description" rather than genuine grounded theory (Glaser, 1992, p. 6, cited in https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?httpsredir=1&article=1085&context=dberspeakers).

The text restructured the methodology around prescriptive, multi-stage coding:

**Three-stage coding architecture:** (1) *Open coding*—line-by-line or word-by-word scrutiny producing concepts; (2) *Axial coding*—"intense analysis done around one category at a time in terms of the paradigm items" (Strauss, 1987, p. 32); (3) *Selective coding*—selecting a core category and relating all categories to it. In the third edition (Corbin & Strauss, 2008, 2015), the final stage was renamed "theoretical integration" (Rieger, 2019, Table 2).

**The coding paradigm:** A structured scaffolding of conditions, interaction among the actors, strategies and tactics, consequences—intended to make relations between codes explicit, especially during axial coding (Strauss, 1987, pp. 27–28; Strauss & Corbin, 1990). The conditional/consequential matrix extended this to macro–micro links.

---

## 4. The Three Contested Areas: Direct Comparison

### 4.1 Pre-existing theoretical frameworks in coding

| Glaser (1978) | Strauss & Corbin (1990) |
|---|---|
| Pre-existing frameworks contaminate emergence; the researcher should hold "as few predetermined thoughts as possible" (Glaser & Strauss, 1967; Glaser, 1978). | Researchers may—and should—bring accumulated disciplinary knowledge to coding; an "open mind" does not mean "an empty mind" (Strauss & Corbin, 1998). |
| Literature review is delayed; the only legitimate use of prior theory is *emergent fit*—comparing an emerging category with a pre-existing one and keeping only what fits the data (Glaser, 1978; Wuest, 2000). | Technical literature and disciplinary knowledge can legitimately sensitize the researcher and guide analysis from the start. |
| Coding families are sociological scaffolding deployed **after** open coding, when categories have already emerged (Glaser, 1978, 2005). | The coding paradigm is applied **during** axial coding—mid-analysis—to impose structure on the data. |

Kelle's crucial observation is that Glaser's own commitment to pre-existing coding families is inconsistent with his dismissal of pre-existing frameworks—a point he documents carefully in his *Forum: Qualitative Social Research* review (https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/download/467/1001).

### 4.2 Legitimacy of forcing data into categories

| Glaser (1978, 1992) | Strauss & Corbin (1990) |
|---|---|
| "Emergence vs. forcing" became the title of the 1992 polemic; forcing is the cardinal methodological sin. Theory must be "discovered" via constant comparison alone. | The coding paradigm is explicitly a scaffold to organize messy data; structured coding is necessary to overcome the "common tendency [of novices] simply to take a bit of the data… and translate that into a précis of it" (Strauss, 1987, p. 29). |

Glaser's 1992 letter to Strauss demanded: "your work is fractured and scattered…distorts and misconceives grounded theory, while engaging in a gross neglect of 90% of its important ideas… You wrote a whole different method so why call it 'grounded theory'?" (Glaser, 1992, p. 2, cited in https://nsuworks.nova.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1416&context=tqr). The paradigm model "focuses the researcher on the conditions of the phenomenon, actions/interactions and emotions of participants, and consequences" (Rieger 2018), dictating what kinds of relationships must exist before the data have spoken.

Strauss and Corbin defended their approach: researchers may "inadvertently attempt to place data into a category where it does not analytically belong, but by means of making systematic comparisons, these errors will eventually be located" (Strauss & Corbin, 1990). They also redefined theorizing as construction: "Theorising is the act of constructing… from data an explanatory scheme" and theories are "interpretations made from given perspectives" (Strauss & Corbin 1998, p. 25; quoted in Mills, Bonner & Francis, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/160940690600500103). Kelle's verdict: Glaser "points out some existing weaknesses of STRAUSS' concepts but vastly exaggerates the risks" (https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/download/467/1001).

### 4.3 Verification procedures

| Glaser (1978, 1992) | Strauss & Corbin (1990) |
|---|---|
| Verification belongs to deductive/quantitative paradigms; in GT, constant comparison internally "assumes verification" but the goal is theory generation (Glaser & Strauss, 1967, p. 28). | Hypothesis-testing and verification of emerging theoretical claims are legitimate throughout the analytic process; the conditional matrix, axial coding paradigm, and "waving the red flag" / "flip-flop" techniques are explicitly verificational tools (Strauss & Corbin, 1990). |
| Evaluation criteria: *fit, work, relevance, modifiability* (Glaser, 1978). | Evaluation criteria expanded to seven: fit, applicability, concepts, contextualization of concepts, logic, depth, integration (Corbin & Strauss, 2008, 2015). |

Glaser wrote: "The goal of grounded theory is to generate a conceptual theory that accounts for a pattern of behavior which is relevant and problematic for those involved. The goal is not voluminous description, nor clever verification" (Glaser 1978, p. 93). Strauss (1987) explicitly re-integrated verification: "Induction, deduction, and verification… all three processes go on throughout the life of the research project" (https://staibabussalamsula.ac.id/wp-content/uploads/2024/05/QUALITATIVE-ANALYSIS-staibabussalamsula.ac_.id_.pdf). Strauss and Corbin's canon 9 states: "Hypotheses About Relationships among Categories Should Be Developed and Verified as Much as Possible during the Research Process" (https://studylib.net/doc/28755861/corbinstrauss).

After 1991, the dispute became irretrievable: "the exchange of letters ensued with myself pleading and Anselm saying 'no' to a pulling and correction of Basics of Qualitative Research" (Glaser, 1992, p. 3).

---

## 5. Charmaz's Constructivist Reformulation (2006): Resolution by Epistemological Relocation

Kathy Charmaz, a UCSF doctoral student trained under both Glaser and Strauss, published *Constructing Grounded Theory: A Practical Guide through Qualitative Analysis* (Sage, 2006; 2nd ed. 2014). The book has ~60,209 Google Scholar citations (https://scholar.google.com/scholar_lookup?title=Constructing+Grounded+Theory), roughly 2.5× Glaser's *Theoretical Sensitivity* and far exceeding *Emergence vs. Forcing*, making it the single most cited grounded-theory methodology monograph.

Her resolution operates at three levels:

**Epistemological shift: from objectivist to constructivist.** Charmaz repositioned GT squarely in social constructionism. She argued that the title *The Discovery of Grounded Theory* encodes an assumption she rejects, that data and theory exist "out there" awaiting observation. Her constructivist alternative: "data and theorizing about these data…are constructed, not discovered" (Charmaz, 2017, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1609406917719350). The researcher is "the author of a reconstruction of experience and meaning" (Mills, Bonner & Francis, 2006).

**Bridging the Glaser/Strauss impasse:**

- *Pre-existing theory:* Charmaz keeps Strauss & Corbin's allowance of bringing disciplinary knowledge but frames it as part of the researcher's positional reflexivity, not as a procedural scaffold.
- *Forcing:* She keeps the core Glaserian commitment to emergence but relocates it ontologically; categories "emerge" from the interaction of researcher and participant, not from a mind-independent reality.
- *Verification:* She preserves constant comparison while relocating it under reflexivity: the researcher interrogates "data, nascent analyses, research actions, and themselves each step along the way" (Charmaz, 2017).

**Methodological innovations.** Charmaz introduced *initial* and *focused* coding (replacing open/axial/selective), abolished the axial coding/paradigm machinery that Glaser abhorred (Charmaz, 2006, p. 61), emphasized memowriting and theoretical sampling, and incorporated symbolic interactionism explicitly. She retained GT's pragmatist heritage through Strauss while discarding the positivist residue, situating CGT "in the social constructionist tradition" (Charmaz, 2017).

Critiques persist. Duchscher and Morgan (2004), Evans (2013), and Glaser (2002) view the constructivist turn as an erosion of GT's analytical power (Rieger, 2019).

---

## 6. The Paradigm Wars Context (1990s–2000s)

The Glaser–Strauss–Charmaz dispute mirrors the broader "paradigm wars" in qualitative research. According to the standard periodization (Teddlie & Tashakkori, 2003; Lincoln & Guba, 1985, 1994, 2000, 2005; Denzin & Lincoln, 2011; https://us.sagepub.com/sites/default/files/upm-binaries/51015_ch_1.pdf):

1. **Postpositivist–constructivist war against positivism (1970–1990):** Ended symbolically with Guba's (1990) *The Paradigm Dialog*.
2. **Conflict between competing postpositivist, constructivist, and critical-theory paradigms (1990–2005):** The "handbook wars"—Denzin & Lincoln's *Handbook of Qualitative Research* editions (1994, 2000, 2005, 2011, 2018) became the canonical battlefield. Charmaz (2000) and Bryant & Charmaz (2007a, 2007b, 2007c) explicitly grounded their GT reformulation within this contested terrain.
3. **Evidence-based vs. mixed-methods/interpretive/critical schools (2005–present):** The current phase, marked by politicized disputes over "scientifically based research."

Babchuk's taxonomy makes the alignment explicit: Glaserian GT = positivist/objectivist; Straussian GT = postpositivist; Charmaz = interpretive/constructivist; Clarke's situational analysis = postmodern (https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?httpsredir=1&article=1085&context=dberspeakers). The Bryant & Charmaz *SAGE Handbook of Grounded Theory* (2007) canonized the pluralist settlement by describing GT as a "family of methods" sharing core features while differing epistemologically. By the 2005 Handbook edition, Guba & Lincoln reported that "the number of qualitative texts, research papers, workshops, and training materials has exploded" and that the "legitimacy of postmodern paradigms is well established and at least equal to the legitimacy of received and conventional paradigms" (http://www.iot.ntnu.no/innovation/norsi-common-courses/Lincoln/Guba%20&%20Lincoln%20(2005).pdf)—the intellectual environment in which constructivist GT flourished.

---

## 7. Citation Patterns 2020–2024: Which Position Now Dominates?

The empirical evidence converges on a **discipline-dependent pattern with a clear secular trend toward Charmaz's constructivist version as the epistemological default**, while Straussian procedural vocabulary persists in applied health research.

**Finding 1: Charmaz's constructivist GT dominates nursing, library/information science, and social/health-research methods.** A 2023 review of three high-impact Library and Information Science journals (*Journal of Documentation*, *JASIST*, *Library & Information Science Research*) found that "Charmazian (constructivist) grounded theory approach was the most popular version," with grounded theory used predominantly as "a research design or methodology" employing constant comparative analysis (https://distantreader.org/stacks/journals-ojs/aliseacp/aliseacp-1297.pdf). Multiple 2020–2024 studies in nursing and health research methodology journals cite Charmaz (2006/2014) as their primary methodological reference (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/16094069231186257).

**Finding 2: Straussian GT remains dominant in education and information systems, but is losing ground.** An 18-year review of 210 studies across 15 top education journals (Timmins et al., 2021, https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/16094069211052203) concluded: "While educational researchers appear to prefer Straussian approaches to the design and analysis of grounded theory studies, Charmaz's constructivist approach has increased in popularity over the last decade." Similarly, an IS-field study found that "the Strauss and Corbin version of grounded theory…have found most adherents in the IS discipline" (https://aisel.aisnet.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1960&context=jit).

**Finding 4: Pure Glaserian GT has negligible presence in mainstream methodology journals.** Across disciplines, OpenAlex and Google Scholar both show that *Theoretical Sensitivity* and *Emergence vs. Forcing* are cited overwhelmingly in methodological discussion and historiography of GT, not as primary references for new empirical work.

**Quantitative citation summary (late 2024, approximate):**

| Work | Google Scholar | OpenAlex/other |
|---|---|---|
| Charmaz (2006/2014), *Constructing Grounded Theory* | ~60,209 | ~18,700–29,000 (combined editions) |
| Strauss & Corbin (1990), *Basics of Qualitative Research* (all eds.) | ~14,051 (Scispace) | — |
| Glaser (1978), *Theoretical Sensitivity* | ~24,252 | ~6,120 |
| Glaser (1992), *Emergence vs. Forcing* | ~16,002 | — |

**Synthesis:** Charmaz's constructivist GT now dominates qualitative methodology training programs in nursing, education, library science, sociology, social work, and health-research methodology courses, as evidenced by (a) citation asymmetry in 2020–2024 methodology journals; (b) the explicit findings of the Timmins et al. (2021) 18-year education journal review and the 2023 LIS review; and (c) the institutional embedding of *Constructing Grounded Theory* in third-edition course adoptions (Sage, October 2024, https://uk.sagepub.com/en-gb/hkg/constructing-grounded-theory/book255601). Straussian GT persists as the procedural default in management, IS, and a portion of educational research, while Glaser's classic GT has been largely pushed to the disciplinary margins of the *Grounded Theory Review* and into methodological-historical writing.

---

## 8. Conclusion

The Glaser–Strauss debate of the late 1980s and 1990s was not merely procedural but paradigmatic: it staged the encounter between residual positivism, pragmatist symbolic interactionism, and the emerging constructivist turn. Charmaz's 2006 reformulation effectively absorbed the legitimate concerns of all sides—the Strauss/Corbin acknowledgement that researchers cannot enter the field empty-headed, the Glaserian insistence that data should not be forced into pre-existing categories, and the post-1990s consensus that researchers are not external observers of an objective reality—while relocating the entire enterprise within social constructionism.

The result, judged by 2020–2024 citation patterns in major methodology journals, is the contemporary dominance of constructivist grounded theory in qualitative research training, with Straussian GT holding a substantial but declining procedural foothold in management, IS, and parts of education, and pure Glaserian GT confined to a specialized methodological niche sustained by the Grounded Theory Institute and its journal. The "dual equilibrium" is notable: constructivist epistemology dominates training discourse, while Straussian procedural vocabulary still dominates field practice—particularly in applied nursing and health research, where the citation of Strauss & Corbin (1990) persists even as researchers interpret their practice through a constructivist lens.

# WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II for ADHD in Children Aged 8–12: A Comprehensive Literature Review with Emphasis on Working Memory Sensitivity and Ecological Validity

## 1. Executive Summary

**Bottom-line answers to the clinical questions:**

1. **Working memory sensitivity.** The WISC-V Working Memory Index (WMI) is the more sensitive and construct-valid standardized index for detecting WM deficits in children aged 8–12 with ADHD. The NEPSY-II provides no WM composite; its "WM" coverage is confined to a single verbal subtest (Word List Interference), and the largest NEPSY-II ADHD effect sizes (d ≈ .64–.73) come from vigilance/inhibition tasks (Response Set, Inhibition), not WM tasks. Meta-analytic evidence (Martinussen et al., 2005) shows visuospatial WM deficits are the largest (d = 0.85–1.06) and verbal WM deficits the smallest (d = 0.43–0.47); the WISC-V's Picture Span samples the high-effect modality while NEPSY-II does not.

2. **Ecological validity (EV).** No published head-to-head review by pediatric neuropsychologists comparing the EV of NEPSY-II versus WISC(-V) was located—this absence is itself a reportable research gap. The NEPSY-II enjoys higher *verisimilitude* (classroom-analogous tasks, behavioral observation, contrast/process scores) by design; the WISC-V has stronger reliability, normative precision, and replicated group effects. *Veridicality* (prediction of real-world functioning) is weak for both, with performance-based EF tests correlating only at median r = .19 with real-world ratings (Toplak, West, & Stanovich, 2013).

4. **Clinical recommendation.** Neither instrument is diagnostically sufficient. Best practice combines WISC-V (cognitive-ability/WM profile, exclusionary) with NEPSY-II (EF process analysis), supplemented by behavior ratings (BRIEF-2/Conners 3) and continuous performance tests, consistent with AAP (2019) and NICE NG87 guidelines stating that neuropsychological testing complements but does not replace clinical diagnosis.

---

## 2. Search Strategy

Systematic searches were conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, PsycINFO-indexed outlets (APA, Springer, Wiley, Taylor & Francis, Sage, Cambridge Core, Elsevier/ScienceDirect, Hogrefe), Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex-derived citation services, ERIC, MDPI, Frontiers, and institutional repositories (Antioch, Ball State, Sapienza, UNT, Texas Woman's University). Search strings combined instrument terms ("WISC-V," "WISC-IV," "NEPSY-II") with condition terms ("ADHD"), construct terms ("working memory," "executive function," "sensitivity," "specificity," "ecological validity," "meta-analysis"), and methodological terms ("measurement invariance," "incremental validity"). Prioritized evidence: meta-analyses and systematic reviews; test-standardization clinical validity data; peer-reviewed empirical studies of children approximately 6–16 (emphasis 8–12); and authoritative clinical guidelines. Dissertations and non–peer-reviewed sources were retained only when filling gaps and are flagged as such.

---

## 3. Theoretical Frameworks

Three models structure this literature:

**(i) Executive Function (EF) Deficit Theory.** ADHD symptoms arise from primary deficits in EF—neurocognitive processes maintaining goal-directed problem-solving. Willcutt, Doyle, Nigg, Faraone, & Pennington (2005) demonstrated all 13 EF tasks show significant ADHD–control differences (d = .46–.69), but EF weaknesses are "neither necessary nor sufficient to cause all cases of ADHD" (https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract).

**(ii) Baddeley's Multi-Component WM Model.** Phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive. This licenses the verbal/spatial × storage/central-executive taxonomy used throughout the meta-analytic literature (Martinussen et al., 2005; Kasper et al., 2012).

**(iii) Luria's Functional-Systems Theory.** The NEPSY-II is explicitly grounded in Luria: "assessing a cognitive disorder requires separately assessing all the components that make up a functional system" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8). NEPSY-II's designers argue that factor analysis is *incompatible* with Lurian theory—an important methodological asymmetry: the WISC-V is judged by factor-analytic standards; the NEPSY-II is judged by content/process-validity standards.

**ADHD-specific frameworks:** Barkley's behavioral-inhibition/EF model; Castellanos, Sonuga-Barke, Milham, & Tannock (2006) "beyond executive dysfunction," which cautions that cool-EF deficits are group-level phenomena not universally present (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1364661306000283).

---

## 4. Seminal Papers and Citation Analysis

| Work | Role | Citation count |
|---|---|---|
| Martinussen, Hayden, Hogg-Johnson, & Tannock (2005), *JAACAP* 44(4):377–384 | Field-defining WM meta-analysis (26 studies; 1997–2003); spatial storage d = 0.85, spatial central-executive d = 1.06, verbal storage d = 0.47, verbal central-executive d = 0.43 (https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(09)61489-1/abstract) | Foundational; cited by virtually all subsequent WM–ADHD work |
| Willcutt et al. (2005), *Biological Psychiatry* 57(11):1336–1346 | 83 studies; ADHD N = 3,734, controls N = 2,969; EF effect sizes .46–.69, strongest for response inhibition, vigilance, WM, planning | ~3,000 citations; canonical citation for EF theory of ADHD |
| Kasper, Alderson, & Hudec (2012), *Clinical Psychology Review* 32(7):605–617 | Moderator meta-analysis; large WM effects; significant moderators include % female, trial count, recall vs. recognition, central-executive demands (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979) | Standard citation for WM effect-size moderation |
| Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013), *JCPP* 54(2):131–143 | 20 studies, 286 correlations; only 24% significant; **median r = .19** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/) | The reference point for EV/performance-vs-ratings debate |
| Pievsky & McGrath (2018) | Umbrella review of 34 meta-analyses; WM = .54, inhibition = .52, RT variability = .53–.66 | Highest-level synthesis of ADHD neurocognition |
| Korkman, Kirk, & Kemp (2007), NEPSY-II manual | Primary source for NEPSY-II validity; contains the only published ADHD validity study | Anchor of NEPSY-II literature |
| Brooks, Sherman, & Strauss (2010), *Child Neuropsychology* 16(1):80–101; Davis & Matthews (2010), *J. Psychoeducational Assessment* 28(2):175–182 | Independent test reviews of NEPSY-II; flag structural validity and standardization concerns (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716) | Davis & Matthews: 74 citations |
| Castellanos et al. (2006), *Trends in Cognitive Sciences* 10:117–123 | "Beyond executive dysfunction"; paradigm-shifting corrective | Highly influential theoretical critique |

---

## 5. WISC-V/WISC-IV Evidence in ADHD (Ages 8–12)

### 5.1 Group-level performance and sensitivity for WM

- **German WISC-V study** (n = 103 ADHD vs. matched controls): significantly lower performance on all five indices and FSIQ; **largest effect sizes in Working Memory, Fluid Reasoning, and FSIQ**; WISC-V characterized as "a valid and sensitive instrument" for capturing cognitive deficits in ADHD (https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/pdf/10.1026/0942-5403/a000256).

- **Spanish sample** (N = 188; controls n = 56; ADHD-C n = 57; ADHD-I n = 75; ages 6–16): WMI, PSI, CPI, FSIQ all significantly lower (p < .001 except FSIQ p = .005). Logistic regression: **WMI B = −0.067 (p < .001), PSI B = −0.043 (p = .007), CPI B = −0.091 (p < .001)** predicting ADHD vs. control membership; ADHD-I showed lower WMI than ADHD-C (p = .016) (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42343738/).

- **WISC-V structural/clinical analysis** (n = 241, ages 6–17; *BMC Psychology*, 2026): WMI and PSI significantly lower than reasoning indices with **medium-to-large within-subject effect sizes**; CPI < GAI; but discrepancy patterns are "neither sensitive nor specific enough to serve as diagnostic markers" (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0).

- **WISC-IV study** (N = 719; 363 ADHD): WMI, PSI, CPI significantly lower after covariates; logistic model Nagelkerke R² = 0.44 (https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/9/1279).

- **ADHD+SLD comorbidity** (WISC-V, n = 159): ADHD+SLD group impaired on WMI, PSI, FSIQ, AWMI, CPI versus controls (https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948).

- **German WISC-V MGCFA** (n = 91 ADHD vs. n = 91 controls): only **partial scalar invariance** achieved—intercept non-invariance on Digit Span, Picture Span, Coding, Symbol Search, Vocabulary, and the WM and PS factors; "clinical interpretations based on the WISC-V primary indexes are limited" for ADHD–control comparisons (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/).

- **WISC-IV, ages 7–8, population sample** (n = 865): 22% of children had WM deficits, but only 4% combined WM deficit with behavioral regulation/hyperactivity-inattention problems, and only about one-third of those met inattentive ADHD criteria—**low WMI has poor positive predictive value for ADHD in the general population** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/).

### 5.2 Counterevidence

- **Iranian diagnostic-validity study** (WISC-V, n = 250 ADHD vs. 250 controls, ages 7–9): **only Processing Speed exceeded critical thresholds for diagnostic validity (p < .001); Working Memory, Verbal Comprehension, Visual-Spatial, and Fluid Reasoning subtests failed to distinguish ADHD from controls** (https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf). [Quality concern noted: this paper misattributes WISC-V authorship to "Edith Kaplan, 2015."]

- **Multinomial classification study** (WISC-V, n = 133, ages 6–16, ADHD vs. SLD vs. ADHD+SLD vs. controls): cross-validated classification accuracy = .32, near chance; neither GAI–CPI discrepancy nor intra-individual profile configuration differentiated groups (https://www.peeref.com/works/90867940; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/).

- **Digit Span administration limitation:** Standard WISC Digit Span Backward "failed to predict WM or achievement" in 34 children with ADHD ages 8–13; modified administration (counting all digits correct rather than discontinue rule) substantially improved validity (r = .58 with WM reordering; r = .49 with KTEA-2 achievement) (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/).

### 5.3 Quantitative synthesis

Aggregating across studies, meta-analytic and primary-study effect sizes for ADHD–control differences on the WMI in school-age children cluster around **d = 0.50–0.85**, with digit-span backward alone showing **Hedges' g = 0.56** (95% CI [0.49, 0.64]) across 49 studies, with effect size decreasing by 0.05 for every additional year of age (https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/routledg/clin/2020/00000034/00000005/art00002). Pievsky and McGrath (2018) identify WM as the **second-largest ADHD-related neurocognitive deficit after reaction-time variability** (weighted mean SMD ≈ 0.54) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bkyymp4jqzv).

---

## 6. NEPSY-II Evidence in ADHD (Ages 8–12)

### 6.1 Standardization clinical-group data (primary psychometric source)

The NEPSY-II standardization included ~260 special clinical cases; ADHD n ≈ 51–55 (DSM-IV Combined Type, non-comorbid, IQ > 85). For the ADHD group in the Attention/Executive Functioning domain: significant differences (p < .01 to p < .05) on **over 80% of scores from Auditory Attention and Response Set, Clocks, and Inhibition**, with effect sizes d = .42–.73; largest:

| NEPSY-II score | d |
|---|---|
| **Response Set Total Correct** | **.73** |
| **Response Set Combined** | **.70** |
| **Inhibition–Inhibition Total Completion Time** | **.64** |
| Inhibition Combined | .58 |
| Auditory Attention Combined | .54 |
| Auditory Attention Total Correct | .46 |
| Animal Sorting Combined | .32 |

Sources: manual excerpts (https://studfile.net/preview/21682932/page:20/); Brooks, Sherman, & Strauss (2010) review (https://www.scribd.com/document/1021058334/BrooksShermanandStrauss-NEPSY-IITestReviewforChildNeuropsychology). **These are small-to-moderate effects by Cohen's conventions—sensitive at group level, but far below thresholds for individual diagnostic classification.**

### 6.2 Independent empirical studies

- **MDPI *Children* (2025; n = 48, ages 8–15; ADHD vs. anxiety vs. comorbid; WISC-IV + NEPSY-II):** **no significant group differences in attention or working memory**; differences emerged only on inhibition (children with ADHD took longer to inhibit automatic responses) (https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1741790; https://www.mdpi.com/2227-9067/12/6/798).

- **Sjop (2024): ADHD vs. SLD** (n = 72, ages 5–15; WISC-IV + NEPSY-II): ADHD group significantly more impaired than SLD on NEPSY-II inhibition, cognitive flexibility, short-term verbal memory, and **verbal working memory**, and on WISC-IV FSIQ (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/sjop.12562).

- **Cardinal Scholar (2015):** In clinically-referred children, canonical correlations between WISC-IV composites and NEPSY-II Inhibition were mostly non-significant—evidence that WMI/PSI–EF coupling is weaker in clinical samples than healthy samples. However, WISC-IV WM and PS tasks were significantly related to NEPSY-II Inhibition-Naming and Inhibition-Switching Combined scores (https://cardinalscholar.bsu.edu/items/1393f480-5723-49c0-b220-23237bd85e25).

- **Brazilian validation** (n = 30 ADHD, ages 6–14): significant impairments across NEPSY-II subtests (https://repositorio.unifesp.br/items/3a3d79b2-848b-487d-aef6-4317f2270bb5/full).

- **CFA of norming sample** (N = 600, ages 7–12): best model = general factor + four first-order factors; general-factor loadings mostly < .50 (M = .44); domain-specific effects lower; **strong subtest-specific variance of unclear meaning** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38873994/). The NEPSY-II has "no domain scores" by design: "Domain scores are not derived in the NEPSY-II due to these psychometric issues and the clinical sensitivity and utility of the individual subtest scores" (Pearson manual, https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf).

### 6.3 Structural limitation for WM assessment

NEPSY-II's Attention/EF domain contains **no subtest designed to measure working memory storage/manipulation directly**; WM is engaged incidentally (e.g., Response Set requires holding rules online), and the Memory & Learning domain targets episodic memory (Memory for Designs/Faces, Word List Interference), not Baddeley-style WM. This is why studies seeking WM assessment pair NEPSY-II with a Wechsler scale. For ages 8–12, Statue (a strong preschool ADHD indicator) is not normed, further narrowing the battery's ADHD-relevant span.

---

## 7. Direct Head-to-Head Comparison: Effect-Size Benchmarking

The single most pertinent direct comparison is **Newberry, K. E. (2025). *Pay Attention! A Comparative Analysis of Psychological Assessments and Neurological Mechanisms for ADHD Within a Pediatric Population* (Doctoral dissertation, Antioch University Seattle; PsyD)** (https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/; https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=antioch1744236100254081&disposition=inline).

- **Sample:** 272 children aged 8–16; grouped by ADHD subtype.
- **Measures:** WISC-V (GAI, CPI, VSI, WMI, PSI), NEPSY-II (Animal Sorting, Auditory Attention, Response Set, Inhibition, Word Generation), Conners CPT-3, CATA.
- **Findings:** Lower CPI and lower NEPSY-II Animal Sorting and Response Set scores predicted ADHD diagnosis; **WISC-V WMI in isolation was not a robust predictor**; NEPSY-II contributed incremental validity beyond WISC-V.
- **Author's conclusion (verbatim):** "These results support using NEPSY-II, CATA, and CPT-3 for targeted, efficient ADHD assessments over traditional tools like the WISC-V."

**Critical caveats:** (i) This is a PsyD dissertation, not a peer-reviewed publication; (ii) the sample age range is 8–16, extending beyond the requested 8–12 band; (iii) archival, cross-sectional design; (iv) no ROC/sensitivity–specificity analyses; (v) the conclusion that NEPSY-II "outperforms" WISC-V for diagnostic prediction is not warranted by a single binary logistic regression without cross-validation or head-to-head metric comparison.

**Effect-size benchmarking** (computing common-language effect size, CL = Φ(d/√2), the probability that a randomly selected ADHD child scores below the median control):

| Source / Measure | d | CL |
|---|---|---|
| Spatial central-executive WM (Martinussen 2005) | 1.06 | 0.77 |
| Spatial storage WM (Martinussen 2005) | 0.85 | 0.73 |
| NEPSY-II Response Set Total Correct | 0.73 | 0.70 |
| NEPSY-II Inhibition time | 0.64 | 0.67 |
| Willcutt 2005 mean EF | 0.54 | 0.65 |
| Verbal storage WM (Martinussen 2005) | 0.47 | 0.63 |
| Verbal central-executive WM (Martinussen 2005) | 0.43 | 0.62 |

**Key inference:** The largest available NEPSY-II ADHD effects (d ≈ .64–.73) are on Response Set—a task blending sustained attention, set-shifting, inhibition, and WM—not on pure WM. The modality with the largest meta-analytic deficit is *visuospatial* WM (d ≈ 0.85–1.06); the WISC-V WMI samples this via Picture Span while NEPSY-II provides no visuospatial WM subtest for ages 8–12. This is a **structural sensitivity advantage for the WISC-V**.

---

## 8. Ecological Validity

### 8.1 Conceptual foundations

A 2024 *Journal of the International Neuropsychological Society* systematic review found that of 90+ EF EV studies, only 28% (28 studies) provided a formal EV definition; the term conflates **veridicality** (criterion validity, prediction of real-world behavior) with **verisimilitude** (face validity, similarity to real-world tasks). The authors call for replacement with concrete terminology (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0). A 2023 systematized review (82 studies) operationalizes EV along **representativeness** (artificial↔natural, simple↔complex) and **generalization** dimensions (https://recipp.ipp.pt/server/api/core/bitstreams/38c55a7c-8c8e-4791-aa12-40892605f885/content).

### 8.2 NEPSY-II vs. WISC on EV

**No published review directly compares the EV of NEPSY-II versus WISC(-V)**—this is a documented research gap.

**NEPSY-II's EV claims (verisimilitude side):** Independent reviews (Davis & Matthews, 2010; Brooks, Sherman, & Strauss, 2010) highlight features associated with ecological relevance: Luria-based **process/qualitative observation**, **behavioral-observation base rates** (e.g., out-of-seat behavior, asking for repetition), **contrast and process scores**, **flexible administration order**, and classroom-analogous tasks (sustained auditory attention, inhibitory control, motor persistence). Reviewers flag modest reliability for some subtests (internal consistency α = .21–.91; test–retest "generally adequate"), which caps veridicality (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716; https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ879056).

**WISC-V's EV claims (veridicality side):** The publisher documents correlations between WISC-V scores in the ADHD special group and real-world behavior rating scales (BASC-2, Brown ADD) and adaptive functioning (Vineland-II in ID samples), explicitly framed as ecological-validity evidence (https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/wisc-v/wisc-v-tech-manual-supplement.pdf). WMI/PSI deficits map plausibly onto classroom functioning, but the test itself is maximally structured and decontextualized—low verisimilitude by design.

**The decisive cross-cutting finding:** Toplak, West, & Stanovich (2013) found performance-based EF measures correlate with real-world EF ratings at only **median r = .19** (24% of 286 correlations significant), concluding that the two methods capture different constructs ("efficiency of cognitive abilities" vs. "success in goal pursuit") and that neither proxies the other in ADHD assessment. In children with ADHD specifically, BRIEF parent ratings discriminated ADHD from controls better than performance measures, and BRIEF indices were essentially uncorrelated with performance-based EF (Gioia et al., 2002). Yet a 2020 study of 136 children (ages 8–13) found performance tests showed higher cross-method predictive validity for academic achievement than ratings, with both contributing unique variance (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7483691/).

**Pediatric-specific EV conclusion:** Reviews (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330) find child EV research lags the adult literature substantially and issues a research agenda rather than endorsing any battery.

**Synthesis:** NEPSY-II has an edge in **verisimilitude and process-oriented behavioral observation**; WISC-V has better-documented criterion correlations and psychometric rigor. Neither has demonstrated strong prediction beyond rating scales. Any publication should use dimensional (verisimilitude vs. veridicality) rather than categorical claims.

---

## 9. Methodological Rigor of Key Studies

| Study | Design/N | Strengths | Limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| Martinussen et al. (2005) | Meta-analysis, 26 studies | Component-wise WM decomposition; independence from IQ/LD | Dated (1997–2003); included preschool and adult samples |
| Willcutt et al. (2005) | Meta-analysis, 83 studies, N ≈ 6,703 | Largest aggregate; moderator analyses | Task heterogeneity; not diagnostic-level |
| Pievsky & McGrath (2018) | Umbrella review, 34 meta-analyses, 253 SMDs | Highest-level synthesis | Cannot resolve test-level sensitivity |
| NEPSY-II manual ADHD validity study | Matched case-control, n ≈ 55 | Demographically matched; effect sizes reported | Small n; DSM-IV; IQ > 85; **comorbidity excluded** (atypical); not peer-reviewed |
| BMC Psychology (2026) | WISC-V CFA + discrepancy, n = 241 | Model-fit rigor; explicit sensitivity/specificity framing | Single-country clinical sample |
| German WISC-V invariance study (PubMed 38248904) | MGCFA, n = 91 + 91 | Tests validity of index comparisons | **Partial scalar invariance only**—undermines naive index comparisons |
| MDPI *Children* (2025; n = 48) | WISC-IV + NEPSY-II differential diagnosis | Anxiety comparator | Very small n; WM null may reflect power |
| Newberry (2025) dissertation | Archival, n = 272, ages 8–16 | Only direct WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II multivariate comparison | **Unpublished dissertation**; no ROC/AUC; age range extends past 12 |

Common methodological concerns: (a) most studies cross-sectional; (b) clinic-referred samples with elevated base rates of comorbidity; (c) the Newberry dissertation is the only direct comparison; (d) measurement invariance of the WISC-V in ADHD is partial; (e) the NEPSY-II ADHD validity sample is small and non-comorbid, limiting generalizability.

---

## 10. Conflicting Evidence Requiring Synthesis

1. **WMI sensitivity:** German (n = 103) and Spanish (n = 188) studies → WMI robustly lower and predictive; Iranian diagnostic-validity study → WMI **failed** to discriminate, only PSI did. **Synthesis:** Group-level sensitivity does not entail individual-level diagnostic utility; sample composition (comorbidity, subtype mix), analytic approach, and possible measurement non-invariance drive discrepancies. Cross-validated classification is near chance.

2. **NEPSY-II WM signal:** 2025 MDPI study found no WM/attention differences but an inhibition difference; standardization data show moderate attention/inhibition effects. **Synthesis:** Small clinical samples + NEPSY-II's lack of direct WM measurement → attenuated WM signal; inhibition is the more reliable NEPSY-II ADHD marker.

3. **Performance tests vs. ratings:** Toplak 2013 (median r = .19); Toplak 2008 (ratings, not tests, predicted ADHD status); but a 2020 study showed performance tests predicted academic achievement better than ratings. **Synthesis:** The two assess different levels of functioning; both are needed.

4. **EF deficits: necessary vs. contributory:** Willcutt 2005 (deficits significant, d = .46–.69, but not universal) vs. clinical lore of EF as ADHD's core. Castellanos 2006 resolves: group-level cool-EF deficits coexist with substantial heterogeneity; hot-EF and motivational pathways matter for real-world outcomes.

5. **Diagnostic utility overall:** Publisher/instrument literature emphasizes clinical sensitivity; AAP (2019) and NICE NG87 guidelines state neuropsychological testing does not improve diagnostic accuracy (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7067282/; https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87/chapter/Recommendations/). **Synthesis:** Both correct at different levels—tests profile associated deficits; diagnosis remains clinical, multi-method, multi-informant.

---

## 11. Research Gaps (Prioritized)

1. **No peer-reviewed, adequately powered head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy trial** of WISC-V vs. NEPSY-II for ADHD classification in 8–12-year-olds with ROC/AUC and sensitivity–specificity endpoints. The only direct multivariate comparison is Newberry (2025), an unpublished dissertation.

2. **Near-absence of pediatric veridicality studies:** prospective prediction of academic/functional outcomes from NEPSY-II vs. WISC-V scores in ADHD (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330).

3. **Terminological standardization of "ecological validity"** (JINS 2024 call to action).

4. **Measurement invariance** of both batteries across ADHD/control groups is rarely tested before index-level comparisons; existing WISC-V evidence shows violations.

5. **NEPSY-II lacks a WM composite**—a structural gap limiting standalone use for WM-deficit referral questions. Additionally, the NEPSY-II revision removed Tower (a planning measure)—precisely the domain Willcutt found among the strongest ADHD effects.

6. **Structural validity of NEPSY-II** domains (CFA/EFA/network) remains unsettled; the manual's six-domain structure is partially recoverable only at ages 7–12, and Social Perception is not reliably located.

7. **Subtype and sex moderation** (Kasper 2012 found % female moderates WM effect sizes) is under-analyzed at the instrument level.

8. **Cross-cultural validity is poorly characterized** for both instruments; Iranian diagnostic-validity studies (Brieflands 2025; Maherpub 2025) raise questions about generalization beyond Western populations. Several non-English validation studies (Spanish, German, Portuguese) exist but were not accessed in full text.

9. **Comorbidity moderation** (ADHD+SLD, ADHD+anxiety) differential-diagnosis sensitivity is only beginning to be addressed (MDPI 2025; Sustainability 2021; Sjop 2024).

10. **Treatment-prediction validity is unstudied**—no identified study has compared whether WISC-V WMI or NEPSY-II Animal Sorting/Response Set scores predict response to behavioral, pharmacological, or cognitive-training interventions.

---

## 12. Recommendations for Clinical Practice and Publication

**For clinical assessment (ages 8–12):**
1. **WM-deficit referral:** Use WISC-V WMI (Digit Span + Picture Span), supplemented by AWMI; interpret Digit Span Backward and Picture Span as most ADHD-sensitive (manipulation and visuospatial; "good holders, bad shufflers" pattern: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/abs/good-holders-bad-shufflers). Evidence-based expectation: medium-to-large group differences, but never use WMI alone diagnostically.
2. **Inhibitory/vigilance profile with behavioral observation:** Use NEPSY-II Auditory Attention and Response Set, Inhibition, Clocks, Animal Sorting, Design Fluency (all normed for 8–12). Standardization effect sizes: d ≈ .42–.73.
3. **Best practice for comprehensive ADHD work-up:** WISC-V + NEPSY-II are *complementary*; add BRIEF-2/Conners 3 ratings, CPT-3, and DSM-5-based clinical evaluation. Neither instrument is diagnostic alone.

**For a peer-reviewed publication:**
1. Treat WISC-V WMI as a **profile and exclusionary tool**, not a diagnostic marker.
2. Use NEPSY-II Attention/EF subtests as the **process-level EF screen**, with WISC-V providing the cognitive-ability frame.
3. Report subtest-level data, not just index scores, to capture modality-specific deficits.
4. Use modified Digit Span Backward scoring (count all digits correct) per Kofler/Wells until publishers update standard procedures.
5. Define "ecological validity" operationally (Pinto et al. 2023 framework; JINS 2024); distinguish verisimilitude from veridicality.
6. Frame claims dimensionally with effect sizes rather than categorical "sensitivity," given absence of ROC data.
7. Acknowledge the Newberry dissertation's evidentiary limits in any comparative claim.

---

## 13. Limitations of This Review

This is a rapid evidence synthesis rather than a registered PRISMA systematic review. Full-text access was restricted for several paywalled primary sources (WISC-V Technical Manual Supplement, *Biological Psychiatry* 2005, *Clinical Psychology Review* 2012, *Assessment* 2023 review). Several key studies are recent (2024–2026) and await replication. The pooled sensitivity comparisons necessarily bridge experimental-task meta-analyses with clinical-index studies—an acknowledged inferential step. Cross-cultural literature is incompletely covered; no Spanish, German, or Portuguese NEPSY-II validation studies beyond cursory mention were retrieved in full text.

---

## Key Sources (Selected)

- Newberry (2025) dissertation: https://aura.antioch.edu/etds/1127/ ; https://etd.ohiolink.edu/acprod/odb_etd/ws/send_file/send?accession=antioch1744236100254081&disposition=inline
- WISC-V ADHD: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40359-026-05191-0 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42343738/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38248904/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42501447/ ; https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/13/17/9948 ; https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/15/9/1279 ; https://brieflands.com/journals/ijpbs/articles/153741.pdf ; https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/pdf/10.1026/0942-5403/a000256
- WISC-IV/ADHD population: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36780371/
- NEPSY-II: https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1741790 ; https://cardinalscholar.bsu.edu/items/1393f480-5723-49c0-b220-23237bd85e25 ; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40817-024-00158-8 ; https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0734282909346716 ; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/09297040903146966 ; https://studfile.net/preview/21682932/page:20/ ; https://www.scribd.com/document/1021058334/BrooksShermanandStrauss-NEPSY-IITestReviewforChildNeuropsychology ; https://www.pearsonassessments.com/content/dam/school/global/clinical/us/assets/nepsy-ii/nepsy-ii-design-and-purpose.pdf
- Digit Span Backward / WM: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5743590/ ; https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/abs/good-holders-bad-shufflers
- Meta-analyses: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0272735812000979 ; https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(09)61489-1/abstract ; https://www.biologicalpsychiatryjournal.com/article/S0006-3223(05)00171-X/abstract ; https://exa.ai/library/publication/bkyymp4jqzv
- Ecological validity: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-the-international-neuropsychological-society/article/conceptualization-of-the-term-ecological-validity-in-neuropsychological-research-on-executive-function-assessment/01C595F6F8931798F9053A0628260BA0 ; https://recipp.ipp.pt/server/api/core/bitstreams/38c55a7c-8c8e-4791-aa12-40892605f885/content ; https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/21622965.2012.686330 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23057693/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7483691/

# How to Become a Nail Tech in PA: Your Step-by-Step Guide

**Title tag (56 characters):** How to Become a Nail Tech in PA: 2026 Step-by-Step Guide

**Meta description (143 characters):** Learn how to become a nail tech in PA: 200 training hours, exam steps, costs, salary outlook, and PA cosmetology board requirements explained simply.

**URL slug:** /how-to-become-a-nail-tech-pa

---

## Introduction

If you're researching how to become a nail tech in PA, here's some encouraging news: Pennsylvania makes it faster and more affordable than almost any other licensed beauty career. You only need 200 hours of nail tech training at a licensed school, a 10th-grade education, and a passing score on the state exam to earn your nail technician license PA. Most students finish school in two to four months, take the exam, and start earning tips within a single season. Whether you're a recent grad, a parent re-entering the workforce, or switching careers, this guide walks you through every step, from day one of school to your first paying client. For a broader view of beauty career paths before you commit, browse these [career resources](https://insightcortex.com/career-resources). Let's get started.

![Pennsylvania nail technician working on client nails in salon](pa-nail-tech-station.jpg)

## Nail Tech Training Pennsylvania: What You'll Actually Learn

Your first big step in figuring out how to become a nail tech in PA is picking an approved school. The Pennsylvania State Board of Cosmetology requires your 200 hours to come from a state-licensed cosmetology school, with hours spread over at least one month (49 Pa. Code § 7.129). The curriculum breaks down into four blocks: professional practices (25 hours), sciences (75 hours), nail treatments (75 hours), and pedicuring (25 hours). Expect theory and hands-on practice in:

- Manicures, pedicures, and hand and foot massage
- Artificial nail application (tips, acrylics, gels, sculptured forms)
- Nail art, color theory, and design
- Sanitation, sterilization, and Pennsylvania state law
- Nail anatomy, skin conditions, and product chemistry
- E-file operation and safety

Approved programs run at private cosmetology schools, community colleges, and dedicated nail academies in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Harrisburg, Allentown, Lancaster, and Erie. Many offer day, evening, and weekend tracks. Full-time students finish in 6 to 10 weeks; part-timers take 4 to 6 months. Tuition runs roughly $2,800 to $5,600, with most programs near $5,500 once you add kits and fees.

![Nail tech student practicing manicure techniques at a Pennsylvania cosmetology school](nail-tech-training-pa-school.jpg)

## Nail Technician License PA: Licensing Requirements

Once your hours are done, the next step is passing the state exam and applying through the Pennsylvania Licensing System (PALS). Here are the PA cosmetology board requirements, in order.

### Step 1: Confirm Eligibility

You must be at least 16 years old with a 10th-grade education or equivalent. The education rule is waived if you are 35 or older or a military veteran (49 Pa. Code § 7.32f).

### Step 2: Apply Through PALS

Create an account at [pals.pa.gov](https://pals.pa.gov), select the State Board of Cosmetology, and choose the nail technician application. Upload your transcript, notarized school affidavit, ID, and a Criminal History Records Check for any state where you lived in the past five years. Pay the $26 application fee.

### Step 3: Pass the Theory Exam

Pennsylvania lets you sit for the exam after just 150 hours, then finish the remaining 50 while your results process. Register through Pearson VUE and pay the $93 exam fee. The test is computer-based and multiple choice: 75 questions (60 scored plus 15 unscored pretest items), 1 hour and 45 minutes, with a scaled passing score of 75. Since November 25, 2014, the exam is theory only, covering sanitation, nail anatomy, Pennsylvania law, and procedures. There's no separate practical portion.

### Step 4: Get Your Wall License

Once you pass and your school certifies all 200 hours, the Board issues your nail technician license PA. You're legal to work in any licensed PA salon. For the full official breakdown, visit the [Pennsylvania State Board of Cosmetology nail technician licensure requirements page](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/dos/department-and-offices/bpoa/boards-commissions/cosmetology/nail-technician-licensure-snapshot).

### Renewing

Your license renews every two years for $97, with no continuing education requirement. Renewals are due by January 31 of even-numbered years, so keep your PALS contact info current.

## Costs & Timeline: What to Budget

Wondering how to become a nail tech in PA without breaking the bank? Here's a realistic budget:

- Tuition (200-hour program): $2,800 to $5,600
- Professional nail kit: $300 to $1,100 (often included)
- State application fee: $26
- Theory exam fee: $93
- Textbooks and uniforms: $200 to $400
- Total all-in: $3,000 to $7,000

Timeline: training takes 2 to 6 months, application processing 3 to 10 business days, exam scheduling 2 to 4 weeks, and license issued a few days after passing. Most students go from day one of school to a working license in 3 to 6 months.

![Licensed nail technician displaying finished gel nail art design on client in PA salon](pa-nail-tech-gel-art.jpg)

## Career Outlook: What You Can Earn in PA

Pennsylvania's beauty industry is steady and growing, and nail techs are in real demand. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 7% job growth for manicurists and pedicurists from 2024 to 2034, much faster than the average occupation, with about 1,100 job openings per year statewide. Here is what the latest figures show:

- PA median annual wage: $27,990 (BLS via O*NET)
- Entry-level (10th percentile): $20,520
- Top earners (90th percentile): $43,890
- Philadelphia-area techs: ~$31,200 median

Tips add 15 to 30% on top, and commission or booth-rental models let experienced techs scale past six figures in busy urban salons. Your license covers nail services only, so adding hair or skincare later requires a separate cosmetology license.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Q: How long does it take to become a nail tech in PA?**
Most students finish a 200-hour program in 6 to 10 weeks full-time or 4 to 6 months part-time. Add 2 to 4 weeks for the state exam, and you can usually go from day one of school to a working license in 3 to 6 months. State rules require your hours to span at least one month.

**Q: How much does nail tech school cost in Pennsylvania?**
Tuition for an approved 200-hour program runs $2,800 to $5,600. Greater Johnstown Career & Technology Center sits near $2,800; Paul Mitchell Monroeville totals about $5,554 including kits and exam fees. All-in, most students spend $3,000 to $7,000.

**Q: Do I need a high school diploma to get a PA nail tech license?**
You need a 10th-grade education or its equivalent. The rule is waived for applicants 35 or older, or military veterans. Most schools ask for proof during enrollment, so bring a transcript, GED certificate, or another accepted document before you start.

**Q: Can I take the exam before finishing all 200 hours?**
Yes. Pennsylvania allows early testing once you've completed 150 hours. You still must complete all 200 hours, and your school must certify your training, before the state issues your license, but early testing can shave weeks off your timeline.

**Q: Can I transfer an out-of-state nail tech license to Pennsylvania?**
Yes, through reciprocity. You'll need proof of at least two years of licensed work experience in your current state, plus an $89 application fee. Note that Pennsylvania has no reciprocity with Alabama, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, or West Virginia, so check the board's list first.

**Q: Do I need a license to do nails at home in PA?**
Yes. Anywhere you get paid for nail services, even a home studio, counts as a salon and must be licensed by the Board. Working without a license risks fines, so check the salon licensure rules before you take your first paying client.

**Q: How much do nail technicians earn in Pennsylvania?**
Per the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the median annual wage for manicurists and pedicurists in Pennsylvania is $27,990. Entry-level techs start around $20,520, while the top 10 percent earn $43,890 or more. Tips, commissions, and booth rental can raise income significantly.

**Q: Is there a continuing education requirement for PA nail techs?**
No. Pennsylvania does not require continuing education hours to renew a nail technician license. You must renew every two years for $97 by January 31 of even-numbered years and keep your contact info current in PALS so renewal notices reach you on time.

## Conclusion

Figuring out how to become a nail tech in PA is simpler than most expect. Complete 200 hours at a licensed school, pass the Pearson VUE theory exam, and apply through PALS, and you're officially a licensed nail technician in one of the country's most affordable beauty careers. With median wages near $28,000, room to grow past $43,000, and a 7% job-growth outlook through 2034, Pennsylvania is a strong market. Pick your school, book a tour this week, and start building a career you enjoy.
