# Designing Collaborative Learning Interfaces for Secondary Students in South Korea, Finland, and Mexico

## 1. Cultural Baseline: Hofstede Dimension Scores

| Dimension | South Korea | Finland | Mexico |
|---|---|---|---|
| Power Distance (PDI) | 60 | 33 | 81 |
| Individualism (IDV) | 18 | 63 | 30 |
| Masculinity (MAS) | 39 | 26 | 69 |
| Uncertainty Avoidance (UAI) | 85 | 59 | 82 |
| Long-Term Orientation | 100 | 38 | 24 |
| Indulgence (IVR) | 29 | 57 | 97 |

Sources: Korea PDI 60, IDV 18, MAS 39, UAI 85 (https://www.internationalbusinesscenter.org/geert-hofstede/hofstede_south_korea.shtml); Mexico PDI 81, IDV 30 (https://www.internationalbusinesscenter.org/geert-hofstede/hofstede_mexico.shtml); Finland PDI 33, IDV 63 (https://classwrites.com/cultural-dimensions-analysis-tool/mexico, https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/bitstreams/881d70fc-586a-4f90-9952-19facacd774c/download).

Key quantitative gaps: PDI spread = 48 points (Mexico 81 vs Finland 33). Mexico/Finland PDI ratio = 2.45×; Korea/Finland PDI ratio = 1.82×; Mexico/Korea PDI ratio = 1.35×. Korea's closest Hofstede correlate is El Salvador (PDI 66, IDV 19), not any Western European country (https://www.internationalbusinesscenter.org/geert-hofstede/hofstede_south_korea.shtml). Korea and Mexico share collectivist lean (IDV 18 vs 30), but diverge on Indulgence (29 vs 97, a 68-point spread) and Masculinity (39 vs 69), predicting that even though both are high-PDI, their interactional texture differs: Korea is restrained, Mexico is warmly expressive.

**Cross-cultural caveat**: A 12-school (six Finnish, six Korean) comparison found that student agency is "intensively constrained" in both countries (https://www.utupub.fi/items/843415d1-e9d7-4393-9fe8-a57a5e2325f7; *Education Inquiry* 12(1):54–72, doi:10.1080/20004508.2020.1744350). Finnish students paradoxically "do not welcome increasing their agency" through student-oriented lessons. This warns against assuming naïve low-PDI freedoms for Finnish students.

PISA-based multilevel evidence confirms that power distance (not collectivism) predicts lower school belonging in 31–41 countries, mediated by student–teacher relationship quality (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2017.00056/full; https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12144-023-05280-y). Teacher-presence features are a lever on belonging everywhere, but calibration differs by PDI.

---

## 2. Documented Platform Implementations

### 2.1 Classting (South Korea)

Scale: 8.9–9 million cumulative users, 400,000+ teachers, 1 million+ classes, 95–98% Korean school market share (https://business.classting.com/; http://www.businessreport.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=46940; https://blog.classting.com/news-etnews-230419/). Classting AI is deployed in 4,600+ schools, with AI-adopting schools growing 4.86× year-over-year (https://www.classting.com/).

**Engagement metrics (university deployments):**
- **Ulsan University:** posts +4×; Q&A activity +2×; learning-material utilization +37.4 percentage points; AI teaching assistant response rate 96.8% (https://www.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2025042813260545377).
- **Baewha Women's University:** AI response rate ~90%; student-initiated posts = 84.4% (https://www.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2025042813260545377).

**Documented secondary-school empirical findings:**
- 40 sixth-graders (Icheon, 6 weeks): cooperative learning with SNS reflection produced higher academic achievement vs. control (https://sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877042813037877/pdf).
- 19 fifth-graders (8 weeks Classting vs. textbook): significant gains in "exchanging feedback" and "correcting errors," plus self-directed writing, interest, confidence (https://kci.go.kr ART002000065). Affective-domain gain was not statistically significant — a learning gain without emotional-affinity gain consistent with collectivist restraint.
- 23 experimental vs. 22 control (8 PBL sessions): achievement gains strong; no effect on subject interest (https://dbpia.co.kr/journal/detail?nodeId=T13519745).

**Interaction patterns:**
- **Teacher-gated structure.** Only class administrators can distribute AI assessments; teacher dashboard shows per-student progress, right/wrong item detail, and class comparisons (https://www.classting.com/features/data-driven-instruction).
- **Classting feature: "선생님만 보이게 글쓰기"** (writing visible only to the teacher) is documented as a core primitive that gives students a private channel to surface confusion to authority without losing face (https://resources.classting.com/8c906f75-8267-4bc5-a406-cadfa99ed9e5).
- **Private error management.** The "오답 보관함" (wrong-answer notebook) is private by default with immediate explanations; teachers can broker selective sharing for "같이 배움" (learning together) (https://www.classting.com/features/self-directed-learning).
- **Peer-first, teacher-second feedback ordering.** Documented teacher case studies intentionally group peer-feedback givers and receivers, with peer teaching ("또래 교수법") as the first feedback layer before teacher feedback (https://blog.classting.com/ai-courseware-routine/).
- **Gamified collective competition.** "Quiz Battle" plus class-level/national learning rankings rather than individual error exposure — channeling competition through effort/quantity metrics (https://blog.classting.com/ai-learning-2023-july-01/).
- **AI as face-saving intermediary.** The CLST knowledge-tracing engine reports up to 91.5% correctness prediction; the platform processes 100M+ learning data points/day (https://www.classting.com/features/self-directed-learning).
- **Anonymity + empathy button study (Seoul engineering students, AECT 2023):** Anonymous-vs-real-name question posting combined with a "저도 궁금해요" ("I'm wondering too") empathy reaction button raised class satisfaction and induced active questioning from introverted students, raising academic self-efficacy. The empathy button lets students piggyback on others' questions without individual exposure (https://aitimes.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=29369).
- **Real-time teacher monitoring.** Teachers can see on-task status during AI assessments, send participation nudges, and organize 모둠 (small groups) (https://blog.classting.com/product-update-2506/).
- **3-step hint scaffold.** Three-step hint system delivers the first two hints before the third — a scaffolded rather than direct-answer model (https://aidt.classting.com/).

### 2.2 Wilma (Finland)

Scale: 2 million+ users, 300,000+ messages per week, used in 95%+ of Finnish primary and secondary schools since 2001 (https://www.visma.com/newsroom/wilma-tayttaa-25-vuotta-vakiintunut-osa-suomalaista-kouluarkea; https://ijoc.org/index.php/ijoc/article/download/11357/2878).

**Wilma is not a collaborative learning platform.** Its feature set is administrative: per-learner grade entries, private teacher–student–guardian messaging, absence handling, support-need records (https://wilma.fi/opettajalle/; https://omnia.fi/en/systems-and-applications/wilma-en/; https://www.hel.fi/). Peer-to-peer interaction is structurally absent.

**Documented research findings:**
- A survey of 558 parents (32.6% with special-support children) found Wilma perceived as "a good technical tool, but an ambiguous pedagogical tool that lacked common practices." Pupils receiving special support got more daily Wilma markings than chance predicted (https://noredstudies.org/index.php/nse/article/view/6972).
- Qualitative research on Finnish high schools (https://ijoc.org/index.php/ijoc/article/view/11357) found Wilma formalizes and renders traceable work processes that were previously informal; enables "faster and more colloquial communication" but intensifies day-to-day work for teachers; advances a "normalization of surveillance practices" because all messages, grades, and attendance entries are timestamped and archived.
- Uitto & Lutovac (2024) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0742051X24003238) found Wilma disrupts teachers' "stories-to-live-by" in their relationship with parents — the mediated channel changes the relational contract.
- Anu Alanko (University of Oulu) flagged a critical gap: no national, municipal, or school-level rules govern Wilma usage; "feedback given via Wilma can in the worst case damage a student's trust, motivation, or self-belief" because students treat Wilma lesson notes as a mirror of their learning identity (https://www.larorikt.fi/eleverna-far-inte-likvardig-aterkoppling-i-wilma-forskare-efterlyser-riktlinjer/).
- A 2019 MA thesis (https://jyx.jyu.fi/jyx/Record/jyx_123456789_66974/Details) found most-used features were quick messages, lesson notes, tests, and assessment; the most-requested improvement was a better mobile app — not new peer features.
- Ketonen's dissertation (JYU) found that Finnish lower-secondary students are "unequally challenged" by peer assessment and that "judging others' work was difficult for some students regardless of the egalitarian culture" — agency gates peer critique, not only power distance (https://jyx.jyu.fi/bitstreams/aea465f4-8ed5-4f46-80c7-0b8341e54f19/download).

### 2.3 Google Classroom in Latin America / Mexico

Adoption scaled massively during COVID-19: Google Classroom doubled to 100M+ users globally in the first pandemic month, reaching 150M by early 2021 (https://9to5google.com/2020/04/09/google-classroom-meet-integration/; https://iblnews.org/story/google-classroom-adds-40-million-users-and-includes-new-mobile-features). Mejoredu data show 65.5% of Mexican students used Google for Education during the pandemic; only 50% of secondary students had computer access (https://revistasincronia.cucsh.udg.mx/index.php/sincronia/article/download/432/626).

**Documented Mexican deployments:**
- **Baja California** was the first Mexican state to adopt Google for Education. Initially only 3% of teachers used it daily; after sustained training, in March 2025 it became the first state to purchase Education Plus licenses — now 162,000+ students across 480 public secondary schools with 175,000+ licenses (https://blog.google/intl/es-419/actualizaciones-de-producto/informacion/nueva-era-en-la-ensenanza-google-for-education-mexico/).
- **Jalisco**: 45,000 teacher Chromebooks (>90% of teachers), 32,000 student Chromebooks, 1.3 million students able to work simultaneously, participate in shared projects, and receive "more agile and immediate feedback" (https://edu.google.com/intl/ALL_mx/resources/customer-stories/mexico-jalisco/).
- **CBTIS 276** (industrial-technical baccalaureate, 30 students + 8 teachers, one semester, mixed methods with platform log analysis): higher frequency of access and consistent use correlated with greater academic compliance, better time management, and lower task accumulation. Researchers identified "limitations in the use of educational analytics and formative feedback" (https://pablolatapisarre.edu.mx/revista/index.php/rmiie/article/download/337/263).
- **Universidad Autónoma de Zacatecas secondary, 2021–22:** deployment framed explicitly around "helping teachers to control and manage at a distance the educational progress of their students" — language that foregrounds teacher authority (http://ricaxcan.uaz.edu.mx/xmlui/handle/20.500.11845/3836).
- **Veracruz technological institutes, n=479:** 83.5% "agree/totally agree" that the platform positively impacted teaching-learning (https://exa.ai/library/publication/gnxjm4ybtsw). A separate n=81 study noted Classroom "facilitates interaction of students and teachers" and "generates a competitive environment" (https://revistas.milpaalta.tecnm.mx/index.php/IPSUMTEC/article/download/74/117/130).
- **Colegio Anáhuac Garibaldi, n=102 (UTAUT2/PLS-SEM):** direct determinants of behavioral intention = **habit > performance expectancy > social influence**. Effort expectancy, facilitating conditions, and hedonic motivation were not direct determinants — but facilitating conditions were indirect through habit (https://revistas.uadec.mx/RIIIT/en/article/download/1117/855/1979).
- **Chihuahua public university, n=72, 16 weeks:** performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and intrinsic regulation drove continued-use intention (https://dialnet.unirioja.es/descarga/articulo/6888317.pdf).
- **Secundaria Técnica 73 (Zacatecas math):** pretest/posttest (Mejoredu diagnostic) with Wilcoxon and comparative mean tests reported improved learning in mathematical "saberes y pensamiento científico" (http://ricaxcan.uaz.edu.mx/jspui/handle/20.500.11845/4003).
- **CBTA 144** agricultural baccalaureate: Google Classroom "motivated and generated greater interest in the various subjects, helping to improve the academic performance of students" (https://cosac.sems.gob.mx/Proyectos_apoyados/Art%C3%ADculos_ejercicio_2020/DGETAyCM/159.20-P03.pdf).

**Shadow layer — WhatsApp**: In Tlaxcala, the most-used tool was WhatsApp (48.1%), ahead of educational TV (23.3%) and printed materials (21.0%) — relational, warm, teacher-to-group messaging carried the system, not LMS-native discussion (https://www.redalyc.org/journal/1941/194173996027/html/). A 299-student Hidalgo study found WhatsApp worked best in *small groups* with concrete tasks, with off-topic distraction as the main failure mode (https://apertura.cugdl.udg.mx/index.php/apertura/article/view/1911/0).

The documented Mexican pattern: teacher as broadcaster and content distributor; student-to-student interaction rare; comments stream used as teacher Q&A rather than peer discussion.

---

## 3. The Three Cultural Variables That Drive Interface Decisions

### 3.1 Peer Feedback: Anonymity as the Load-Bearing Variable

**Strongest quantitative evidence:**

- **Systematic review of 14 controlled studies (N=1,224):** Anonymous peer assessment produces more critical feedback, higher perceived learning value, better self-reported social effects, and a slight performance advantage (**effect sizes d = .14 to .27**). Non-anonymous peer grading correlates more highly with teacher grades (accuracy trade-off). A fading design (Rotsaert et al. 2018) showed quality remained stable after anonymity was removed (https://ernestopanadero.es/Publications/Articles/040_Panadero_&_Alqassab_2019_An_empirical_review_of_anonymity_effects_in_peer_assessment.pdf).
- **Vanderhoven et al. 2015** (*Computers & Education* 81:123–132), four *secondary* classes, Belgium: anonymous peer scoring via classroom-response technology vs. public score cards → pupils felt more positive toward peer assessment and reported **less peer pressure and fear of disapproval** under anonymity (https://sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360131514002218).
- **van den Bos & Tan 2019** (*Computers & Education* 142, n=114 Dutch L2 university): anonymous assessors produced significantly more *directive higher-order* feedback (substantive critique) and less directive lower-order feedback; assessees in the anonymous condition processed significantly more higher-order feedback and **scored significantly higher final grades** (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0360131519301915).
- **40 Chinese university EFL students (8 weeks, 4 anon / 4 identified):** "overwhelmingly favoured the anonymous mode," with significantly higher comfort ratings at peer and class levels; giver-role comfort highest. Students compared the experience to "a masked ball" (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02602938.2022.2089348).
- **German–Mexico virtual teams study (n=74, 9 teams, 8 weeks):** peer ratings correlated with visible participation (r = 0.66) but not with cognitive contribution (r = 0.14; r = −0.28). Evaluator nationality shifted ratings (**d = −0.43, p < 0.001**) — culture measurably distorts peer-evaluation behavior in digital settings (https://exa.ai/library/publication/cswqvrtn2tq).
- **CHI 2020 (150,000 logged online interactions across two sites):** being identifiable significantly changed how students accessed and rated peer content; under identifiability, **cultural differences became more prominent**, some students avoided content created by classmates of certain nationalities, and **negative gender effects appeared under identifiability and disappeared under anonymity** (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3313831.3376283).
- **Slido anonymous Q&A (n=39):** verbal baseline participation 15.38%; anonymous digital intervention lifted it to 54.54% (**3.55× increase**). 92.8% of contributions submitted anonymously; *all* primary Q&A contributors were international students. Researchers concluded "anonymity is a fundamental requirement for inclusion" (https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/s10639-026-13956-8).
- **Coursera cross-cultural MOOC study:** "in cultures with high power distance, students expect the teacher to outline paths. Status is important and hierarchies are well accepted… especially learners from cultures with high power distance might prefer to have more information [about their peer reviewers]" (https://alexandria.unisg.ch/server/api/core/bitstreams/0c1d0334-4581-4c09-8386-119fb38ed860/content).
- **Korean counter-evidence:** a small-n study (6 Korean teenage EFL learners) found *identified* peer feedback was slightly **more effective for revision quality** than anonymous; multi-peer review beat single-peer (https://kci.go.kr ART002936213). In a face-to-face vs. anonymous feedback comparison, Korean college students *produced more* anonymous feedback (especially in-text form-focused comments) but *adopted more* face-to-face feedback for revision — they trusted identified feedback more (https://exa.ai/library/publication/cfcr1wdqww1). In design education, 13 Korean students valued anonymity for removing emotional burden but criticized its time cost (https://exa.ai/library/publication/gpy53pjbb21).
- **Mexican co-evaluation longitudinal evidence:** A 70.7% initial fear rate of evaluating/being evaluated by peers dropped to 82.9% improvement in study activity and 78.1% reporting better teamwork after structured implementation (https://revistascientificas.uach.mx/index.php/qvadrata/article/view/1366). A separate study at Universidad de Sonora found resistance rooted in "perceptions of lack of reliability and knowledge from peers as well as the power relations among peers" that improved after structured training (http://end-educationconference.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/2020end004.pdf).
- **Greek EFL college study:** "students from countries that uphold power distance appear to have less regard for peer feedback than those from countries that exhibit lower power distance" (https://publications.coventry.ac.uk/index.php/joaw/article/download/447/705/3118).
- **Academy of Management evidence (Mexican–U.S. samples):** "when a team member was perceived to be an in-group member, collectivists evaluated that member significantly more generously than did individualists" — the in-group generosity bias (https://journals.aom.org/doi/10.5465/1556338).

**Synthesis:** Anonymity raises *composition and quality* of critique; identified feedback drives *adoption and use* of critique. Anonymity reliably increases comfort in the giver role and higher-order feedback volume (Dutch n=114, Chinese n=40, Japanese Ritsumeikan, CRT secondary n=4 classes). Effect sizes are modest (d = .14–.27) — anonymity is a lever, not a silver bullet, and must pair with accountability (rubrics, teacher oversight, helpfulness ratings).

**Predicted peer-feedback friction and anonymity recommendation:**

| Market | Predicted friction | Default |
|---|---|---|
| South Korea (PDI 60, IDV 18, UAI 85) | High; sunbae/hoobae hierarchy amplifies face threat | Anonymous *default*; identified after trust builds |
| Mexico (PDI 81, IDV 30) | Highest; teacher-centered tradition strong | Anonymous *default*; identified only with teacher endorsement |
| Finland (PDI 33, IDV 63) | Low; flat hierarchy, individualist | Identified *default*; anonymity as option for sensitive topics |

### 3.2 Teacher Authority: The Moderation Gradient

**Direct evidence on the direction of teacher-presence effects:**
- Thai/German comparative study: "the presence of the lecturer in break-out rooms increased Thai students' voicing behavior, [while] German students opened up as the lecturer was absent." Thai students also more concerned about classmates' judgment; camera use affected them negatively (https://exa.ai/library/publication/77x9rztdpst). The direction of teacher-presence effects is PDI-dependent and designable.
- Korean EFL learners report lowest willingness-to-communicate *inside* the classroom vs. digital/out-of-class settings (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1362168819890825). Computer-mediated teacher dialogue "helped provide lower-proficiency students with voice" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/bthqc575v0h).
- Confucian-heritage learners in US online courses were "intimidated to interact with their instructors" and instead sought help from peers, particularly those sharing similar cultural and linguistic backgrounds (https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/b6d0/e6cd2f1d887dbc8f4609de489a39af8c641d.pdf).
- Korean flipped-learning study: students missed the teacher's immediate feedback enough to prefer traditional instruction — removing the teacher from the feedback loop has measurable cost (https://scienceon.kisti.re.kr DIKO0014471477).
- Chinese MBA students posted fewer online-discussion messages than Southeast Asian peers and Westerners (https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1052569905276669).
- Thai students in Thai universities showed significantly inhibited knowledge-sharing vs. Thai students in Australian universities, with **power distance and uncertainty avoidance as significant inhibitors** — the effect is contextual and designable, not fixed by nationality (https://so04.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/NDJ/article/view/2912).
- Arab distance learners preferred significantly more structure and more instructor interaction than Americans (n=95+95) (https://exa.ai/library/publication/qcxt9k9cp40).
- A 1,040-student statistics-course survey: **prioritizing group harmony predicted greater help-seeking avoidance**, moderated by competitive individualist values (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00220973.2025.2565175).

**Moderation summary by market:**
- **Korea:** Heavy teacher moderation as engagement lever (Classting posts 84.4% student-initiated with AI proxy as first-line; Kanuri-style teacher-mediated AI butler documented at 96.8% response rate). The Korean flipped-learning result implies teacher presence is participation-enabling, not just suppressing.
- **Mexico:** Visible teacher moderation as trust scaffold (Baja California's 3% → mass daily use hinged on sustained teacher training; UAZ implementation explicitly framed as teacher-control). Mexican co-evaluation research says students want teacher to judge peer readiness and fear teacher retaliation — moderation must be visible and protective.
- **Finland:** Wilma's design is administrative, not moderating — teacher is information source, not chat moderator. Wilma research shows that overly instrumented surveillance features generate resistance in a trust-based culture ("boundary turbulence" of teachers; "normalization of surveillance" critique).

Kim and Bonk's cross-cultural comparison (https://digitalrepository.unm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1170&context=ulls_fsp) found Korean students were "more social and contextually driven" online; Finnish students "more group-focused as well as reflective and, at times, theoretically driven"; US students "more action-oriented and pragmatic." The design implication: Korean students need a *relationship-rich* container, Finnish students a *cognitive-rich* container, Mexican students a *teacher-endorsed* container.

### 3.3 Public vs. Private Correction Displays

**Korea (PDI 60, IDV 18, UAI 85):**
- Korean students' classroom-presentation anxiety study: **negative feedback from peers was a major anxiety source, while making mistakes, audience attention, and teachers' feedback were *not* major sources** (https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1203707.pdf). This inverts the standard PDI narrative: in Korea it is peer-group judgment, not teacher hierarchy, that suppresses critique among peers.
- Korean EFL writer-identity study (12 college students, 15-week peer review): identified six writer identities — face negotiator, evaluator, junior (hoobae) and senior (sunbae), facilitator, audience, opinion-holder. The hoobae/sunbae identity is itself a moderation requirement — a junior cannot directly correct a senior (https://www.earticle.net/Article/A354578).
- Korean students use "politeness, and face-saving strategies, which are centred on listening and implicitness" to avoid direct confrontation; they prefer collaborative learning in *informal* environments outside the classroom; formal classroom settings produce "unease" (https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1120643.pdf).
- Classting design: public recognition on *effort/quantity* (class/national learning-volume rankings, journey maps), private AI-mediated correction on *quality* (wrong-answer notebook, revision cycles) (https://www.classting.com/features/self-directed-learning).

**Finland:** Finnish Wilma research shows that *even private teacher notes* carry psychological weight in low-PDI Finland — public correction in a peer group is acceptable, but the teacher-set tone matters. A 9th-grade self-assessment intervention (36 students) improved self-regulated-learning perceptions but reflection remained superficial without scaffolding (https://converis.jyu.fi/converis/portal/detail/Publication/182824048). Wilma's per-learner comments are visible to the learner and guardians, not the class.

**Mexico (PDI 81, IDV 30, UAI 82, IVR 97):** Indulgence of 97 makes a public "exemplar" wall a positive social-display surface (consistent with the Veracruz students' value on visible peer comment streams); a public "wall of shame" must not exist. CBTIS 276 study explicitly identified "limitations in the use of educational analytics and formative feedback" — public mistake display is the failure mode that creates that limitation.

**Leaderboard and public ranking evidence:**
- Two fully online-course experiments (n=50 postgraduates): absolute leaderboards intensified comparison; **students ranked in the bottom third preferred anonymous over public comparison**; only top-third students sustained motivation under relative ranking (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1016/j.compedu.2021.104297).
- Japanese university EFL 14-week quasi-experiment: the *non*-leaderboard class **completed more homework beyond the weekly target** than the leaderboard class; the leaderboard shifted motivation from intrinsic toward extrinsic and capped effort at the reward threshold (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1016/j.compedu.2022.104605).
- Badges/leaderboards in two physics-course experiments (N=102, N=88) showed **no effect on academic performance** despite positive student attitudes (https://exa.ai/library/publication/9vj4tdzt4nj).

---

## 4. Power Distance Manifestations in Digital Learning Environments

The literature converges on three observable behaviors in high-PDI digital classrooms (synthesized from https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2210656125000583, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2210656126000413, https://exa.ai/library/publication/4yfs2k7ykc2, https://publications.coventry.ac.uk/index.php/joaw/article/download/447/705/3118):

1. **Reluctance to challenge peers' work publicly.** In Chinese and Vietnamese studies, students explicitly prefer teacher feedback because the teacher is the legitimate evaluator. In Korean EFL studies, students self-identified as *face negotiators* before they could perform as evaluators. In Mexico, the documented Google Classroom pattern is overwhelmingly student→teacher, not student→student. In-group generosity bias inflates peer scores (AOM study).

2. **Reluctance to request help publicly.** Korean students' documented face-saving strategies and the broader high-PDI evidence imply that a public "I need help" channel will be underused. The Chinese anonymity study found comfort ratings "significantly higher" in the anonymous condition across *both* peer-level and class-level dimensions (https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02602938.2022.2089348). The Slido study found a 3.55× increase in participation when anonymity was introduced.

3. **Sensitivity to publicly displayed error.** Korean students' "junior" identity is a vulnerability when their mistakes are public; Mexican students' high uncertainty avoidance (82) amplifies the same effect. Finnish students treat public mistakes as learning material — but Wilma research shows that *teacher-made* public notes about errors are processed as identity statements, not as neutral feedback.

**Friction ranking by market** (PDI-based heuristic): Mexico (PDI 81) > Korea (PDI 60) > Finland (PDI 33). Korea–Mexico differ on restraint-vs-warmth axis despite both being high-PDI; design templates should not treat them as the same market.

---

## 5. Summary Comparison of Measurable Outcomes

| Metric | Classting (Korea) | Wilma (Finland) | Google Classroom (Mexico) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deployment scale | 9M+ users; 95–98% school share; 4,600+ AI schools | 2M+ users; 95%+ schools; 300k messages/week | Most-used LMS in Mexico per UAZ; 65.5% of students in Mejoredu data; 480 secondary schools in Baja California alone |
| Documented engagement lift | Posts +4×; Q&A +2×; learning material +37.4 pp (Ulsan Univ); student-initiated 84.4% (Baewha) | Not measured in engagement terms (administrative system) | Higher access frequency ↔ higher academic compliance, better time management, lower task accumulation (CBTIS 276) |
| AI response rate | 96.8% (Ulsan); ~90% (Baewha) | n/a | n/a |
| Peer-feedback primitive | None native; AI-mediated question + empathy button | None (only teacher-channel feedback) | Limited (comment stream used as teacher Q&A) |
| Anonymous-feedback primitive | Yes (anonymous question posting + "저도 궁금해요" empathy button) | None | None (identified by design) |
| Determinants of use | Performance + AI convenience (qualitative) | Routine + administrative necessity | **Habit > performance expectancy > social influence** (UTAUT2) |
| Acceptance rate | n/a (vendor-reported adoption) | "Ambiguous pedagogical tool" (558-parent study) | 83.5% agree/totally agree (Veracruz n=479) |

The pattern: Korean platforms drive engagement *through* teacher-mediated authority with AI proxy; Mexican platforms drive compliance *through* habit and social conformity to teacher-set routines; Finnish platforms drive administration through a low-friction channel that doesn't try to gamify peer interaction. None of the three markets has a documented, well-functioning, culturally-adapted native peer-feedback primitive in production.

---

## 6. Specific Interaction-Pattern Recommendations

### Group Project Workspaces

**Korea:** Use a teacher-visible mirror of all activity (Classting dashboard pattern). Make AI Tutor first line of student questions (3-step hints). Avoid open public team chat; use a *threaded, role-typed* model where contributions are tagged "question," "answer," "evidence," "summary" so face is managed by content type rather than who said it. Encode hoobae/sunbae asymmetry as a first-class design object — two-track feedback channels (upward junior→senior, downward senior→junior) with different defaults. Group-level progress visible to class; individual contribution visible to teacher only.

**Finland:** Mirror Wilma philosophy — low-touch teacher channel, high-trust student channel. Open team chat, identified by default, no AI filter. Finnish flat hierarchy means peer-to-peer coordination is the norm; teacher's job is to set the assignment, not to monitor. Don't add surveillance feel (cf. Wilma's "normalization of surveillance" critique). Match Wilma's transparent shared-record model where teachers and students see the same information.

**Mexico:** Default to teacher-broadcast, student-respond; add a *small-group breakout* primitive that the teacher *endorses*. UTAUT2 evidence shows habit and social influence are the strongest drivers — optimize workspace for familiar routine and peer conformity (default templates, suggested group sizes of 3–4, teacher-vetted prompts). Avoid free-form public chat. Design mobile-first with low-bandwidth modes (only 50% of secondary students had computer access during remote schooling).

### Peer Review Systems

| Feature | Korea | Finland | Mexico |
|---|---|---|---|
| Default reviewer identity | Anonymous | Identified | Anonymous |
| Anonymity fading path | Identified after 2–3 cycles, after trust builds | Anonymity for sensitive topics only (self/well-being) | Identified only after teacher endorsement |
| Rubric | 4-point with separate "kindness" and "accuracy" axes | Standard 4-point | 4-point + teacher-endorsed exemplar |
| Public display of review | Only "exemplar" reviews (curated) | Full transparency | Only teacher-endorsed excerpts |
| Response window | Asynchronous, ≥48h | Synchronous OK | Asynchronous, ≥48h |
| Mandatory training | 15-min module first time | Optional orientation | 10-min module first time |
| Multi-peer requirement | Yes (multi-peer beat single-peer; KCI ART002936213) | Optional | Yes |

Universal accountability safeguards: rubric-anchored criteria, teacher-visible attribution for accountability, helpfulness ratings to deter loafing. Mitigation for anonymity's fairness penalty (Panadero 2018): surface rubrics and published exemplar feedback.

### Real-Time Collaboration Features

- **Korea:** Default to asynchronous co-editing with a "raise hand for live help" path. 3-step hint scaffold from Classting AI transfers directly. Live-cursor displays opt-in per user. Anonymity + empathy-reaction mechanism ("저도 궁금해요") for question channels. Cameras optional.
- **Finland:** Synchronous co-editing acceptable and consistent with flat-hierarchy culture. Wilma's lack of real-time features is a gap, not a virtue. "Invite teacher" button rather than teacher-presence default.
- **Mexico:** Default to asynchronous with teacher-mediated live option. Cameras optional. Integrate or interoperate with messaging-style interaction (the WhatsApp lesson) — relational warmth is a documented adoption driver. Mobile-first design.

### Public vs. Private Correction Displays

- **Korea:** Private correction default. Two-track feedback (junior→senior anonymous/mediated, senior→junior more direct). Public ranking on collective effort only. Classting-style "오답 보관함" (private wrong-answer notebook) with optional teacher-brokered sharing.
- **Finland:** Public correction default, but student-controlled visibility (one-click "make private to me" toggle). Wilma research shows even private teacher notes carry weight; student agency over visibility matters.
- **Mexico:** Private correction default. Public "exemplar wall" viable (Indulgence 97); "wall of shame" must not exist. CBTIS 276 study identifies "limitations in the use of educational analytics and formative feedback" — public mistake display is precisely the failure mode.

### Help-Request Behavior

Across all three markets, but especially Korea and Mexico, "ask the teacher" must be *private by default* and *one click from any task*. The Classting model (AI Tutor handles 90%+ of student questions, escalates rest to teacher) is the proven pattern. In Mexico, where Mexican co-evaluation research shows students want teacher to judge peer readiness, this transfers directly. In Finland, the same path can be public without anxiety costs.

---

## 7. Limitations and Uncertainty

Several caveats apply:

- **Hofstede scores are population-level averages** from IBM employee data (1968–1973) with later replications; younger Korean and Mexican users may diverge (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/311974431). Mexico PDI is reported as 81 in the current Culture Factor dataset but 94 in the older IBM data.
- **Classteng's engagement numbers** (4× posts, 96.8% AI response, 84.4% student-initiated) come from vendor case studies; independent replication is limited. The secondary-school empirical work (Cooperative SNS n=40, EFL writing n=19, PBL n=23+22) shows achievement gains but mixed affective effects.
- **The strongest anonymity evidence** comes from Chinese (n=40), Dutch (n=114), Belgian secondary (4 classes), and US/Japanese L2 university settings — transfer to Korean/Finnish/Mexican secondary is by analogy.
- **Veracruz Google Classroom study** is the largest Mexican study cited (n=479), but it measures self-reported satisfaction, not learning gain.
- **Wilma research is qualitative**; no quantitative engagement deltas comparable to Classting exist. Wilma is not a collaborative platform — Finnish conclusions about peer interaction come from adjacent low-PDI cultures (Netherlands, Sweden), not platform-internal data.
- **No published study directly compares the three platforms** on the same outcome metrics in the same time window. The cross-platform comparison is triangulated, not head-to-head.
- **Effect sizes for anonymity are modest** (d = .14–.27); anonymity is a lever among several, not a silver bullet.
- **Hofstede scores don't capture within-country variance** (urban/rural, school type, socioeconomic); Mexico's connectivity divide (50% computer access) is itself a within-country gap that dwarfs some cross-national ones.

**Bottom-line synthesis:** The strongest evidence-supported prescriptions are (1) make anonymity a cultural default in Korea and Mexico, not the exception; (2) mirror the Classting AI Tutor 3-step scaffolded-hint model; (3) treat Wilma's lack of peer features as Finnish comfort — improve teacher-channel mobile, don't add surveillance; (4) code hoobae/sunbae asymmetry in Korean UI as a first-class design object; (5) optimize Mexican UX for habit and social conformity, not curiosity; (6) treat public and private correction as two distinct surfaces, with different defaults per market; (7) embed the help-request path inside the task, private by default, with AI-first triage. Where measurable deltas are concerned, the strongest available numbers are the anonymity effect sizes (d = .14–.27), the Slido 3.55× anonymity participation lift, the Mexican completion-by-access finding, the German–Mexico rater nationality effect (d = −0.43), and peer-rating validity splits (r = 0.66 visible vs. r ≈ 0.14 cognitive) — cited at source.

# The Neoanalysis–Oralist Divide on the *Iliad* and the Epic Cycle

## 1. The Two Schools in Profile

The methodological split was diagnosed by Wolfgang Kullmann in his 1984 *Greek, Roman, and Byzantine Studies* article "Oral Poetry Theory and Neoanalysis in Homeric Research" (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/5411/5311/15193): the two programs developed on opposite sides of the post-war Atlantic — oralism (Parry, Lord) in Anglophone scholarship, neoanalysis (Kakridis, Pestalozzi, Schadewaldt, Kullmann) predominantly in Germanophone Homeric research. Margalit Finkelberg summarizes in "Homer and His Peers" (2003 / 2011 reprint) that both schools converged on a single substantive finding — that the Homeric poems presuppose a much wider epic tradition about the Trojan War, of which the lost *Epic Cycle* is the most important surviving witness — but they sharply disagree about Homer's position within that tradition (http://old-eclass.uop.gr/modules/document/file.php/LITD328/Homer_and_His_Peers.pdf).

- **Neoanalysts** (Kakridis, Kullmann, Schadewaldt, Dowden, **Burgess**, **Currie**, **Tsagalis**, Danek) treat the *Iliad* and *Odyssey* as textually interacting with the larger Trojan tradition, giving Homer a "metacyclic" or meta-traditional status. The Cycle poems are "essentially just…verse manifestations" of the wider oral mythological tradition, but Homer's poems engage with them through motif transference (Burgess, "Neoanalysis, Oral Theory, and the Textual Transmission of Greek Epic," *Oral Tradition* 21 [2006]: 148–189, https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf). Kullmann's *Faktenkanon* — the constraint that certain basic plot elements could not be altered — was the working hypothesis distinguishing neoanalysts from the older Analysts, while preserving the assumption of a single authorial intelligence (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2013/2013.09.21/).

- **Oralists** (Nagy, Foley, Bakker, Foley and Arft) treat the *Iliad*, *Odyssey*, and Cycle poems as "instances of the epic stories surrounding the Trojan War… which once existed as malleable story-patterns that featured and fostered variation within limits" (Foley and Arft, "The Epic Cycle and Oral Tradition," https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/14397ED473238E742B12447115062E67/9780511998409c3_p78-95_CBO.pdf/epic_cycle_and_oral_tradition.pdf). Homer has no special status vis-à-vis the Cycle; similarities reflect shared inheritance, not borrowing. Finkelberg crystallized the difference: "from the standpoint of oral formulaic theory Homer and the Cycle should nevertheless be placed on the same plane as independent variants of a common tradition" (http://old-eclass.uop.gr/modules/document/file.php/LITD328/Homer_and_His_Peers.pdf).

The key methodological fault lines, as Burgess isolates them, are (i) **texts vs. typology**, (ii) **motif priority**, and (iii) **the source-language question** (Burgess 2006). Early neoanalysis postulated written poems Homer had "before his eyes" — Kakridis's pre-Homeric *\*Achilleis*, Schadewaldt's *\*Memnonis* — reconstructed from intertextual inference. The "Memnon theory," that the Patroclus plotline mirrors the Memnon story of the *Aethiopis*, remains "probably the most frequently cited and characteristic topic raised in Neoanalysis" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homeric_scholarship). Oralists counter that motifs are freely adaptable across performances and that "no instance of a motif can be shown to have priority over another" (Burgess 2006, summarizing Lord 1960:159; Fenik 1964, 1968; Nagy 1990b:130–31). Foley's "traditional referentiality" and the "immanent meaning" of formulaic typology became the standard oralist counter-model: shared phraseology and scenes evoke the tradition as an anonymous ensemble, not a specific text (Currie's framing of Foley 1999 in BMCR 2018.01.27, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2018/2018.01.27/).

## 2. Cypria Motifs in *Iliad* 1

### 2.1 The Διὸς βουλή (*Iliad* 1.5) and the *Cypria*'s Zeus-plan

The proem announces that "the plan of Zeus was being fulfilled" (Διὸς δ' ἐτελείετο βουλή, *Il.* 1.5). The most important thing to grasp about this verse is that its disputed Cypria parallel exists in two distinct versions. Cypria fr. 1 Bernabé = fr. 1 West = fr. 1 Davies is preserved by the **D-scholion** on *Iliad* 1.5 and tells of Zeus pitying the overburdened earth and resolving to relieve it "by fanning into flame the great strife that was the Trojan War" (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/1-the-origins-of-the-trojan-war/), where the fragment ends with the *same formula* as *Iliad* 1.5. The D-scholion then adds that Zeus took counsel with **Momus**, who advised against flood or thunderbolt and instead proposed "the marriage of Thetis to a mortal and the birth of a beautiful daughter" (Helen) (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/1-the-origins-of-the-trojan-war/; https://repositories.lib.utexas.edu/bitstreams/7b12a320-62aa-4c08-a825-1e8bdcf75f41/download). Proclus' *Chrestomathy* summary, by contrast, has Zeus "plan with Themis" (βουλεύεται μετὰ Θέμιδος), and **P.Oxy. 3829** matches this Themis version (https://papyri.info/dclp/60552; https://exa.ai/library/publication/lqktm7mhdqn).

For **Kullmann** (*Die Quellen der Ilias*, 1960, https://www.persee.fr/doc/reg_0035-2039_1961_num_74_351_3677_t2_0484_0000_2), the *Iliad*'s Διὸς βουλή is the flagship case for a shared pre-Homeric epic plan; the Iliad's plot is a slice of a longer known narrative. **Burgess** reads the Zeus-Thetis consultation in Book 1 as reverberating "against the wider tradition" while remaining free-standing in the Iliad (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf). **Tsagalis** treats the entire Apollonian plague of Book 1 (1.44–53), with its connection to the voyage from Aulis and Kalchas' prophecies, as a sequence presupposing the *Cypria*'s arrangement (https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/61673/chapter/550533582). A recent Oxford study proposes a "middle road": the *Iliad* 1 plague allusively replays the sacrifice of Iphigenia at Aulis, "not by quoting a fixed text but by reworking an established oral tradition" with stable fabula elements, acknowledging design "even if it is only constructed at the level of audience reception" (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:98754c9f-8187-43e3-9da4-f04f19447cb8/files/swp988m14s).

For **oralists**, the *Dios boulē* is a typological event, not a unique Cyprian invention. Nagy traces a deliberate translation shift across his corpus: "Will of Zeus" in *The Best of the Achaeans* (1979), *Pindar's Homer* (1990), *Homeric Responses* (2003), *The Ancient Greek Hero in 24 Hours* (2013); "Plan of Zeus" in *Homer the Classic* (2009) and *Homer the Preclassic* (2010) — precisely to "concentrate on the differences in plot that we see at work in two different epics, that is, in the Homeric *Iliad* and in the *Cypria*… two different plots corresponding to two different Plans of Zeus" (https://classical-inquiries.chs.harvard.edu/trying-to-read-the-will-of-zeus/). In *Homer the Preclassic* he argues that the older *Iliad* (arkhaia Ilias) had **no** Plan of Zeus, while the newer *Iliad* subsumes Apollo's anger under Zeus's plan (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/5-iliadic-multiformities/) — a prooemion type shared with *Homeric Hymn* 23 *to Zeus* and the *Cypria*, demonstrating competitive variation rather than derivation.

**Reception-oriented critique.** E. Barker shows that the D-scholion — the *actual* source for Cypria fr. 1 — "already betrays the gravitational pull of the Homeric poems, around which the rest of the epic cycle comes to revolve." Proclus' second-century-AD summary "critically recasts" the *Cypria* "at the service of reading Homer." Both schools therefore depend on evidence already Homerized (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:a8c2061b-0bee-4f57-aa2d-0de7f1a2d306). The overpopulation motif is a widely diffused folkloristic and Near Eastern *topos*: Schwartzbaum (*Numen* 4 [1957] 59–74), Scodel (*HSCP* 86 [1982] 33–50), Burkert's *Die orientalisierende Epoche* (1984), Mayer (*AJPh* 117 [1996] 1–15), Vielle's comparison of the divine prologues of the Trojan War and the *Mahābhārata* (1998), and West's *The East Face of Helicon* (1997) — a parallel repertoire cutting against uniquely Greek or uniquely Homeric priority. Jim Marks adds that Cypria fr. 1 "belongs to a flashback," complicating any simple narrative reconstruction (https://classics-at.chs.harvard.edu/classics6-jim-marks-inset-narratives-in-the-epic-cycle/).

### 2.2 The Thetis Supplication (1.493–533)

Tsagalis treats Il. 1.493–516 as the case study for "the rhetorics of supplication and the epic intertext" (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/part-iv-intertextuality-and-intratextual-sequences-10-the-rhetorics-of-supplication-and-the-epic-intertext-iliad-i-493-516/). The standard neoanalytic reading identifies the divergence from older epic: "what Thetis asks Zeus to give Achilles is the opportunity to become the [best of the Achaeans]" — which she knows will kill him — and Thetis, despite her resemblance to Eos, "will not grant immortality to Achilles as Eos did to Memnon in the post-Homeric *Aethiopis*" (Tsagalis, ibid.). For **Burgess** (2006) the scene is the engine of motif transference; Homeric epic is "metacyclic," a "respectful and dependent outgrowth of earlier myth and epic" — yet, as Burgess himself concedes, "Homeric motif transference is therefore an example of how Homeric technique extends oral poetics yet is not independent of it" (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf). For **oralists** the scene participates in the Indo-European pattern of the "chariot of the goddess," with Thetis rising from the sea to Olympus cognate (per Nagy's review of West's *Indo-European Poetry and Myth*) with Parmenides' proem and Indic ascetic imagery (https://chs.harvard.edu/curated-article/gregory-nagy-the-origins-of-greek-poetic-language-review-part-ii-of-m-l-wests-indo-european-poetry-and-myth/) — typologically inherited, not textually allusive.

## 3. Achilles' Awareness of His Own Death

The interpretive crux is the "two fates" passage at *Iliad* 9.410–416, where Achilles tells the embassy: "my mother, silver-footed Thetis, tells me that I bear a dual fate (δισσαὶ κῆρε) towards the end of death: if I stay and fight around Troy, my homecoming is lost but my glory will be undying; if I return home, my great glory is lost but a long life will be mine" (https://web.viu.ca/johnstoi/homer/iliad9.htm). *Iliad* 18.9–11 repeats the pattern ("my mother once warned me… that the best of the Myrmidons would be torn from the light of the sun by Trojan hands while I was still alive," https://sententiaeantiquae.com/2026/04/21/schrodingers-companion-productive-dissonance-in-iliad-18/), again prophesying a fact Thetis never delivers on-stage.

- **For neoanalysts**, this is a structurally transgressive moment. Burgess's *The Death and Afterlife of Achilles* (2009) treats Achilles as a "dead man walking" from Book 1 onwards: "the Patroclus–Memnon analogy — Sarpedon's death at Patroclus' hands (*Iliad* 16) 'reflects' the duel of Achilles and Memnon from the *Aithiopis* — gives the entire *Iliad* the quality of an 'anticipatory' narrative pointing to the death that the *Iliad* itself never depicts" (https://www.rorotoko.com/micro-interviews/20090310-burgess-jonathan-death-afterlife-achilles-1-1). Currie's *Homer's Allusive Art* (2016) formalizes a one-to-two correspondence: "Achilleus in *\*Memnonis* (*Aethiopis*) corresponds to Achilleus in *Iliad*"; and "Achilleus in *\*Memnonis* corresponds to Patroklos in *Iliad*" (https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9780191081491_A30390078/preview-9780191081491_A30390078.pdf). Tsagalis' *Oxford Classical Dictionary* entry on neoanalysis captures the strict sense: motif transference is the recognition of features in the *Iliad* that "naturally" belong to the *Aithiopis* (https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/61673/chapter/550533582). A *Mnemosyne* study, "The Death of Achilles in the Iliad," argues the poem surrounds Achilles with "numerous structural and thematic similarities [that] reflect and foreshadow elements of the traditional story of the death of Achilles," so that "through constant foreshadowing Achilles achieves the highest glory a Homeric warrior can hope for, dying in battle and earning immortal fame without actually dying" — while explicitly hedging on sources: "it is not necessary to presuppose a fixed or even written version of this poem as a source of our *Iliad*… the mere existence of the Cyclic subject matter in an earlier form is enough" (https://brill.com/view/journals/mnem/74/1/article-p1_1.xml).

- **For oralists**, the dual-fate passage is a standard Indo-European *kleos aíphor* motif. Nagy's *Comparative Studies in Greek and Indic Meter* (1974) treats κλέος ἄφθιτον as cognate with Rigvedic *śráva(s) ákṣitam*, reconstructible as *\*klewos n̥dhgwhitom* (https://chs.harvard.edu/book/nagy-gregory-comparative-studies-in-greek-and-indic-meter/); the choice-of-fates episode belongs to a deep Indo-European poetic archive of which the *Iliad* is but one variant. Foley/Bakker add the linguistic-oralist layer: in Bakker's *Pointing at the Past*, the deictic οὗτος, augment, and aorist are grammatical markers making narrated events "immediate" rather than displaced (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/chapter-7-similes-augment-and-the-language-of-immediacy/; https://chs.harvard.edu/book/bakker-egbert-j-pointing-at-the-past-from-formula-to-performance-in-homeric-poetics/) — Bakker himself calls "the oralist position in principle no less than the scripsist position" both "anachronistic and ill-taken" (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/chapter-3-how-oral-is-oral-composition/).

- **Davies' counter-neoanalytic position.** Malcolm Davies' *The Aethiopis: Neo-Analysis Reanalyzed* (2016) re-examines the standard arguments for *Iliad* dependence on the *Aethiopis* and concludes that in many cases the *primacy of the Aethiopis* "is not susceptible of proof," and that "generic, oral-traditional motifs cannot be used to establish source-derivative relationships" (https://crossworks.holycross.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1084&context=necj). Davies' *The Cypria* (2019, CHS) extends this anti-neoanalytic pole among recent editions (https://chs.harvard.edu/book/davies-malcolm-the-cypria/); an Italian *Emerita* study notes that fr. 1's language "has rather late linguistic characteristics compared to the other fragments of the Cycle" (https://emerita.revistas.csic.es/index.php/emerita/article/download/1089/1136), complicating the chronology of the recovery.

## 4. Cypria Motifs in *Iliad* 24

The Priam–Achilles ransom scene of *Iliad* 24 is read by Burgess and Currie as a programmatic inversion of the *Cypria*'s marriage of Peleus and Thetis: a god on Olympus (Zeus) relents, a second human supplication is approved, "and this is the only world in its turn by a complete reversal of the order of meetings between Achilles-Thetis-Zeus in the beginning" (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/part-iv-intertextuality-and-intratextual-sequences-10-the-rhetorics-of-supplication-and-the-epic-intertext-iliad-i-493-516/). The Judgement of Paris flash at 24.25–30, where Hera, Poseidon, and Athena "remained hostile to sacred Ilios… because of Alexander's folly (ἄτης)" in praising her who "provided his grievous lust" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/classical-quarterly/article/abs/iliad-24-and-the-judgement-of-paris1/45F7669651D636F1F0B3063F17648D82), is read by neoanalysts as a pointed allusion paired with the binding-of-Zeus motif at 1.393–407, the *Iliad*'s only explicit reference to the Judgement (which "most likely received its first detailed treatment in the *Cypria*," Davies, *The Cypria*, https://chs.harvard.edu/book/davies-malcolm-the-cypria/).

The Niobe exemplum at 24.599–620 — Achilles urging Priam to eat by telling of Niobe's eternal grief — is exactly the kind of paradigmatic material oralists treat as typological. A recent *Classical Quarterly* note re-reads the notorious "epic τε" + aorist at line 602 as a **timeless/gnomic aorist**, framing Niobe's grief as "an eternal consequence of a grieving process gone wrong" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/classical-quarterly/article/thought-for-food-on-niobes-eternal-brooding/725D6374B5DCB0AD6FEE06BB26F31F36). J. B. Hainsworth's study of 24.559–70 exemplifies the oralist counter-approach: the "enormous expansion and elaboration" of type-scene patterns (arrival, clasping knees, kissing hands, twofold plea) is "the interpretation of a theme in oral epic," generating meaning through traditional patterning rather than allusion to a lost poem (https://exa.ai/library/publication/0225nb0msrz). Tsagalis' "Priam's Catabasis" reframes the ransom episode as evoking "the epic journey to Hades in *Iliad* 24," explicitly claiming this illuminates "Homer's use of traditional themes and his aesthetic and ideological competition with other epic traditions" (https://www.academia.edu/1157780/Priams_Catabasis_Traces_of_the_Epic_Journey_to_Hades_in_Iliad_24): a synthesis formulation, since "competition with other epic traditions" is neoanalytic in substance but oral-traditional in mechanism. The 2024 BMCR review of Zieliński's *The Iliad and the Oral Epic Tradition* shows the debate still live at the level of close reading: Zieliński argues Achilles yields to Priam because Priam "comes to him personally, unlike Agamemnon in Book 9" — an intratextual, audience-response argument rather than a source-critical one (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2024/2024.08.25/).

Thetis' lament of *Iliad* 18 ("Would that you could live your life without sorrow, without tears, since now your life must be brief and bitter beyond all men's," 18.54–56, Lattimore) is for neoanalysts a transferred motif from the *Aethiopis*, where Eos laments Memnon — Tsagalis on "intertextuality and intratextual distality" (https://chs.harvard.edu/chapter/11-intertextuality-and-intratextual-distality-thetis-lament-in-iliad-xviii52-64/) and the *Aethiopis* argumentum at the Odyssey Online record (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:f6f16918-26f2-4035-be4e-675b40c0bf7d/files/m873fb86eabff593b51421a245495e580). Oralists object that the Nereid-lament type-scene and mother-mourning-son motif may be so traditional that the *Aethiopis*, *Odyssey* 24.43–66, and *Iliad* 18/24 are simply three instantiations of a shared pattern, with no derivational arrow.

## 5. The Evidence Base: Bernabé, Venetus A, and Indo-European Poetics

### 5.1 The Bernabé / West edition of the *Cypria* fragments

Alberto Bernabé's *Poetae Epici Graeci* I (1987/1996) and Martin West's *Greek Epic Fragments* (2003, https://eclass.upatras.gr/modules/document/file.php/LIT2211/Επικός%20Κύκλος/1%20West%202003%2C%20Greek%20Epic%20Fragments%2C%20Loeb.pdf) reconstruct a coherent-enough text base for inference of *Iliad*ic dependence; West's edition contains approximately 27 items of the *Cypria* including testimonia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Cypria, indicative), while West's *verbatim* reconstructible verse totals only ~50 lines (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cypria). West places **P.Oxy. 3829** immediately after Proclus' summary of the *Cypria*, noting that "Strife's appearance and the consequent dispute are paralleled in Proclus' summary, and the mention of Chiron is paralleled in frr. 3* and 4" (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.35/).

The standard **neoanalytic** use is the *Brill Yearbook of Ancient Greek Epic* summary: "the *Iliad*'s consistent use of flashbacks in Books 2–7 to recall mythic episodes that (a) precede the poem's narrative and (b) later appear in the post-Homeric *Cypria* indicates (for Neoanalysis) that the *Iliad* is drawing on an earlier, pre-Homeric epic tradition… rather than that the poet of the *Cypria* retroactively assembled them from scattered allusions in the *Iliad*" (https://brill.com/downloadpdf/view/journals/yago/10/1/article-p1_1.pdf). The **oralist** counter is that verbatim fragments "display a high degree of correspondence with Homeric phraseology" — but, in Foley and Arft's view, this is the consequence of "the typology of oral composition," not of Cyclic imitation of Homer or vice versa (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf). Davies sharpens the objection: many motifs allegedly transferred from the *Aethiopis* to the *Iliad* are "generic and traditional" enough to be interdependent rather than source-and-derivative (https://crossworks.holycross.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1084&context=necj).

A striking priority test-case is the **Sidon problem**: Herodotus says Helen and Paris sailed home in three days without interruption, whereas the *Iliad* has them stop at Sidon (6.288–292) and Proclus' *Cypria* has them *sack* Sidon. A neoanalyst can make either Herodotus or Proclus the original; an oralist treats the three-day voyage as a typical easy-journey formula (*Il.* 9.362–363) and the *Cypria* as "an authentic witness to a still-thriving tradition of oral composition" (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:5202fd4d-7d33-4b9c-972b-a0f3a2013525/files/r73666524n).

### 5.2 The Venetus A scholia and Proclus' *Chrestomathy*

The **Venetus A** (Marciana 822 = Z. 454, 10th c., https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venetus_A) preserves damaged excerpts from Proclus' *Chrestomathy* giving summaries of the Cycle except the *Cypria* — and the *Cypria*'s absence is itself the reason fragmentary evidence and the *Iliad* scholia carry disproportionate weight (Monro's 1883 JHS study remains foundational, https://www.jstor.org/stable/623376). Kullmann stated the asymmetry plainly: "the summaries of Proclus' *Chrestomathy*: for the *Cypria* these are preserved in various Homeric manuscripts, but for the other Cyclic epics only in the manuscript Venetus A" (https://exa.ai/library/publication/lqktm7mhdqn). The decisive *Cypria* fragment is not from Venetus A but from a **D-scholion** to *Iliad* 1.5 — Barker argues that this source is itself a reception artifact of the Alexandrian period, already under Homer's gravitational pull (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:a8c2061b-0bee-4f57-aa2d-0de7f1a2d306).

The **Homer Multitext Project's** digital reconstruction of the scholia (2010–2018, https://www.homermultitext.org/VenA-Introduction-2014.html; http://homermultitext.github.io/chsseminar/scholia-2018/) has transformed the evidence base. Topic-modelling of the scholia's vocabulary identifies the Aristarchan stratum as the dominant tradition, with Zenodotus and Aristophanes of Byzantium prominent in the editorial layer, supporting finer-grained attribution of the *Viermännerkommentar* (VMK) sources (https://classics-at.chs.harvard.edu/recovering-the-history-of-iliadic-scholia-architecture-and-initial-results-from-the-homer-multitext-project/).

### 5.3 Comparative Indo-European poetics

Watkins, Nagy, and West are the comparativist resources both sides mobilize, with opposite interpretive payoffs. Nagy uses the κλέος ἄφθιτον / *śráva(s) ákṣitam* cognate to argue that the dual-fate passage is an Indo-European traditional phrase, not a Cyprian invention (https://chs.harvard.edu/book/nagy-gregory-comparative-studies-in-greek-and-indic-meter/). West's *Indo-European Poetry and Myth* (2007) is taken up by Nagy as confirmation of the chariot-as-ascent motif connecting Thetis' rising to Olympus with Indic parallels (https://chs.harvard.edu/curated-article/gregory-nagy-the-origins-of-greek-poetic-language-review-part-ii-of-m-l-wests-indo-european-poetry-and-myth/). Currie's *Homer's Allusive Art* (2016) combines comparative IE material with neoanalytic method, including Mesopotamian parallels (Gilgamesh) — the chapter on the *Iliad*, Gilgamesh, and neoanalysis was originally published in the 2012 volume *Homeric Contexts* (https://homerica-agora.prod.lamp.cnrs.fr/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Currie_Homer_AllusiveArt.pdf). Burgess' 2006 article similarly frames "comparative evidence from Mesopotamian literature" within the neoanalytic frame, citing Burkert, West, and Cook (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf).

The divergent conclusions: for **oralists**, deep IE/Near-Eastern parallels show the motif is *traditional and diffuse* — precisely the material that cannot be used to establish textual priority. For **neoanalysts** and West, the same parallels show that the *Cypria*'s Zeus-plan and overpopulation motif are *ancient* and therefore plausibly pre-Homeric — supporting the influence thesis. Davies reports that West "declined to explain the Greek–Indian parallel by Indo-European inheritance," concluding instead that "the Greek and Indian poets were both using a motif somehow derived from Mesopotamia" (https://classics-at.chs.harvard.edu/classics6-malcolm-davies-folk-tale-elements-in-the-cypria/).

## 6. P.Oxy. 3829 and the Post-2000 Papyrological Record

### 6.1 *P.Oxy.* 3829: publication history

The single most consequential papyrus in the debate was **published in 1989**, not since 2000: P.Oxy. LVI 3829, edited by L. Kappel, AD 150–199, provenance Oxyrhynchus (http://archive.csad.ox.ac.uk/POxy/papyri/vol56/pages/3829.htm; https://papyri.info/dclp/60552; catalogue: CEDOPAL MP³ 01157.010, http://www.cedopalmp3.uliege.be/cdp_MP3_display_en.aspx?numNot=01157.010). What is genuinely post-2000 is its **editorial canonization** (West 2003 prints it among the *Cypria* testimonia), its **digitization** (Trismegistos TM 60552; DCLP; Oxyrhynchus Online), and its **reinterpretation** in reception-aware scholarship (Barker 2008; Christopoulos; the Brill *YAGO* survey).

The papyrus divides into three sections: (a) lines 1–7a, the end of a catechism listing characters of the *Iliad*; (b) lines 7b–38, a prose narrative of **antehomerica**, from Zeus' plan to destroy the heroic generation to the Judgement of Paris; (c) lines 39–44, the first line of *Iliad* 1 followed by a hypothesis of Book 1 (http://archive.csad.ox.ac.uk/POxy/papyri/vol56/pages/3829.htm). The preserved Greek of column 2 lines 7b–11 reads, in West's reconstruction: "τῆς Ὁμήρου Ἰλιάδος ἡ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ὑπόθεσις˙ ὁ Ζεὺς ἀσέβειαν καταγνοὺς τοῦ ἡρωϊκοῦ γένους βουλεύεται μετὰ Θέμιδος ἄρδην αὐτοὺς ἀπολέσαι… θύων δὲ ἐν τῷ Πηλείῳ ὄρει παρὰ Χείρωνι τῷ Κενταύρῳ τοὺς Θέτιδος καὶ Πηλέως γάμους" (https://papyri.info/dclp/60552). The Zeus agent is **Themis** (matching Proclus), not **Momus** (matching the D-scholion on *Iliad* 1.5).

### 6.2 Interpretive consequences

For **Christopoulos' "Casus belli,"** the impiety-motif (ἀσέβειαν καταγνοὺς τοῦ ἡρωϊκοῦ γένους) is decisive: "the *Iliad*'s Διὸς βουλή is more closely associated with Thetis' subsequent request to Zeus and much less or not at all with Momus' advice" (https://classics-at.chs.harvard.edu/classics6-menelaos-christopoulos-casus-belli-causes-of-the-trojan-war-in-the-epic-cycle/) — a stronger match to the *Iliad*'s terse plan of Zeus than the Proclus-summary version of the *Cypria*.

For the oralist "Momos advises Zeus" paper, however, the *significance* of P.Oxy. 3829 is opposite: the antehomerica is "a prose narrative" presupposing a Hellenistic *hypothesis-tradition* in which the *Iliad* and Cycle material have already been retro-fitted to one another, so the papyrus does not witness a pre-Homeric *Cypria* but a Proclus-style scholarly synthesis of *Cypria*-plus-*Iliad* (https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid:a8c2061b-0bee-4f57-aa2d-0de7f1a2d306). The same Momus/Themis multiformity that helps Christopoulos is, for Barker, evidence that the tradition was genuinely multiform and any single-source reconstruction is heroic.

### 6.3 Other post-2000 papyrus work

The Cambridge *New Surveys* overview of fragments catalogs further accessions: **P.Oxy. 5094** (2011; Colomo–Perale, *ZPE* 181 [2012] 1–3, https://air.unimi.it/bitstream/2434/1149075/2/Colomo_Perale_ZPE_2012.pdf; West, "The Daughter of Dymas," *ZPE* 183 [2012] 11–13) — a prose mythographic text naming the *Cypria* in connection with the grammarian Demetrius of Scepsis and the daughter of Dymas (Hecuba's father); **P.Oxy. 4708**, Archilochus' Telephus elegy, which "vindicates" Kullmann's fifty-year-old claim in *Die Quellen der Ilias* that the *Iliad* was aware of the Teuthranian expedition (BMCR 2013.09.21); and mythographic Philodemus and *New Jacoby* 18 F 1–2 accessions (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/new-surveys-in-the-classics/article/abs/v-fragments/7E9B4FBC7E5519633940A012D36439EC).

The cumulative effect has been to widen, not narrow, the divide: neoanalysts have a more concrete text-base than ever (the West/Christopoulos antehomerica, the HMT scholia, the Bernabé/West editions), but oralists can argue that this text-base is the textualized residue of a Hellenistic reception process that already presupposed Homer's centrality. The *YAGO* survey's verdict captures the impasse: any reading of the *Cypria* is "a composite act: reconstruction of narrative sequence; evaluation of witnesses whose agendas are rarely neutral; and… interpretation of a poetic object that we cannot access in continuous and full form," and the history of scholarship is "a sequence of shifting methodological settlements—each defining anew what the *Cypria* is allowed to be" (https://brill.com/downloadpdf/view/journals/yago/10/1/article-p1_1.pdf).

## 7. Current Status of Synthesis

The dominant trend since roughly 2000 has been explicit, and explicitly acknowledged, convergence — though not consensus:

1. **Kullmann (1984)** was the cross-fertilization landmark, acknowledging that the sources on which Homer drew were oral even if recorded late (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/download/5411/5311/15193).
2. **Finkelberg, "Homer and His Peers" (2003/2011)** mediates: both trends now agree the Homeric poems evoke Cyclic episodes; the real disagreement is whether this implies Homer's unique, writing-enabled status. Her own resolution: the uniqueness is real, but "it is of little relevance whether it was in oral or in written form that they attained this position" (http://old-eclass.uop.gr/modules/document/file.php/LITD328/Homer_and_His_Peers.pdf).
3. **Burgess, *The Tradition of the Trojan War in Homer and the Epic Cycle* (2001)** reversed the usual perspective: the Cycle poems "well represent pre-Homeric oral traditions," and the *Iliad* is "metacyclic" (https://journal.oraltradition.org/wp-content/uploads/files/articles/21i/Burgess.pdf). Burgess' 2006 article abandons textual sources: "it is not advisable to portray identifiable texts as the influences on the Homeric poems"; the source is Level A (oral mythological tradition), not Level B (specific cyclic poems).
4. **Tsagalis, *The Oral Palimpsest* (2008)** and "Towards an Oral, Intertextual Neoanalysis" (2011, https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/tcs.2011.011/html) propose three criteria for synthesis: (i) entextualisation (a dynamic oral process), (ii) external criteria for identifying allusion to identifiable oral traditions, and (iii) the transfer of motifs, themes, and phraseology (https://openurl.ebsco.com/contentitem/gcd:67328177). Intertextuality is "an innate feature of the web of myth," not an authorial policy.
5. **Montanari–Rengakos–Tsagalis (eds.), *Homeric Contexts: Neoanalysis and the Interpretation of Oral Poetry* (2012)** institutionalized the merger — 24 contributions, opening with Kullmann's programmatic essay, declaring that "*Motivforschung*, Epic Cycle" and "song-traditions, formula, performance, multiformity… may not be so incompatible as we often tend to think" (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2013/2013.09.21/; https://www.akademika.no/dokumentar-og-fakta/kunst-og-kultur/homeric-contexts/9783110271959).
6. **Currie, *Homer's Allusive Art* (2016)** is the counter-current: a "vigorous vindication of Neoanalysis, and a powerful challenge to conventional oralist understandings of Homer" (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2018/2018.01.27/), arguing that archaic Greek poets practiced allusion "as sophisticated as that of Hellenistic and Roman poets." Currie shores up "the old hypothesis of a pre-Iliadic *\*Memnonis*… with a novel argument (ironically itself typological): that the Sumerian [epic tradition provides parallels]" (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2013/2013.09.21/). The "curious fact" about Currie's reception, as the BMCR reviewer notes, is that the split inside the volume rather signals the unsettled state of the field.
7. **Zieliński, *The Iliad and the Oral Epic Tradition* (reviewed 2024)** embodies the synthesis in close reading — "fully committed as a neoanalyst but also as an oralist" — inviting comparison with Currie while differing sharply from him (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2024/2024.08.25/).

**Three residual disagreements remain open.** (i) *Target specificity*: does Homeric allusion aim at particular poems (Currie's hard position) or at fabulae/traditions (Burgess, Tsagalis, the Iphigenia paper)? (ii) *Direction and dating*: Davies' linguistic case for a post-Homeric *Cypria*, and the late language of fr. 1 (https://chs.harvard.edu/book/davies-malcolm-the-cypria/), directly contradict the neoanalytic chronology. (iii) *Source neutrality*: Barker's reception argument implies that much of the evidence both camps use (Proclus, scholia, hypotheses, P.Oxy. 3829 itself) is already a product of Homerocentric ancient scholarship, so any reconstruction of a "pre-Homeric Cycle" is partly a reconstruction of ancient reading practices.

Finkelberg crystallizes the current impasse: "contrary to the oralists' opinion, the position of the Homeric poems in Greek epic tradition was indeed unique. Contrary to the Neoanalysts' opinion, it is of little relevance whether it was in oral or in written form that they attained this position" (http://old-eclass.uop.gr/modules/document/file.php/LITD328/Homer_and_His_Peers.pdf). Whether this is a *paradox* or a *paradigm* is the question on which the next generation of monographs — Currie, Burgess, Tsagalis, Zieliński — is currently divided.
