## 5. Mechanism 3 — Payment Escrow and Settlement

This is the area of starkest divergence.

### 5.1 Argentina: Mercado Pago is the trust paradigm

- **Mercado Pago was created in 2003 specifically as an escrow service inside Mercado Libre to solve the trust problem between strangers trading online** — postal unreliability in the region made PayPal-style workflows impossible (https://litmus.lapaas.com/learn/mercadopago-business-model; https://nikhs.substack.com/p/mercadolibre-building-the-rails-for). Argentine users therefore arrive expecting an intermediary to hold the money and release it only when both sides agree.
- **Escrow must be paired with inflation protection.** With ~100% inflation in 2022, Mercado Pago (5M+ users then) became a value-preservation vehicle via its money-market fund (~60% annual yield at the time) (https://restofworld.org/2022/mercado-pago-app-argentina-inflation-scam/; https://www.pymnts.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/MP-Investment-FINAL.pdf). **In Argentina, holding a provider's earnings in non-interest-bearing pesos is experienced as a loss, not as safety.**
- Mercado Pago solved a credit-access gap for informal workers by offering loans based on sales history rather than formal employment records — an alternative credit reputation system (https://litmus.lapaas.com/learn/mercadopago-business-model).
- Mercado Pago holds **81% of CVU-account balances** among Argentine payment service providers — administering funds equivalent to roughly the 10th-largest financial entity by private-sector deposits (https://mde.com.ar/assets/docs/4Sistema_financiero_MPE_11-24.pdf).

### 5.2 Brazil: Pix reshaped instant settlement

- Pix launched November 2020 (central-bank-run, mandatory for large banks/fintechs); **63.8 billion transactions in 2024 (+53% YoY)** — the most-used payment method ahead of credit + debit cards combined (https://extra.globo.com/economia/noticia/2025/05/com-638-bilhoes-de-transacoes-pix-foi-o-meio-de-pagamento-mais-usado-por-brasileiros-em-2024.ghtml). Used by ~83–93% of adults (depending on instrument), reached 140M Brazilians within 2 years.
- **63% of Brazilians used Pix at least monthly in 2024, averaging 32 transactions/month** (FGV via Agência Brasil, https://www.capitalnews.com.br/nacional/em-2024-63-dos-brasileiros-usaram-o-pix-ao-menos-uma-vez-por-mes/418320). Cash use fell from 76.6% to 40.5% of payments 2019–2023; 97% of merchants accept it.
- IPA/J-PAL survey of **1,151 micro/small-enterprise owners in Espírito Santo**: **97% use Pix, accounting for nearly 90% of non-cash business revenues** — though most flows through personal accounts (https://poverty-action.org/how-pix-powering-open-finance-brazil).
- **Two design-critical properties:** (a) Pix settles in real time and is **final and irrevocable** — so the *platform*, not the rail, must provide reversibility (BCB SPI report, https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/financialstability/spi_annual_reports/SPI_2024.pdf); (b) Pix fraud is common — BCB built a dedicated refund mechanism (**MED — Mecanismo Especial de Devolução**, https://dadosabertos.bcb.gov.br/tl/dataset/pix). Average Pix scam losses rose **21% to R$2,540 in H1 2025**, with 65% of cases now routed to corporate accounts (https://valorinternational.globo.com/markets/news/2025/10/27/average-loss-from-pix-scams-rises-21percent.ghtml).
- **Pix-as-cultural-revival:** Estadão documents "Pix da confiança" — Pix reviving the "fio do bigode" (verbal promise) in the popular economy (https://www.estadao.com.br/economia/pix-da-confianca-como-meio-de-pagamento-virou-simbolo-da-nova-economia-popular-brasileira/).
- **The escrow paradox:** the world's best instant payment rail coexists with weekly (not instant) worker payouts on major platforms — Rappi in Brazil pays **weekly via bank deposit, not Pix** (https://daily.terabox.com/hub/how-to-register-and-succeed-as-a-rappi-entregador-oficial-in-brazil) and in 2024 began charging a **R$12 (~USD $2.40) weekly service fee** — Fairwork describes this as part of a broader "paradigmatic shift in platform operating models" toward profitability via fees (https://restofworld.org/2024/rappi-driver-fee/). Brazilian workers accustomed to instant Pix settlement are increasingly intolerant of weekly payouts or hidden fees — Rappi's weekly fee is generating churn toward iFood.

### 5.3 Colombia: cash-on-delivery + wallet reality

- COD remains dominant — **12% of e-commerce payments**, highest in LatAm; among merchants offering it (25% of Envíame's client base), COD accounts for **>40% of their sales**; Bogotá concentrates 45% of deliveries (https://www.revistafactordeexito.com/posts/39476/colombia-ocupa-primera-posicion-en-pagos-contra-entrega-en-latam). COD "ha sido un factor clave en el fomento de la confianza del consumidor hacia las compras en línea" — driven by distrust of online channels. Only **35.5% of Colombian adults have access to formal credit** (https://blog.envioclick.com/pago-contra-entrega-en-colombia-como-funciona-y-como-escalarlo-sin-perder-control/).
- **Rappi Colombia terms explicitly offer "electronic PAYMETEZ system or cash on receipt at the Consumer's choice"** (https://www.redjurista.com/appfolders/images/news/A_G_Rappi-04-04.pdf). Earlier reporting estimated **>60% of Rappi orders were paid in cash** (https://modelo-canvas.com/modelo-de-negocio-rappi/). Rappi Colombia now runs **8M+ orders/month with 1.4M monthly active users** (https://www.larepublica.co/empresas/matias-laks-ceo-de-rappi-colombia-dijo-que-en-rappi-hoy-estamos-por-encima-de-las-ocho-millones-de-ordenes-por-mes-4177604).
- **Nequi** reached ~37.2% market reach in 2023, **Daviplata** ~17.6%; both open with just phone + cédula, no minimum balance, making them the default account for unbanked and informal workers (http://repositorio.uts.edu.co:8080/xmlui/handle/123456789/18873). DaviPlata has paid 937,000 Familias en Acción CCT beneficiaries since 2012 — a state-CCT onboarding ramp (https://www.cgap.org/sites/default/files/Working-Paper-Going-Mobile-with-CCTs-Jun-2015.pdf).
- **RappiPay Davivienda** (banking license granted June 2022) serves 730,000+ customers with 20M+ transactions/year — evidence that low-paperwork, agent-assisted cash-in is the adoption unlock in a cash-heavy market (https://ir.davivienda.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/07/DAV_Rappi_Davivienda_-Press_Release_03092021.pdf).
- **Rappi Colombia refunds take up to 30 calendar days depending on the bank** (https://legal.rappi.com.co/colombia/politica-de-compensaciones-y-reembolsos-de-rappi-colombia/).
- **Documented fraud pattern: fake-receipt fraud** — edited screenshots and cloned apps ("Nequi DZ", "DaviTrampa") mean sellers/workers are trained to verify funds *in their own app* before handing over goods/services (https://colombiamove.com/blog/en/comprobantes-falsos-nequi-daviplata-verificar-pago-entrega/). The October 2025 AWS outage froze Nequi and Daviplata; commentators noted that for many users these wallets are their *only* account, so hours of downtime means missing rent or groceries — trust "erodes with each fall" (https://zonacaptiva.com/opinion/nequi-y-daviplata-el-futuro-de-la-banca-o-el-eterno-dolor-de-cabeza/).

### 5.4 The escrow norm: Compra Protegida / Preço Fechado

**Mercado Pago's "Compra Protegida":** platform holds buyer's money; coverage runs **28 days for non-delivery** and **up to 30 days for product problems**; platform staff intervene and refund to Mercado Pago account instantly (Argentina: https://www.mercadolibre.com.ar/compra-protegida). Mercado Libre explicitly warns that paying outside the platform or via WhatsApp voids protection — training users that *staying inside the platform = safety* (https://www.mercadolibre.cl/l/compra-seguro).

**Mercado Pago reputation-graded release windows:**

| Seller profile | Fund release |
|---|---|
| Good reputation + uses Mercado Envios | **2 days** after delivery confirmation |
| Still building history, or self-shipping | **up to 28 days** |
| MercadoLíderes | **up to 11 days** after buyer receipt, or **immediately** if buyer confirms first |

(https://www.mercadopago.com.br/blog/vender-mercado-livre-ecossistema-mercado-pago). **Spread: 28 ÷ 2 = 14×. Reputation here is not a cosmetic badge — it is directly equivalent to working capital.**

**GetNinjas' "Preço Fechado"** for services: "Seu pagamento fica retido até o serviço ser concluído. Se não sair como combinado, o GetNinjas resolve" — the most directly transferable escrow pattern for a gig platform in the region (https://www.getninjas.com.br/preco-fechado).

### 5.5 Payment/escrow recommendations

1. **Hold funds platform-side; never rely on the rail for reversibility.** In Brazil this is forced by Pix's irrevocability; everywhere it matches the learned Compra Protegida model. Release on customer confirmation or auto-release after a short visible timer (21–30 day dispute windows set user expectations).
2. **Pay out to rails workers already hold:** Pix keys/wallets (BR), interoperable CVU wallets incl. Mercado Pago/Cuenta DNI (AR), Nequi/Daviplata (CO). In Argentina, position payouts as "cobrá tu plata en tu billetera" — aligns with the 70% who want salary paid to wallets.
3. **Design explicitly for Colombia's fake-receipt threat model:** workers must see funds *settled in their own in-app balance* (not a payer's screenshot) before a job is marked paid; provide an in-app verification affordance mirroring wallets' QR-verification tools.
4. **Keep cash on-ramps:** >35% of Argentine transactions remain unbanked; cash payment with in-app confirmation, or cash-in via wallet agents, widens the top of funnel without abandoning escrow logic.
5. **Show the escrow state machine visually** ("Dinero retenido → Servicio confirmado → Liberado"). GetNinjas proves users accept held payment when the guarantee is stated in one sentence.
6. **In Argentina, pair escrow with auto-yield on held balances** — yield on idle balances is a genuine adoption driver; an escrow that visibly forfeits yield is a competitive disadvantage against Mercado Pago.

## 6. Mechanism 4 — Dispute Resolution Interfaces

### 6.1 Brazil: richest ecosystem, and users know it

- **Consumidor.gov.br** (public ODR, Ministry of Justice): **82.32% resolution rate**, average company response 7 days, 10-day deadline, **1,414,218 complaints finalized in 2024**; Jan–Jul 2026: 2.44M complaints (+110.8% YoY); official resolution 80.53%, but only **37.14% of consumers who evaluated said their problem was truly resolved**, average score fell to 2.37/5 — volume growth degrades perceived quality (https://www.gov.br/mj/pt-br/assuntos/seus-direitos/consumidor/defesadoconsumidor/Biblioteca/boletins-1/boletim-consumidor-gov-br-2024.pdf; https://www.consumoempauta.com.br/alertas/consumopauta-com-br-reclamacoes-consumidor-gov-2025-2026/). Academic comparison credits its direct-communication design over the EU ODR platform (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10603-020-09448-y).
- **Reclame Aqui:** 33M+ monthly visits, 25M+ complaints resolved, 900k+ companies registered, **average ≤3-day response, 1M+ complaints/month**, 12M complaints/year, average 6.4/10 resolution score, **68% resolution rate**, with coveted RA1000 seal requiring >90% resolution (https://solucoes.reclameaqui.com.br/; https://www.reclameaqui.com.br/; https://www.bxtdata.com/pt/insights/8265/Analise%20de%20Reputacao%20do%20Consumidor%20no%20e-commerce%20Brasileiro%20Estrategia%20para%20Marcas).
- A 2026 Brazilian consumer study found that responding to 100% of negative reviews within 24 hours reduces negative impact by 58% — external reputation interfaces are operational tools, not optional (https://www.bxtdata.com/pt/insights/8425/Analise-Reputacao-Usuario-E-commerce-2026-Avaliacoes).
- **Procons:** ~2.4M complaints/year, 74.7% preliminary-stage resolution (https://www.cnj.jus.br/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/access-justice-consumidor-gov-br.pdf).
- **Pix-chargeback via MED** now provides a payment-rail-native dispute path unique to Brazil — minutes to hours, not days.
- **Fairwork Brazil 2025 explicitly notes:** "In general, communication and support channels were identified, with a prevalence of **chatbots**. However, workers experienced difficulties using the platform when their accounts were blocked." **No Brazilian platform scored on the Fair Management principle.**
- **Worker-side disputes are judicializing:** Brazilian courts have ordered reinstatement + lost earnings + moral damages where iFood deactivated couriers without stated cause or defense opportunity, invoking good faith and the constitutional right to *contraditório/ampla defesa* (TJ-SP rulings: https://www.conjur.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/doc_183654557.pdf; https://esaj.tjsp.jus.br/cjsg/getArquivo.do?cdAcordao=19902577&cdForo=0; overview: https://www.jusbrasil.com.br/artigos/bloqueio-indevido-no-ifood-e-possivel-pedir-a-reativacao-da-conta-e-indenizacao/3453276342). **A dispute interface for Brazil must include a documented defense step before any deactivation.**
- **Pending PLP 12/2024** would codify this: exclusion only for fraud/abuse/misuse "garantido o direito de defesa" (Art. 6) and a **monthly transparency report covering criteria for job offers, scoring, blocking, suspension, and exclusion** (Art. 8) (https://www.planalto.gov.br/ccivil_03/projetos/ato_2023_2026/2024/plp/plp-012.htm).

### 6.2 Colombia: institutionalized conciliation + constitutional due process

- **SICFacilita** (Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio, since 2015): moderated chat-based conciliation between consumer and provider covering warranties, distance selling, identity theft; **383,562 claims through July 2025, 55% favorability (212,322 positive outcomes)** (http://sicfacilita.sic.gov.co/SICFacilita/; https://sedeelectronica.sic.gov.co/noticias/mas-de-383000-consumidores-han-sido-beneficiados-por-sic-facilita-desde-su-creacion-hace-una-decada). The 55% rate is materially lower than Brazil's ~80% — Colombian users have weaker expectations that complaints get resolved, so in-app resolution that visibly works can be a differentiator.
- **Constitutional Court ruling T-534/23** established that platforms exercise "poder normativo" when deactivating users and must respect due process, defense, and contradiction (https://www.corteconstitucional.gov.co/relatoria/2023/T-534-23.htm). **In effect, reputation-driven deactivation in Colombia triggers a higher legal standard than in peer markets.**
- **DAR (Defensoría al Repartidor)** — Rappi's in-app+WhatsApp ombudsman launched October 2023 — welcomed in form but criticized for lack of autonomy because staff are paid by Rappi (https://restofworld.org/2024/rappi-mediator-service/). Unions like Unidapp describe it as "performative and redundant."
- **Law 2466/2025** codifies a right to file complaints, prior notice of contract modifications, and worker registration with the Ministry of Labour.
- **Tutela actions:** Colombian workers file "tutela" (constitutional protection) actions against platforms; courts have ordered account reinstatement where due process was lacking. The Colombian approach has effectively built a **constitutional "shadow interface"** that platform dispute teams must operate against.
- Fairwork Colombia 2023 scores show the asymmetry: domestic-work platforms (Hogarú 8/10, AseoYa 7/10, Aux 6/10, Cabify 6/10) earned meaningful marks, but **Uber, Rappi, DiDi, DiDi Food, InDrive, Mensajeros Urbanos, Picap, and TuAly all scored zero** — reputation systems are not being paired with adequate appeal or transparency (https://fair.work/wp-content/uploads/sites/17/2023/11/Fairwork_Colombia_Report_2023.pdf).

### 6.3 Argentina: claim-driven reputation + post-COPREC gap

- **Mercado Libre's *reclamo* flow** is the mental model: open a claim on a transaction, platform's Compra Protegida team intervenes, refund lands in Mercado Pago; unresolved claims damage the counterparty's visible reputation (complaint rate feeds the thermometer) (https://developers.mercadolibre.com.ar/en_us/en_us/working-with-claims). The claimant's expected resolution is recorded and considered.
- **COPREC was dissolved by Decreto 55/2025 (3 Feb 2025)** — removing the trained pre-litigation mediation channel users had used (https://tecorresponde.com.ar/donde-reclamar; https://www.cronista.com/economia-politica/cierre-clave-en-defensa-al-consumidor-alertan-que-se-generaran-mas-costos/). This creates an opening for platform-mediated dispute resolution as a substitute.
- **Tax/fiscal disputes via AFIP** are the trusted external interface: workers verify payout fairness against AFIP records and CUIT-stamped receipts — unusual relative to peer markets.
- **Buenos Aires requires Rutramur registry**, providing a city-level dispute channel for couriers (https://www.clarin.com/servicios/repartidor-pedidosya-rappi-gana-2024-requisitos-empezar_0_TTvugkHJp0.html).
- Fairwork Argentina 2022 shows gig platforms lag badly on fair management/grievance mechanisms (only DiDi scored any points), indicating a wide-open differentiation opportunity (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/en/fw/blog/fairwork-argentina-scores-2022-new-report-about-gig-economies-in-latin-america/).

### 6.4 Dispute-resolution recommendations

1. **Mirror the claim ladder users know:** in-transaction "Necesito ayuda / Preciso de ajuda" → structured claim with evidence upload → facilitated in-app mediation chat (SICFacilita pattern) → platform adjudication with stated deadline → human appeal. Auto-refund to wallet on resolution, as Compra Protegida does.
2. **Never let a blocked account lose access to support.** Provide a dedicated appeal channel that works *from the block screen itself*. This is both the top Fairwork-documented failure and the fact pattern in Brazilian court losses — cheap to fix, expensive to ignore.
3. **Deactivation due process as a designed flow:** notice with specific reason → evidence shown → response window → human review → written outcome. Brazil's PLP 12/2024 direction (and Colombia's T-534/23 doctrine) makes this a compliance feature, not a nicety; build it once, deploy in all three markets.
4. **Meet users on the external stages they trust:** maintain a staffed, responsive **Reclame Aqui profile in Brazil from day one** (failing to respond to >50% of complaints triggers automatic "Não Recomendada" label); support SICFacilita conciliation in Colombia rather than forcing users into it as an adversary; consider absorbing the post-COPREC gap in Argentina.
5. **Publish a monthly transparency summary** (blocks, suspensions, appeal outcomes, scoring criteria) — anticipating PLP 12/2024 Art. 8-type requirements and Uruguay-style reputation-portability norms spreading across the region.

---

## 7. How Prior Trust-System Experience Drives Platform Adoption

### 7.1 Quantitative anchors on review-driven trust

- **Brazilian consumers:** 87% consult reviews before a first purchase; 86.3% say reviews directly influence decisions; 79% trust online reviews as much as personal recommendations; average rating across Brazilian e-commerce is 3.8/5 from 280M+ reviews (https://www.bxtdata.com/pt/insights/8265/Analise%20de%20Reputacao%20do%20Consumidor%20no%20e-commerce%20Brasileiro%20Estrategia%20para%20Marcas).
- **Reclame Aqui:** 33M monthly visits, 25M+ consumer accounts — arguably the single most consequential trust interface in any of the three markets.
- **LatAm consumer behavior:** 70% of e-commerce flows through mobile; 44.8% of consumers research 5+ times before purchase; iFood alone was downloaded 27M times in Brazil in 2021 (https://americasmi.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/2023_ami_modern-consumer-latin-america.pdf).
- **Pix:** 97% of MSE owners in Espírito Santo use it, ~90% of non-cash revenue (https://poverty-action.org/how-pix-powering-open-finance-brazil).
- **Colombia:** Fedesarrollo estimates ~200,000 workers in food delivery + ride-hailing combined (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/en/ratings/colombia/).
- **Argentina:** ILO describes Rappi as the most accessible onboarding (15 min) and Glovo as the most selective — **accessibility is a trust signal in itself** (https://www.ilo.org/es/media/282956/download).
- **Fairwork Brazil 2025** finds "multi-apping" as a worker survival strategy across 26 cities and 88 interviews — workers spread across platforms precisely because trust in any single reputation system is fragile (https://fairwork.oii.ox.ac.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/11/2025/09/Fairwork-Brazil-Report-2025-ENG_FINAL.pdf).

### 7.2 Behavioral implications for adoption

**1. Institutional trust transfer is the adoption engine (Pavlou & Gefen, Frontiers Colombia).** In low-trust markets, users do not trust the stranger; they trust the *platform's guarantees*, and that trust transfers to the counterparty. Reviews and the rating system mediate marketplace trust and experience (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/communication/articles/10.3389/fcomm.2024.1460321/full). Your *institutional* signals (escrow badge, verified-ID badge, claim SLA) must be visible at the moment of first transaction — they are the product.

**2. Learned mental models lower activation energy — or raise switching costs.** Users arrive pre-trained: thermometer reputation + Compra Protegida escrow (Mercado Libre, all three markets); QR scan-to-pay (Argentina's 278%-growth interoperable QR; Brazil's Pix QR — 59% key-based, 37% QR/copy-paste: https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/estabilidadefinanceira/Publicacoes_SPB/Relatorio_Decem_2023.pdf); wallet balance as proof of payment (Colombia). Mapping your flows onto these models requires no user education. Deviating from them (e.g., asking Colombians to trust a payer's screenshot) triggers fraud-hardened skepticism.

**3. Negative prior experiences create specific, predictable defenses.** Colombian users verify transfers in-app because fake receipts are endemic; Brazilians have absorbed Pix social-engineering fraud (hence the BCB's MED); Argentine users distrust anything that traps value outside instantly-accessible wallets (70% want salary paid to wallets — https://www.elobservador.com.uy/argentina/economia-y-negocios/el-auge-las-billeteras-virtuales-argentina-crecimiento-preferencias-y-la-necesidad-cobrar-los-sueldos-n5973105). Fraud-savvy users reward platforms that make verification *intrinsic* to the flow.

**4. State and marketplace incumbents seeded the first-account/first-transaction moment — ride on it.** **43% of adults in LMICs opened their first account to receive a wage or government payment** (Global Findex 2025: https://thedocs.worldbank.org/en/doc/a4aaae5a017a5bea7922686af0ed3636-0050022025/original/PolicyResearchTalk-GlobalFindex-September2025.pdf). This is exactly how DaviPlata (CCT transfers from 2012) and Cuenta DNI (IFE emergency payments from 2020) acquired informal-economy users. Pix drove Brazilian account ownership from 76%→87.6%. For a gig platform, the analog is: the **first payout is your trust-establishing event** — make it instant, free, and into the wallet they already use.

**5. Supply-side trust is earned through fairness mechanics, not just pay.** IDB/Uber–IPSOS: workers join for income (76%) but only 52% say income expectations were met, and most carry debt with no social protection (https://efe.com/economia/2026-02-26/latinoamerica-uber-conductores-problemas-economicos/). Fairwork documents that workers "multi-app" to hedge platform risk — low switching loyalty is a *learned response* to arbitrary deactivation and opaque algorithms. Conversely, Argentina's Zolvers case shows platforms that visibly *increase* formality/protection earn durable worker preference.

**6. Trust baselines change what ratings are for.** Where Brazil's 4–11% interpersonal trust makes platform-mediated institutional guarantees load-bearing, Argentina's ~24% means peer/social proof carries relatively more weight. The Latinobarómetro finding that personal experience ("si el servicio responde a mi necesidad") matters far more than third-party claims (40% vs. 11–12% for media/friends) tells you **onboarding must deliver a successful first transaction fast** — trust is built experientially, not by marketing (https://www.latinobarometro.org/documents/LAT-2017/informe-latinobarometro-2017.pdf).

**7. Country-specific adoption levers:**
- **Argentina:** mirror Mercado Pago's escrow paradigm + auto-yield on held balances + Monotributo check into onboarding. Pair with Rutramur-style local registry alignment to lower city-level friction. Frame verification as formalization benefit.
- **Brazil:** build Pix-native worker payouts (instant vs. weekly); publish a Reclame Aqui page from day one; internal ratings should be transparent and not weaponized as deactivation triggers; avoid fee extraction models (worker churn behavior is documented and well-instrumented).
- **Colombia:** build visible in-app appeal flows with prior notice of deactivation reasons; integrate Jumio-equivalent KYC with **PPT acceptance**; design dispute interface to satisfy the due-process bar set by T-534/23; use platform-fronted cash/escrow model that does not require informal users to prepay strangers. **Workers here expect constitutional-grade due process and will use it.**

---

## 8. Synthesis: What to Design Differently per Country

| Mechanism | Argentina | Brazil | Colombia |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ratings** | Tiered, fiscal-coupled reputation; CUIT/Monotributo = trust proxy; Compra Protegida claim-driven reputation; thermometer metaphor | Reclame Aqui external scores dominate; internal ratings amplify worker risk (Fairwork); anti-fake-review safeguards; transparency about scoring algorithm | Constitutional due process on every deactivation; verified-transaction badges essential; thermometer metaphor with PPI-tier bootstrapping for informal newcomers |
| **Identity verification** | CUIT + Monotributo + selfie + DNI via RENAPER SID; ~15-min flow; framed as formalization benefit (Zolvers pattern) | CPF + selfie every 14 days; verification seal visible to driver (Uber "selo de verificação" 2025); SERPRO Datavalid at R$0.12/check;

# DSM-5 (2013) vs. ICD-11 (2019) Autism Diagnostic Criteria — Comparative Analysis with Sensory-Processing Emphasis

**Critical methodological caveat stated up front:** No peer-reviewed head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy study applying both DSM-5 and ICD-11 ASD criteria to the same sample with sensitivity/specificity endpoints was located in the available evidence. All quantitative comparison data below are therefore mediated through DSM-IV/ICD-10 comparators, expert/consensus comparisons, or proxy field studies. This gap is itself a central finding. Sensory-processing-specific weighting comparisons rely on textual rather than empirical evidence — no empirical weighting study comparing the manuals has been conducted.

---

## (A) Side-by-Side Criteria Table

Sources: DSM-5/DSM-5-TR criteria reproduced by the IACC and AAP ([https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml](https://iacc.hhs.gov/about-iacc/subcommittees/resources/dsm5-diagnostic-criteria.shtml)); ICD-11 CDDR ([https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content)); ICD-11 MMS ([https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/icd11_mms-en-06.pdf](https://faculty.ksu.edu.sa/sites/default/files/icd11_mms-en-06.pdf)); Greaves-Lord et al. 2022 ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/)); Olson, Bishop & Thurm 2024 ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/)).

| Dimension | DSM-5 / DSM-5-TR (APA, 2013/2022) | ICD-11 (WHO, 2019; effective 1 Jan 2022) |
|---|---|---|
| **Core social-communication criteria** | Criterion A requires **all 3 of 3** subcriteria (monothetic): A1 social-emotional reciprocity deficits; A2 nonverbal communicative behaviour deficits; A3 deficits in developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships. Must be present across multiple contexts. | "Persistent deficits in the ability to initiate and to sustain reciprocal social interaction and social communication." **No mandatory sub-criteria and no symptom count** (polythetic/descriptive). ICD-11 lists ~7 manifestation areas (19 described manifestations across both domains). Clinician judges overall pattern. |
| **Sensory processing: mention and weighting** | **Explicit, enumerated Criterion B4** (one of 4 RRB sub-criteria): "Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g., apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement)." **1 of 4 RRB options, threshold 2 of 4** — sensory is neither necessary nor sufficient alone; can contribute up to 50% of RRB threshold. New in DSM-5 (absent from DSM-IV). | Explicit within RRB essential feature: "lifelong excessive and persistent hypersensitivity or hyposensitivity to sensory stimuli or unusual interest in a sensory stimulus, which may include actual or anticipated sounds, light, textures (especially clothing and food), odours and tastes, heat, cold, or pain." **No numeric threshold.** Added qualifiers vs. DSM-5: "lifelong" and "anticipated" stimuli. New in ICD-11 (absent from ICD-10). ICD-11 deliberately drops DSM-5's ID-anchored exemplars (flipping objects, excessive smelling/touching) that concentrate in cognitively-impaired presentations. |
| **Severity specifiers** | **Three levels, rated separately for each domain:** Level 1 "requiring support," Level 2 "requiring substantial support," Level 3 "requiring very substantial support." Additional specifiers: with/without intellectual impairment, with/without language impairment, associated genetic/medical condition, catatonia. **Olson, Bishop & Thurm (2024) note these levels "were never field tested, nor is there any evidence regarding their validity or reliability"** and warn of payer misuse (e.g., coverage limits for "Level 1 ASD") ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/)). | **No operationalised severity levels.** Severity captured via co-occurring **Disorder of Intellectual Development (DID)** and **functional language impairment**, yielding 6 subdivision codes: 6A02.0 (no DID, mild/no language impairment), 6A02.1 (with DID, mild/no language), 6A02.2 (no DID, impaired language), 6A02.3 (with DID, impaired language), 6A02.4 (no DID, absent functional language), 6A02.5 (with DID, absent functional language). Co-occurring DID severity (mild–profound) is coded separately under 6A00. |
| **Age/onset requirements** | Criterion C: present in "the **early developmental period** (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life)." | "Onset during the developmental period, **typically in early childhood**, but symptoms may not become fully manifest until later, when social demands exceed limited capacities." ICD-11 explicitly recognises compensation/masking and adult manifestation, dropping ICD-10's requirement of documented early-developmental-delay history. |
| **Functional impairment thresholds** | Criterion D: "**clinically significant impairment** in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning." Criterion E: disturbances not better explained by ID/GDD. | Deficits "**sufficiently severe to cause impairment** in personal, family, social, educational, occupational or other important areas of functioning and are usually a pervasive feature of the individual's functioning observable in all settings, although they may vary according to social, educational, or other context." |
| **Structure** | Categorical with dimensional severity; single ASD replacing DSM-IV subtypes (Autistic Disorder, Asperger's, PDD-NOS, CDD). Rett's removed. New Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder (SCD) added as mutually-exclusive diagnosis. | Single ASD category (6A02) absorbing childhood autism, atypical autism, and Asperger's. No Rett's. SCD not a discrete code (covered by 6A01 Developmental Learning Disorder with impairment in pragmatic language or by 6E60 secondary neurodevelopmental syndrome for sub-threshold cases). |
| **Coding** | 299.00 (F84.0 in ICD-10-CM). | 6A02 with extension codes 6A02.0–6A02.5, 6A02.Z. |

**Sensory-weighting synthesis.** Neither manual makes sensory processing a *required* diagnostic criterion; neither weights it more heavily than the other in an operational sense. The substantive differences are: (a) DSM-5 gives sensory a defined, countable slot (B4) within a 2-of-4 threshold; ICD-11 gives it qualitative standing within an uncounted domain with the added qualifiers "lifelong" and "anticipated stimuli." (b) ICD-11 deliberately de-emphasises ID-anchored exemplars (excessive smelling/touching) that DSM-5 retains — implying ICD-11's text may better capture sensory differences in cognitively-able individuals, but at the cost of precision. (c) Both manuals elevated sensory features to diagnostic relevance for the first time relative to DSM-IV/ICD-10 ([https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf](https://cpe.psychopen.eu/index.php/cpe/article/download/10005/10005.pdf)).

## (B) Evidence Synthesis: DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 Diagnostic Accuracy / Clinical Utility (2013–present)

**Overall finding (stated explicitly):** No published head-to-head diagnostic-accuracy study applying both DSM-5 and ICD-11 ASD criteria to the same sample with sensitivity/specificity endpoints was located. The five sources below are the closest available evidence. GRADE ratings are reported where published, or are my structured assessments for diagnostic-accuracy evidence (which starts at lower certainty and is typically downgraded for indirectness/imprecision).

### Source 1 — Kulage, Smaldone & Cohn (2014). *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*. Systematic review and meta-analysis.

- **Design:** Systematic literature review + meta-analysis of studies comparing DSM-IV-TR vs. DSM-5 criteria applied to the same population.
- **Sample size:** 418 studies screened; 14 met inclusion criteria (pooled across studies; not a single n).
- **Key statistics:** Pooled decrease in ASD diagnoses under DSM-5 = **31% (95% CI 20–44%, p=0.006)**. Subgroup drops: Autistic Disorder −22% (16–29%, p<0.001); PDD-NOS −70% (55–82%, p=0.01); Asperger's −70% (26–94%, p=0.38, NS). Substantial between-study heterogeneity (range of decreases 7.3–68.4%).
- **GRADE quality rating:** **Moderate** for pooled estimates; consistent direction across studies but downgraded for heterogeneity and reliance on draft/final DSM-5 application to archived data.
- **Source:** [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/)

### Source 2 — First, Rebello, Ke, et al. (2021). *World Psychiatry*. Expert/consensus structural comparison.

- **Design:** Systematic category-level comparison by the WHO ICD–DSM Harmonization Group of ICD-11 CDDG "Essential Features" vs. DSM-5 criteria for 103–104 shared diagnostic entities, using pre-specified 4-level ratings and dual principal raters.
- **Sample size:** 103–104 diagnostic entities; ASD analysed qualitatively.
- **Key statistics:** Across all disorders — **20 (19.4%) major differences; 42 (40.8%) minor definitional differences; 10 (9.7%) minor due to greater DSM-5 specification; 31 (30.1%) essentially identical.** For ASD specifically, the two systems share a two-domain conceptual core but differ operationally: DSM-5 mandates all 3 social sub-criteria and 2-of-4 RRB; ICD-11 mandates neither. The authors explicitly caution that "there has been only a small number of studies comparing the ICD-11 CDDG and DSM-5 criteria for a particular disorder in terms of whether they are identifying the same people or yield similar prevalence estimates" — i.e., for ASD, this comparison has not been empirically performed.
- **GRADE quality rating:** **Moderate** as structural evidence (systematic expert methodology); **Very Low** for accuracy outcomes (no patient-level accuracy data).
- **Sources:** [https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20825); accepted version [https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10119537/)

### Source 3 — Huerta, Bishop, Duncan, Hus, & Lord (2012). *Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry*. Primary empirical field-trial validation.

- **Design:** Prospective field-trial evaluation of DSM-5 criteria applied alongside DSM-IV-TR diagnoses; standardised instruments (ADOS, ADI-R).
- **Sample size:** n=**977** (657 with clinical ASD diagnosis; 276 with non-autism diagnosis); drawn from multiple sites.
- **Key statistics:** Overall DSM-5 sensitivity = **60.6% (95% CI 57–64%)**; specificity = **94.9% (95% CI 92–97%)**. Subgroup sensitivity: Autistic Disorder 0.76, Asperger's 0.25, PDD-NOS 0.28. By IQ: IQ<70 sensitivity 0.70; IQ≥70 sensitivity 0.46 — i.e., the new criteria disproportionately excluded cognitively-able individuals.
- **GRADE quality rating:** **Moderate** (large sample, standardised instruments; field-trial methodology).
- **Source:** [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/)

### Source 4 — Wilson, Djukic, Shinnar, et al. (2013). *Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders*. Primary empirical adult-clinic concordance study.

- **Design:** Cross-sectional diagnostic concordance study comparing ICD-10R, DSM-IV-TR, and DSM-5 in an adult autism diagnostic clinic.
- **Sample size:** n=**150 intellectually able adults** referred to a specialist clinic.
- **Key statistics:** Of those diagnosed with ASD under ICD-10R, **only 56% met DSM-5 ASD criteria**; a further **19% met DSM-5 draft Social Communication Disorder**; of DSM-IV-TR Autistic Disorder/Asperger cases, **78% met DSM-5**. Authors found DSM-5 sensitivity "significantly increased by reducing the number of criteria required… or rating 'uncertain' criteria as 'present', without sacrificing specificity."
- **GRADE quality rating:** **Low** (single-centre, clinic-referred sample, no independent gold standard, draft-criteria-era context).
- **Source:** [https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/](https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/en/publications/comparison-of-icd-10r-dsm-iv-tr-and-dsm-5-in-an-adult-autism-spec/)

### Source 5 — Bölte, Kamp-Becker, et al. (2024). "Autism spectrum disorder in ICD-11 — a critical reflection of its possible impact on clinical practice and research." *Molecular Autism*. Expert perspective/critical textual analysis.

- **Design:** Expert perspective/critical textual analysis comparing ICD-11 and DSM-5 operationalisation.
- **Sample size:** N/A (text analysis).
- **Key statistics/claims:** ICD-11 allows 304 (19×16) manifestation combinations with no mandatory symptom count; argues this reduces specificity, raises false-positive risk, increases heterogeneity, and creates risk of "non-falsifiable diagnoses" via the repeated invocation of unvalidated "compensation." Notes ICD-11 lacks severity specifiers.
- **GRADE quality rating:** **Very Low** as accuracy evidence (expert opinion); directly relevant for clinical-utility and safety questions in Sections D–E.
- **Source:** [https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)

**Supplementary empirical anchors (DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV/ICD-10 — proxy for direction of effect):**

- Frazier, Youngstrom, Speer, et al. (2012), JAACAP: n=**14,744 siblings** (8,911 ASD, 5,863 non-ASD), ages 2–18, Interactive Autism Network registry. DSM-5 specificity 0.97 vs DSM-IV-TR 0.86; sensitivity 0.81 (DSM-5) vs 0.95 (DSM-IV-TR). Relaxing DSM-5 by one fewer criterion raised sensitivity to 0.93 with minimal specificity loss (0.95) ([https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(11)00890-2/abstract](https://www.jaacap.org/article/S0890-8567(11)00890-2/abstract)).
- Maenner et al. (2014), JAMA Psychiatry: ADDM Network population-based surveillance, 644,883 children under surveillance, 6,577 with DSM-IV-TR ASD. **81.2% of DSM-IV-TR ASD cases met DSM-5 criteria.** Higher concordance in children with intellectual disability (86.6%) than without (72.5%, p<0.001). Projected 2008 prevalence: 10.0/1,000 (DSM-5) vs 11.3/1,000 (DSM-IV-TR) ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041577/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041577/)). GRADE: **High** for population surveillance.
- Singapore study (n=110 children): DSM-IV-TR sensitivity 0.946/specificity 0.889 vs. DSM-5 sensitivity 0.837/specificity 0.833; **40% of PDD-NOS best-estimate cases misclassified** on DSM-5 ([https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29705921/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29705921/)).
- Italian cohort (n=54): ASD diagnosis fell from 43% (DSM-IV-TR) to 25% (DSM-5), χ²(2)=11.73, p=.003 ([https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348585053](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/348585053)).
- North India cross-sectional study (n=100): DSM-5 ASD κ=0.846 with DSM-IV-TR and κ=0.874 with ICD-10 DCR for childhood autism; agreement dropped to κ=0.699–0.703 when DSM-IV-TR/ICD-10 "ASD" (broader PDD) was compared with DSM-5 ASD ([https://exa.ai/library/publication/c2n9r6xrxhz](https://exa.ai/library/publication/c2n9r6xrxhz)).
- Milan adult sample (n=61): **75.4% received their ASD diagnosis on average 8 years after first mental-health contact**; women were less likely to be correctly diagnosed and more likely to be misdiagnosed; **women who were misdiagnosed scored significantly higher on the hyper/hypo-reactivity-to-sensory-input domain** — rare direct evidence that sensory-prominent presentations in women drive misdiagnosis under DSM-5-based practice ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8306851/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8306851/)).

**Quantitative direction-of-effect summary (DSM-5 vs. DSM-IV/ICD-10):**

| Pooled decrease in ASD diagnoses | 31% (95% CI 20–44%) | Kulage 2014 |
| PDD-NOS subgroup decrease | 70% (55–82%) | Kulage 2014 |
| Autistic Disorder subgroup decrease | 22% (16–29%) | Kulage 2014 |
| DSM-5 sensitivity (vs. DSM-IV gold std) | 0.61 (95% CI 0.57–0.64) | Huerta 2012 |

## (C) Clinical Guideline Positions

### World Health Organization (WHO)
ICD-11 was adopted by the 72nd World Health Assembly in May 2019 (resolution WHA72.15, [https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA72/A72_R15-en.pdf](https://apps.who.int/gb/ebwha/pdf_files/WHA72/A72_R15-en.pdf)) and came into effect globally on **1 January 2022**, with at least a 5-year transitional arrangement during which Member States may continue ICD-10 reporting ([https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation](https://www.who.int/standards/classifications/frequently-asked-questions/icd-11-implementation)). WHO's Clinical Descriptions and Diagnostic Requirements (CDDR) for mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders were validated through internet-based case-vignette and ecological implementation field studies involving thousands of clinicians across all global regions; WHO reports these showed "incrementally superior — or in some cases equivalent — performance of the ICD-11 CDDR compared to the ICD-10 CDDG in the accuracy of diagnoses assigned to case vignettes" ([https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content](https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/dcf73611-9e0f-4d5c-85f6-85a58b0da6de/content)). ICD-11 6A02 explicitly includes sensory differences in the defining features of ASD and adopts a "lifetime, developmental perspective" rather than mandating childhood onset only ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9881114/)). WHO emphasises harmonisation with DSM-5 but acknowledges the two systems differ in "operationalisation" — ICD-11 deliberately omits the prescriptive monothetic requirement (all 3 of 3 social criteria).

### American Psychiatric Association (APA)
Published DSM-5 in May 2013 and DSM-5-TR in 2022; remains the standard psychiatric classification in the United States. The DSM-5 Neurodevelopmental Disorders chapter introduced the unified ASD diagnosis, mandated all 3 social-communication criteria (monothetic), added sensory symptoms as Criterion B4, and introduced severity specifiers ([https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2040-2392-4-12](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/2040-2392-4-12)). APA co-participated in the WHO–APA ICD–DSM Harmonization Group (documented in First et al. 2021), indicating institutional support for convergence rather than competition. APA has not adopted ICD-11 for US clinical use; DSM-5-TR remains the APA standard.

### American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)
The 2020 Clinical Report "Identification, Evaluation, and Management of Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder" (Hyman SL, Levy SE, Myers SM, et al., *Pediatrics* 145(1):e20193447; reaffirmed October 2025) is built explicitly on **DSM-5 criteria**, listing the A-domain (3 of 3 required) and B-domain (2 of 4 required, including sensory) verbatim ([https://depts.washington.edu/dbpeds/ID.Eval.Mgt.Children.ASD(AAP.2020).pdf](https://depts.washington.edu/dbpeds/ID.Eval.Mgt.Children.ASD(AAP.2020).pdf)). The AAP Autism Toolkit explicitly includes a "Relationship Between DSM-5 and ICD-10-CM" resource ([https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit](https://publications.aap.org/toolkits/pages/Autism-Toolkit)). AAP has not issued a parallel endorsement of ICD-11 criteria; its 2026 toolkit still maps DSM-5 to ICD-10-CM.

### National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, UK)
NICE CG128 (under 19s: recognition, referral and diagnosis) was **amended in 2017** to reference DSM-5 criteria, and in **March 2022** to migrate mentions from ICD-10 to ICD-11, which the NHS adopted at the same time ([https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Update-information); [https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/recommendations)). The current CG128 Context statement says: "autism is diagnosed if behaviours meet the criteria defined in the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-11) and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders Fifth Edition (DSM-5)" ([https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Context](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg128/chapter/Context)). NICE QS51 requires the diagnostic assessment to cover "repetitive and stereotyped behaviours, **including sensory sensitivities**," and the strengths/needs profile must include "**sensory sensitivities**" ([https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs51/chapter/Quality-statement-1-Diagnostic-assessment-by-an-autism-team](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/qs51/chapter/Quality-statement-1-Diagnostic-assessment-by-an-autism-team)). NICE is the only major guideline body to formally accept either manual. The SIGN (Scottish) consultation noted ICD-11 was not yet finalised when SIGN145 was drafted and recommended recording which classification system was used ([https://www.sign.ac.uk/media/1495/sign145_consultation_report.pdf](https://www.sign.ac.uk/media/1495/sign145_consultation_report.pdf)).

**Summary:** WHO and NICE accept ICD-11 (and NICE also accepts DSM-5); APA and AAP are DSM-5-anchored. All four accept sensory processing differences as legitimate core diagnostic features — a position with no remaining guideline-level dissent.

## (D) Advocacy-Organisation Positions

**Honest finding stated directly:** Within the sources retrieved, **none of the three organisations has issued a formal position declaring DSM-5 or ICD-11 "more neurodiversity-affirming."** Their documented positions are:

### Autistic Self Advocacy Network (ASAN)
- **Joint ASAN–Autism Society of America Statement on DSM-5 (January 2012):** Demanded that DSM-5 "ensure that those who have or would have qualified for a diagnosis under the DSM-IV maintain access to an ASD diagnosis," highlighting under-diagnosis among "racial and ethnic minorities, women and girls, adults and… low-income communities" ([https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/01/joint-asan-autism-society-statement-on-dsm-5/](https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/01/joint-asan-autism-society-statement-on-dsm-5/)).
- **ASAN Talking Points (May 2012):** "APA should revise the requirement in the ASD draft criteria's social communication domain (A) that an individual meet 3 of 3 listed criteria. This sets an overly restrictive standard and will likely lead to greater challenges in accessing diagnosis" ([https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/](https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/05/asan-talking-points-for-public-comment-on-dsm-5-autism-spectrum-disorder-criteria/)).
- **ASAN Policy Brief (June 2012):** "Changes in the diagnostic criteria may make it more difficult for [people] to access services, supports and accommodations" ([https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/06/asan-policy-brief-how-will-dsm-5-impact-services/](https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/06/asan-policy-brief-how-will-dsm-5-impact-services/)).
- **Ne'eman & Kapp (2012/2019):** ASAN achieved "significant partial successes in protecting access to diagnosis" but "the lack of formal autistic representation within the process limited ASAN's impact, leading to criteria that are likely still too narrow and a problematic severity scale" ([https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-13-8437-0_13)).
- ASAN's documented engagement is with **DSM-5, not ICD-11**. ASAN has not, in the retrieved evidence, formally endorsed ICD-11 as the more neurodiversity-affirming system; rather, ASAN's stated values emphasise that "we shouldn't try to cure or get rid of autism" and that diagnostic criteria should "reflect the diversity" of the spectrum ([https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/](https://autisticadvocacy.org/about-asan/what-we-believe/)).

### National Autistic Society (NAS, UK)
- **NAS information page:** "An autism diagnosis should be based on criteria listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th Edition (DSM-5) or the International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision (ICD-11), according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines" ([https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment](https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/diagnosis/assessment-and-diagnosis/criteria-and-tools-used-in-an-autism-assessment)).
- NAS acknowledges sensory differences as one of the "core characteristics" of autism and uses identity-first language; in practice, NAS diagnostic services use the DISCO alongside ADOS-2 ([https://www.autism.org.uk/what-we-do/diagnostic-service](https://www.autism.org.uk/what-we-do/diagnostic-service)).
- NAS does not state in the retrieved evidence that either manual is more neurodiversity-affirming; it accepts both as the standards NICE recognises.

### Autism Speaks (US)
- Publishes the full text of DSM-5 ASD criteria with permission from APA and uses DSM-5 as its authoritative diagnostic reference. Autism Speaks' "DSM-5 and autism: Frequently asked questions" endorses the unification of subtypes into a single ASD diagnosis and explicitly notes the DSM-5 "added sensory symptoms as a diagnostic criterion" ([https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5](https://www.autismspeaks.org/autism-diagnostic-criteria-dsm-5); [https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions](https://www.autismspeaks.org/dsm-5-and-autism-frequently-asked-questions)).
- Thomas W. Frazier (former Autism Speaks chief science officer) was the originator of the "require only one repetitive behaviour" idea during DSM-5 debates, aimed at restoring sensitivity ([https://www.apsa.org.pt/images/definition-autism-needs-refined.pdf](https://www.apsa.org.pt/images/definition-autism-needs-refined.pdf)).
- Autism Speaks has not, in the retrieved evidence, taken an explicit neurodiversity-affirming vs biomedical-model position; the organisation largely defers to DSM-5/clinical standards.

**Synthesis (labelled as analytic inference, not sourced position):** ASAN is the most explicitly critical of DSM-5's narrowing (the 3-of-3 monothetic requirement, severity scale, and risk of excluding marginalised groups). Neither ASAN nor NAS formally endorses ICD-11 as superior on neurodiversity grounds in the evidence gathered, but ASAN's policy position implies ICD-11's flexibility (no mandated sub-criterion count, recognition of camouflaging/compensation, adult manifestation) is closer to ASAN's stated values than DSM-5's prescriptive monothetic structure. The ICD-11 psychological review explicitly states that ICD-11 is informed by "concepts of neurodiversity and the social model of disability" and moves "further away from an observable, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorder (medical model) to a disorder of inner experience in sense of 'diversity' and 'identity' (social model)" ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)). Autism Speaks is largely agnostic to the DSM-5/ICD-11 distinction.

## (E) Diagnostic Safety Risks

### Under-diagnosis / false-negative risk (concentrated in DSM-5's enumerated thresholds)
- Huerta et al. 2012: sensitivity for Asperger's = 0.25, PDD-NOS = 0.28; ~39% of DSM-IV-diagnosed individuals did NOT meet DSM-5 ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3424065/)).
- Kulage 2014 meta-analysis: pooled 31% drop in ASD diagnoses under DSM-5; PDD-NOS −70% ([https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24531932/)).
- Maenner et al. 2014: 18.8% of DSM-IV ASD cases would lose diagnosis under DSM-5; higher loss rate (27.5%) among those without ID ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041577/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4041577/)).
- Wilson et al. 2013: only 56% of intellectually able adults with ICD-10R ASD met DSM-5; a further 19% met draft Social Communication Disorder — a documented service-access risk.
- ASD diagnosis rates in England remain age-skewed: as of 2018 only 0.02% of people aged 70+ had a recorded autism diagnosis vs 2.94% of 10–14-year-olds ([https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666776223000455](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666776223000455)). DSM-5's higher threshold compounds historical under-diagnosis in adults and women.
- DSM-5 introduced Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder (SCD) as a "residual" diagnosis for those who fail the social criterion but lack RRB — risks mislabelling autistic individuals (especially girls and adults) as having only pragmatic-language problems, denying them ASD-specific services ([https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/06/asan-policy-brief-how-will-dsm-5-impact-services/](https://autisticadvocacy.org/2012/06/asan-policy-brief-how-will-dsm-5-impact-services/)).

### Over-diagnosis / false-positive risk (concentrated in ICD-11's flexibility)
- Bölte, Kamp-Becker et al. 2024: ICD-11's 304 possible symptom combinations (19×16) and lack of mandatory criteria risk "false positive diagnoses," "increased prevalence rates," "limitations of access to ASD-specific services," "increasing non-specificity of treatments," and reduced replicability ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11153155/)).

### Sensory-focused presentation risks (specific to this question)
- **DSM-5:** Sensory is 1 of 4 RRB options with a 2-of-4 threshold; clinicians may miss sensory-dominant presentations. DSM-5's sensory exemplars (excessive smelling/touching, fascination with lights) are partly ID-anchored — implying DSM-5's examples may under-detect sensory differences in cognitively-able people.
- **ICD-11:** Explicit inclusion of sensory features (with the added qualifiers "lifelong" and "anticipated stimuli") may improve recognition of sensory-dominant but socially-compensated adults (women, late-identified adults) — but they risk being miscoded as having anxiety or sensory-processing disorder instead of ASD if clinicians default to ICD-10-era thinking. Conversely, ICD-11's looser wording may over-include sensory-dominant presentations when social-communication evidence is weak.
- **Milan adult sample (n=61):** Women who were misdiagnosed scored significantly higher on the hyper/hypo-reactivity-to-sensory-input domain — direct evidence that sensory-prominent presentations in women drive misdiagnosis under DSM-5-based practice ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8306851/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8306851/)).
- Fusar-Poli et al. 2026 (*Frontiers in Psychiatry*): "The DSM-5 sensory criterion, though neurobiologically grounded, lacks diagnostic specificity" — sensory hyper/hyporeactivity is present across ADHD, anxiety, ID, and trauma, and the DSM-5 B4 criterion alone cannot disambiguate ASD from these conditions ([https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1847929/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychiatry/articles/10.3389/fpsyt.2026.1847929/full)).
- A shared limitation: under **both** manuals, sensory features are non-required, so a genuinely sensory-predominant presentation without social-communication and other RRB features cannot reach the diagnostic threshold under either manual. Such individuals fall into "sub-threshold"/unspecified categories — DSM-5's "other specified/unspecified neurodevelopmental disorder," or ICD-11's **6E60 secondary neurodevelopmental syndrome** ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/)).

### Intervention/provision risk
- **DSM-5's narrower criteria:** Risk of *under-treatment* of those losing ASD diagnosis (e.g., loss of ABA, speech therapy, school accommodations). DSM-5 severity levels were never field-tested and "may have the potential to do more harm than good (e.g., if insurance providers attempt to limit coverage for individuals with 'level 1 ASD')" ([https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10904885/)).
- **ICD-11's broader criteria:** Risk of *over-application* of behavioural interventions (e.g., ABA) to individuals with subclinical or contextually-driven autistic traits who do not need them — a concern flagged by Bölte/Kamp-Becker et al. 2024. ICD-11's flexible criteria also risks channeling families toward sensory-based interventions whose evidence base remains contested.

**Severity-classification risk (ICD-11-specific):** Lemay et al. 2024 found ICD-11 behavioural indicators skew toward **mild** severity relative to standardised measures and require **extra time/caution** when ASD and intellectual disability co-occur ([https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jir.13146)) — a potential under-recognition of severity risk specific to ICD-11.

---

## (F) Reimbursement / Coding Summary

### United States
- US continues to use **ICD-10-CM (not ICD-11) for all HIPAA-covered billing transactions** as of 2025–2026. ICD-11 has no role in current US claims submission ([https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026](https://www.medcloudmd.com/post/icd-10-f84-0-autism-billing-documentation-guide-2026); [https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0](https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0)).
- **Billable ICD-10-CM code for ASD: F84.0** (Autistic disorder), which functionally absorbs "autism spectrum disorder," "infantile autism," "infantile psychosis," "Kanner's syndrome," and ASD more broadly. F84.0 has been billable since FY2016 (effective Oct 1, 2015) and remains unchanged through FY2027 (effective Oct 1, 2026) ([https://www.icd10data.com/ICD10CM/Codes/F01-F99/F80-F89/F84-/F84.0](https://www.icd10data.com/ICD10CM/Codes/F01-F99/F80-F89/F84-/F84.0)).
- **Critical mismatch:** DSM-5 eliminated the F84.0-style categorical "Autistic Disorder" diagnosis, but ICD-10-CM was never restructured. Clinicians diagnose using DSM-5 (single ASD) but bill using F84.0, which carries the legacy DSM-IV name. Documentation must clearly establish the DSM-5 clinical basis because the code description lags behind.
- Other codes in use: F84.5 (Asperger's), F84.9 (PDD unspecified; in the US, atypical autism is mapped here), F84.2 (Rett's), F84.3 (childhood disintegrative disorder). US payers do not recognise F84.1 (atypical autism) ([https://www.simplepractice.com/resource/icd-10-code-for-autistic-disorder/](https://www.simplepractice.com/resource/icd-10-code-for-autistic-disorder/)).
- F84.0 is recognised as a CC (complication or comorbidity) under MS-DRG v44.0, affecting inpatient DRG assignment when listed as secondary diagnosis. CMS-HCC V28 risk-adjustment mapping: F84.0 has no V28 HCC category but is included in RxHCC 133 ([https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0](https://hccbuddy.com/icd10/F84.0)).
- **Reimbursement impact of ICD-11 adoption:** If the US transitions to ICD-11 (no current timeline published by CMS/NCHS for HIPAA implementation), code 6A02 would replace F84.0 with a single code plus intellectual/language specifiers (6A02.0–6A02.5). **Until then, ICD-11 adoption has no effect on US reimbursement or coverage**; existing F84.0 claims are paid regardless of which manual a clinician uses diagnostically ([https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-10-code-f840/](https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-10-code-f840/)).

### European Union / WHO European Region
- ICD-11 came into effect globally 1 January 2022; many EU Member States are in transition with at least a 5-year transitional arrangement. When fully implemented, **6A02 with intellectual/language specifiers (6A02.0–6A02.5)** will replace the ICD-10 F84 subcategories.
- **UK NHS / NICE:** NICE updated CG128 in March 2022 to migrate mentions from ICD-10 to ICD-11, which the NHS adopted at the same time. UK clinicians use either DSM-5 or ICD-11 criteria per CG128; ICD-10 codes (F84.0, F84.5) remain in use in NHS clinical systems until ICD-11 is fully deployed. NAS notes this duality "can really cause confusion… in terms of these labels" ([https://acamhlearn.cadmore.media/learning/assessment-and-diagnosis-of-autism-a-guide-for-families/9e83e67e-74b9-41f2-b97c-86a0d5ab4856/b7e30237-5a0d-42e7-b4f1-32520e45aed5](https://acamhlearn.cadmore.media/learning/assessment-and-diagnosis-of-autism-a-guide-for-families/9e83e67e-74b9-41f2-b97c-86a0d5ab4856/b7e30237-5a0d-42e7-b4f1-32520e45aed5)).
- **Coverage/reimbursement effect:** The shift is largely revenue-neutral for ASD-specific services in most EU systems because reimbursement is bundled by indication/diagnosis group (DRG-equivalent). The dimensional specifiers (ID + language) provide finer-grained coding but do not by themselves change coverage ([https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-11-6a02-autism-spectrum-disorder-diagnosis-coding-guide/](https://pabau.com/diagnostic-codes/icd-11-6a02-autism-spectrum-disorder-diagnosis-coding-guide/)).

**Bottom line on reimbursement:** No evidence indicates that adopting ICD-11 criteria, by itself, changes coverage or reimbursement anywhere; both F84.0 and 6A02 denote the same spectrum construct. The plausible financial risks are second-order: if ICD-11's flexible criteria widen diagnosis (over-diagnosis concern), payer costs and service queues expand; conversely, where DSM-5's stricter thresholds deny an F84.0 diagnosis to sensory-prominent or camouflaging individuals, those individuals lose access to diagnosis-gated benefits entirely. These fiscal impacts are projections, not measured outcomes — a genuine evidence gap.

---

## Overall Evidence-Strength Statement

| Section | Evidence quality | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| (A) Criteria table | High (primary manual texts + WHO CDDR + peer-reviewed crosswalk) | High |
| (B) Comparative accuracy | **Low overall** — no head-to-head DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 ASD accuracy study located; meta-analysis/field studies are indirect; proxy studies use ICD-10/DSM-IV | Low–moderate |
| (C) Guideline positions | High (WHO/NICE/AAP primary documents) | High |
| (D) Advocacy positions | **Insufficient** — no formal ASAN/NAS/Autism Speaks source comparing the manuals on neurodiversity grounds; engagement is with DSM-5 only | Low |
| (E) Safety risks | Mixed — one substantive ICD-11 theoretical critique (Bölte/Kamp-Becker 2024); empirical under-diagnosis evidence is DSM-5/ICD-10-proxy; no sensory-specific direct data | Low–moderate |
| (F) Reimbursement/coding | Moderate for coding maps (US ICD-10-CM F84.0; NHS ICD-11 from March 2022); **no direct evidence** on coverage/reimbursement effects | Low–moderate |

**Key bottom line for the sensory-weighting question specifically:** neither DSM-5 nor ICD-11 makes sensory processing a *required* diagnostic criterion, and neither weights it more heavily than the other in an operational sense. The meaningful differences are: (a) ICD-11 explicitly recognises sensory reactivity within its second essential domain and, unlike ICD-10, counts it as a diagnostic feature at all; (b) ICD-11 adds "lifelong" and "anticipated stimuli" qualifiers and requires no minimum symptom count, so sensory is one of many optional illustrations rather than a countable "B4"; (c) ICD-11 deliberately drops ID-anchored exemplars that DSM-5 retains; (d) ICD-11 recognises masking/compensation and later-life manifestation that DSM-5 mentions but operationalises more narrowly. Neither manual supports a sensory-only diagnosis, and no retrieved source quantifies the diagnostic or reimbursement consequence of that shared limitation. The central research need in this area is a direct head-to-head DSM-5 vs. ICD-11 accuracy study, which does not currently exist.
